title: TabAbax: A Tabular Foundation Model Technical Report
abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) enable in-context prediction on unseen tabular datasets without task-specific training. Mechanistic work has shown that increasing the depth of the ICL Transformer yields weak gains, leaving the main headroom for gains in the synthetic pretraining prior and column-row encoder upstream of the ICL backbone. We introduce TabAbax, a TFM built on TabICLv2 that focuses all modifications on these two upstream components. On the prior side, we further improve the quality and complexity of the synthetic pretraining prior. On the encoder side, a two-pass column-row stack strengthens cross-feature interactions before row compression, using learned Fourier scalar encoding from TabFM and Causilo. Evaluations on BeyondArena and TabArena show strong regression-centric gains: TabAbax reaches 1,238 Elo on the 142-dataset BeyondArena suite (10th of 41 evaluated methods), 1,676 Elo on TabArena's overall 51-dataset suite (11th of 99 methods, +115 over TabICLv2), and 2,024 Elo on TabArena's regression benchmark (7th of 99 methods, +336 over TabICLv2, +21 over TabFM). A prior-only ablation confirms the attribution: the improved prior alone yields +228 Elo for regression, demonstrating that prior quality is the dominant knob for improving regression performance.

title: GameVerse: A Minute-Scale Gameplay Dataset for Long-Horizon Interactive World Modeling
abstract: Recent advances in interactive world models have made it possible to generate controllable, dynamic environments from action inputs. Yet current models struggle to maintain coherence beyond roughly one minute of rollout, a limitation rooted not in model capacity but in the scarcity of long-horizon training data. Existing gameplay video datasets typically consist of clips under ten seconds, with captions that describe whole clips in coarse and undifferentiated text, which is insufficient for controllable long-horizon generation. We address this with GameVerse, a minute-scale gameplay video dataset purpose-built for long-horizon interactive world modeling. GameVerse contains 69.7K clips spanning 1,655 hours and 349.6 million frames across diverse first- and third-person gameplay, including 1,358 hours of continuous two-minute sequences, an order of magnitude longer than prior datasets. Clips pass through a unified pipeline of scene-consistent segmentation, quality filtering, camera pose estimation, and event-based caption annotation. Each clip is paired with a temporally stable camera trajectory that remains coherent across minutes, together with captions that separate static scene context from dynamic foreground events and align to event boundaries rather than fixed time windows. Comprehensive analysis shows that GameVerse surpasses existing public datasets in scale, diversity, and annotation quality. Experiments further demonstrate that training on GameVerse substantially extends the temporal horizon of interactive world models.

title: Efficient multi-basis quantum position verification secure against generalized adversaries
abstract: Abstract Quantum position verification (QPV) enables multiple verifiers to certify a prover’s location using quantum communication and physical assumptions. With experimental demonstrations of QPV becoming increasingly feasible, enhancing the practicality and security of QPV protocols is more important than ever. In this work, we make three key contributions toward this goal. First, we introduce a robust QPV protocol in which the verifier’s state preparation is independent of channel loss, improving reliability in real-world conditions. Second, we refine existing security analysis techniques to bolster protocol resilience against experimental imperfections. Third, we identify and address some implicit assumptions present in existing security analyses, providing a framework to eliminate such assumptions. Additionally, as an example of QPV application beyond location verification, we illustrate how QPV can be leveraged for authenticating classical communication in quantum key distribution.

title: MAESTRO: Adapting GUIs and Guiding Navigation with User Preferences in Conversational Agents with GUIs
abstract: Modern task-oriented chatbots present GUI elements alongside natural-language dialogue, yet the agent’s role has largely been limited to interpreting natural-language input as GUI actions and following a linear workflow. In preference-driven, multi-step tasks such as booking a flight or reserving a restaurant, earlier choices constrain later options and may force users to restart from scratch. User preferences serve as the key criteria for these decisions, yet existing agents do not systematically leverage them. We present MAESTRO, which extends the agent’s role from execution to decision support. MAESTRO maintains a shared preference memory that extracts hard and soft preferences from natural-language utterances and provides two mechanisms. Preference-Grounded GUI Adaptation applies in-place operators (augment, sort, filter, and highlight) to the existing GUI according to preference strength, supporting comparison among options. Preference-Guided Workflow Navigation detects conflicts between preferences and available options, proposes backtracking, and records failed paths to avoid revisiting dead ends. Through a controlled experiment (N = 33), we demonstrated that MAESTRO improved decision quality in movie ticketing: final bookings left fewer hard preferences unmet, and users made fewer selections that violated their stated preferences during the process than in the baseline condition, although task success rate and completion time did not differ significantly. In addition, we showed that using MAESTRO in voice mode can increase users’ active engagement as well as their mental burden, revealing the nuanced tension in agentic interaction design for conversational agents with a GUI.

title: A Quantum-HPC Hybrid Workflow for Reaction-Center Electronic Dynamics: Application to a Cytochrome P450-Inspired Iron-Complex Model
abstract: Abstract We introduce population-transfer dynamics as a practical validation observable for active-state-derived reduced Hamiltonians in multistate reaction-center chemistry. In transition-metal systems, missing couplings or configurations can compromise the reliability of reduced active space models along a reaction coordinate, even when the overall spectrum is reproduced reasonably well. Using a cytochrome P450-inspired Fe-complex model, we construct a reaction-coordinate-dependent effective Hamiltonian from state-averaged complete active-space self-consistent field (SA-CASSCF) calculations, map it to a quantum circuit representation suitable for current hardware, and propagate the dynamics from the reactant-side ground state. At the spectrum level, the reduced Hamiltonian reproduces the SA-CASSCF reference with an RMS deviation of 0.030 eV and a maximum absolute deviation of 0.143 eV. As a dynamics-based diagnostic, the product-manifold population pP(t) identifies a pronounced near-degeneracy window around x ≈ 0.3, where state mixing is strongest; specifically, computed from classical exact time evolution reaches 0.488 at x = 0.3 after 10 fs, compared with 7.26 × 10–2 at x = 0.2 and 5.90 × 10–3 at x = 0.0. To render the workflow executable on current trapped-ion hardware, we quantify the NISQ-relevant trade-off between dynamical fidelity and circuit resources through coupling pruning and first-order Trotterization. A coupling cutoff of ε = 0.02 eV reduces the nonzero coupling set from 32 to 7 while preserving the dominant transfer pathways, and a Trotter step number of M = 30 provides the best practical operating point among the tested values. Finally, we demonstrate the end-to-end workflow on Quantinuum’s trapped-ion quantum computer Reimei. The hardware reproduces the key reaction-coordinate trend identified by the classical reduced model, including the pronounced maximum at x = 0.3, where the measured product population is 0.42 on hardware and 0.43 on the matched emulator. Overall, this work establishes a dynamics-based diagnostic route for assessing the adequacy of active-space-derived reduced Hamiltonians and shows that chemically interpretable multistate electronic dynamics can already be executed on current trapped-ion hardware under realistic device constraints.

title: TeachUp: Facilitating Early-Stage Teachers to Learn Instructional Strategies from Classroom Videos with Reflective Support
abstract: Recorded videos of offline open classes provide good examples for early-stage teachers to learn instructional strategies, e.g., how to organize cooperative learning. However, learning by watching these videos is challenging, as these strategies are implicitly performed, and it lacks in-situ reflective support. In this paper, via a formative study (N=9), we design TeachUp to support the learning of instructional strategies from classroom teaching videos. TeachUp adopts an LLM-powered pipeline to detect nine instructional strategies in videos (precision = 63.4%), provides reflective questions and hints while watching, and generates customized practices with reflective feedback. A within-subjects study (N=16) shows that compared to a traditional video-playing and self-practicing baseline, early-stage teachers with TeachUp are more engaged in learning and perform better in applying learned strategies to new tasks. Interviews with four in-service teachers further generalize our findings and TeachUp’s use cases. We discuss practical implications for fostering video-based learning of instructional strategies.

title: CogChat: Knowledge Graph-Augmented Conversational AI with Heterogeneous Graph Transformer for Cognitive Grounding in Design Generation
abstract: LLM-based chat systems have become valuable tools for design practice, enabling rapid ideation and flexible task support. Yet these systems process designer utterances as generic sequences, maintaining context through recency rather than through any model of how the speaker organizes knowledge. In design conversation, this gap compounds as relational context decays between turns, identical words go unresolved across designers, and the conversation loops or restarts rather than deepens. We present CogChat, a real-time chat framework that grounds conversational AI in a personal heterogeneous knowledge graph constructed from each designer’s input. The system extracts typed entities and relations into a heterogeneous graph, then applies a HGT (Heterogeneous Graph Transformer) to select structurally relevant nodes for response generation and to generate both intentional and exploratory probing questions. Technical evaluation shows that HGT-based entity selection outperforms both ungrounded LLM interaction and naïve KG augmentation, which introduces noise that degrades response quality. A within-subjects study with nine professional designers indicates that grounding conversation in a relationally structured, designer-specific semantic context improves context retention, personalized intent interpretation, and conversational depth while reducing cognitive load. These findings suggest that structuring a designer’s expressed concepts and relations as a dynamic knowledge graph can preserve relational context that fades across turns, pointing toward a graph-grounded approach to long-term context management in LLM-based interaction.

title: Before You Say It: Anticipating Verbal Behavior from Longitudinal Everyday Conversations with LLMs
abstract: Knowing someone deeply means not just understanding what they say or do but also how they will likely think, react, and engage across situations. Such predictions could eventually inform systems to anticipate when the individual is about to deviate from their goal, catch regrettable behaviors before they are made, and surface blind spots before they take hold. While many interactive systems model users to enable more personalized interactions, most cannot make such behavioral predictions, as this often requires longitudinal observation and inference of how the individual’s behaviors unfold across various everyday situations. In this work, we introduce a novel LLM-based predictive behavioral modeling approach that anticipates a user’s likely behavior across everyday conversational situations. We (1) collect a longitudinal dataset of over 1,000 hours of naturalistic conversations from 14 participants using a wearable smartwatch; (2) evaluate LLM-based predictions against ground truth behaviors; and (3) use semi-structured interviews to explore participants’ perceptions of behavioral predictions and their views on possible forms of future behavioral support. Altogether, our findings provide evidence that person-specific verbal behavior can be predicted from longitudinal conversational data. This opens up new possibilities for potential future context-aware, anticipatory, proactive and personalized AI systems.

title: Graphionale: How Graph Visualizations of LLM Rationales Affect Human Decision Making
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly equipped with augmented reasoning capabilities to generate rationales that support human decision-making. Yet these text-dense rationales often impose substantial cognitive burdens. Building on a formative co-design study that identified user preferences for non-linear reasoning representations, we developed Graphionale as a testbed for empirically studying argument-map-style rationale visualization. This system transforms linear LLM rationales into interactive, multi-level graphs. It explicitly structures logical relationships (e.g., conclusions, premises, support, and objections), while further extracting entities and relations within each statement to construct condensed node-link representations. We conduct a large-scale online user study (N = 204) to examine when graphical rationales are more effective than textual ones, across varying task modality (verbal vs. visual reasoning), rationale format (textual vs. graphical), and question difficulty (easy vs. hard). Our results show that graphical rationales do not help uniformly: they improve trust calibration for verbal reasoning yet feel more cognitively demanding and less satisfying; for visual reasoning, they impair calibration yet feel more engaging and helpful. In each modality, the format that better supports calibrated decisions is not the one users prefer, highlighting that matching rationale format to task modality is key to effective AI explanation design. Our findings contribute empirical design knowledge about when and how graphical rationales support human decision making, and inform the next-generation reasoning-aware AI interfaces.

title: The Voice of AI: Consumer Psychology and the Strategic Use of AI-Generated Voices in Marketing
abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence is transforming marketing communication, with AI-generated voices emerging as an increasingly important means through which brands communicate with consumers. This paper examines AI-generated voices from a consumer psychology perspective, focusing on how consumers interpret and respond to synthetic voices used in marketing communication. Drawing on literature from artificial intelligence, marketing, consumer behaviour and human–computer interaction, the paper explores the psychological significance of vocal characteristics such as naturalness, human-likeness, prosody, anthropomorphism and emotional expression. It further examines how these characteristics can shape consumer perceptions of message credibility, authenticity and brand trust. The discussion highlights the growing use of AI-generated voices across advertising, social media, voice commerce and interactive brand communication, with selected examples from the Indian marketing context illustrating their applications in personalisation, engagement and localisation. The paper argues that the effectiveness of AI-generated voices depends not simply on technological sophistication, but on how consumers psychologically interpret the voice and its relationship with the message and brand. The paper concludes by identifying directions for future research on AI-mediated brand communication.

title: Explainable AI in Critical Systems: Techniques, Trust and Challenges
abstract: Abstract In highly sensitive areas like healthcare, cybersecurity, transport and finance, where an unexplainable or incorrect decision could have dire consequences, AI also aids in making decisions. Explainable AI (XAI) has become a widely suggested way to create transparency, accountability and trust, yet the literature is scattered both by technique, domain and evaluation methods. A focused critical review of 14 studies published from 2020 to 2026 is presented, consisting of 11 surveys and systematic reviews, 2 studies that were empirical with an intrusion detection focus and 1 clinician-based evaluation of the heatmap methods. We categorize the various XAI techniques according to scope, timing, model dependence and explanation form, distinguish between the technical trustworthiness of an explanation and the human calibration of trust and combine the evaluation of explanations in practice. The evidence reveals that post-hoc, local methods, in particular SHAP, LIME and Grad-CAM, outstood in terms of applications, explanations have progressed with greater speed than explanation validation, and most of the studies did not focus on quantitative evaluation or user studies, while expert judgements of the plausibility of explanations were not reliably associated with the quality of the models. We argue that explanations in critical systems must be seen as artefacts for safety, which must be validated, and that a research agenda should be pursued in the areas of standardized evaluation, human centered studies, privacy preserving explanation and regulatory alignment.

The evidence reveals that post-hoc, local methods, in particular SHAP, LIME and Grad-CAM, outstood in terms of applications, explanations have progressed with greater speed than explanation validation, and most of the studies did not focus on quantitative evaluation or user studies, while expert judgements of the plausibility of explanations were not reliably associated with the quality of the models. We argue that explanations in critical systems must be seen as artefacts for safety, which must be validated, and that a research agenda should be pursued in the areas of standardized evaluation, human centered studies, privacy preserving explanation and regulatory alignment.

title: AI Hallucinations
abstract: Artificial Intelligence has really transformed areas like healthcare, legal services, education, finance, and business. But its quick spread also brings persistent tech troubles, mainly the confusing issue of AI mistakes, errors, and misinformation. Large Language Models (LLMs) can handle all sorts of tasks, from text creation and code writing to answering questions and summarizing info. Still, despite their big achievements, LLMs sometimes spout incorrect stuff – factually wrong or made-up content – which is called "hallucination." This paper dives deep into AI failures, showing how they differ based on errors in logic, generated fiction presented confidently, and correct data being misinterpreted. It looks at why AI systems act overly sure of themselves, how messy training data messes up, and ideas for fixing this like boosted retrieval methods, cleaner training data, and humans checking the work. What stands out is that these glitches aren't just random tech snafus. Instead, they're a design quirk of big AI language models. Fixing them demands teamwork from folks in various fields, not just developers. So, while there are big issues, figuring out ways to collaborate could make these systems way more reliable in the future.

title: Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference Systems: Architecture, Learning, Input Selection, and Applications - A Survey
abstract: Abstract Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) is a hybrid intelligent modeling framework that fuses the linguistic interpretability of fuzzy if-then rules with the parameter-learning capability of artificial neural networks. Since its introduction by Jang in 1993, ANFIS has become one of the most widely adopted neuro-fuzzy architectures for nonlinear function approximation, system identification, and time-series prediction. This paper surveys the ANFIS framework from three complementary angles. First, it reviews the network architecture and the hybrid learning rule that combines gradient descent with least-squares estimation, drawing on Jang's foundational formulation. Second, it examines a practical challenge in applying ANFIS to real-world, high-dimensional problems determining which candidate variables should serve as network inputs and reviews a computationally efficient input-selection heuristic based on single-epoch training error. Third, it presents a case study of ANFIS applied to high-frequency financial trading, in which an event-based volatility model, the Intraday Seasonality Observation Model (ISOM), is used to pre-filter training data and materially improves trading performance metrics such as return on investment and the Sharpe ratio. The paper closes with a comparative discussion of strengths, limitations, and open research directions for neuro-fuzzy modeling.

title: A Held-Out Site Is a Sample of One: What Random, Spatial and Site-Disjoint Splits Each Estimate, Why Leakage That Differs Between Configurations Reorders a Comparison, and How Many Sites a General Claim Needs
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research A September 2026 study of farm-machinery traversability reports that a forward-facing near-infrared camera appears to beat a colour camera on a paddy-boundary class under its corpus's own sequence-level split, that the advantage disappears once recording sites are held apart, that the near-infrared configuration gained more from having seen a site than colour did, and that two leads the second camera held at one held-out site changed sign when the held-out site was rotated. Each of those findings touches a literature that disagrees with itself: ecologists and remote-sensing researchers dispute whether spatial cross-validation corrects an optimistic bias or introduces a pessimistic one, clinical machine learning had the same dispute over subject-wise splitting, and machine-learning benchmarks report both that rankings survive distribution shift and that they do not. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that these disputes concern three different questions an evaluation can be asked - how accurate a model is at a stated target (level), which of two configurations is better there (order), and whether an advantage holds across the population of sites a deployment will meet (generality) - and that each needs a different design. The level dispute resolves once the prediction target is specified, and the published positions on both sides agree on that resolution more than their titles suggest. The order question has a failure mode the level dispute does not cover: when leakage inflates configurations unequally, a split that shares sites can reverse a comparison, and six published results in four fields show it doing so or coming close: reversals in Kang (2026), Zech et al. (2018), Liang et al. (2017) and, on small margins, Meyer et al. (2019) and Schratz et al. (2018), and a several-fold shrinkage in Milioto et al. (2018). The generality question is a small-sample problem in sites, not in images: one held-out site is one observation. The paper consolidates 24 published results in a table, derives the condition under which leakage preserves an ordering, states a procedure that assigns each evaluation the claim it licenses, and specifies five studies that would settle what remains open.

title: Evaluation of Dialogue Systems Functioning Efficiency based on Using Fuzzy Inference with Neural Network Setting
abstract: The results of the study aimed at improving the process of evaluating the functioning efficiency of dialogue systems based on the development of models of fuzzy inference and neural network learning are presented. Developing tools to assess how virtual assistants actually perform on question-answer tasks is a practical concern in Software Engineering - one the field has not yet solved cleanly. As values for evaluating the functioning efficiency of dialogue systems, it is proposed to use particular indicators that characterize the accuracy, concision and fullness of answers to the questions asked. The resulting performance evaluation is determined by the value of the generalized indicator, calculated taking into account the values of particular indicators. An algorithm for calculating a generalized indicator based on the use of fuzzy inference has been developed. The values of parameters of membership functions and individual conclusions of fuzzy rules necessary for its implementation are proposed to be calculated on the basis of a neural network learning algorithm. The decision to complete the neural network tuning of the fuzzy inference parameters is made based on the calculation and analysis of the current learning error. The results of experimental studies on evaluating the functioning efficiency of dialogue systems based on the proposed algorithms are presented. Across 1,012 conducted experiments, the composite functioning efficiency indicator ranged from 0.395 to 0.912, and the ANFIS training converged after 12 epochs to a minimum error of 0.001996.

title: DeidSharp: de-identification of health data for .NET
abstract: Added Guide (docs/guide.md): how to install, choose a detector stack, de-identify free text and FHIR, add the clinical sidecar or a local language model, pseudonymize, check output, handle errors, run DeidSharp in a service, read its telemetry and measure it on your own data, with a reference of every option. Its examples run as tests (GuideExamplesTests). Samples (samples): three console programs (free text, a FHIR bundle, a local language model), built by CI. Evaluation on MIMIC-IV-Note: --corpus mimic-iv-note builds a corpus of 1,000 MIMIC-IV-Note 2.2 discharge summaries (one per patient, a fixed hashed sample) whose ___ placeholders are filled with made-up surrogates that become the gold spans, typed by context rules; --gold-review writes the gold spans in context for a person to check (evaluation). Its reporting half, measured once under a protocol fixed beforehand, is in the results and findings (F41). Miss profile: the evaluation tool's --miss-profile <label> counts each stack's misses of one corpus label by feature (one word, an ordinary word, found elsewhere in the note), printing counts only; --variants now also wraps the stacks with a language model (findings, F42). Model baselines: tools/baselines/models builds one offline image that runs the Stanford/Penn de-identifier, OpenAI Privacy Filter and GLiNER multi-PII, each at its defaults with its weights pinned by commit, on an NVIDIA GPU, on an --export of a corpus, and writes their spans for --predictions (evaluation). Language-model stacks in the published results: the evaluation tool's --publish now takes --llm (with --llm-prompts, --gazetteer with,without, --clinical-places and the second opinion), and records Ollama's version and each model's digest with the results, read before the run and checked after it; the README's badge shows the recall-first stack beside the one without a model (evaluation). Out-of-scope check: the evaluation tool's --out-of-scope neutral leaves out the predictions that touch only gold outside the scope (a bare year, an age under 90), so tagging them counts neither for nor against a tool; a sensitivity check, never published (findings, F47). Strict span match: EvaluationReport.Strict gives recall, precision and F1 counting only predictions with exactly a gold span's start and end, categories aside, like the binary evaluation of the 2014 i2b2/UTHealth challenge; the evaluation tool shows it on the console and publishes it in results.json. Changed PhiDetectionException.InnerException is now null when a detector throws (and when the Presidio detector's response isn't a result list, or a handler in its HTTP pipeline fails): the message names the original exception's type instead. Code that inspected the inner exception should read the message, or the Presidio detector's HttpRequestException, which is still passed on. See Security below. A release no longer measures the evaluation again when its changes can't alter what the measured stacks find: published results keep the version and commit they were measured at. CI refuses a release tag when the results on the nursing notes (PhysioNet's Deidentified Medical Text) or ASQ-PHI are missing, or when any published result comes from a later version or from code that has changed since, unless the findings record why it still stands (evaluation, D5). The README starts from what a user needs (install, quick start, which stack), and the evaluation README opens with the results at a glance, language-model stacks included. The published results come from one run of record per corpus at version 1.1.0, under a protocol fixed beforehand: the stacks with and without a language model, deid, Philter and the three model baselines, scored together (findings, D6 and F46). The guide's numbers follow it; three stacks move by at most 0.3 points. Stock Presidio, no recommended stack, left the published tables; its numbers stand in the findings (F37, F39, F41). safe-harbor.md lists a gap that was undocumented: in free text, the birth year of someone aged 90 or over is kept, since a date is cut to its year without knowing whose it is (FHIR removes the record's birth date). The guide and the threat model warn that LlmSecondOpinion sends the whole note at once, so the model server's context window must fit the longest note; Ollama cuts a longer prompt from the start, instructions included, without an error. Dependencies: DeidSharp.Fhir requires Hl7.Fhir.R4 6.8.0 and DeidSharp.Llm requires Microsoft.Extensions.AI.Abstractions 10.11.0. Fixed The clinical sidecar no longer returns an empty span when its model tags a token made only of spaces, which made DeidSharp's Presidio detector fail closed on texts with long runs of spaces (form-like headers in discharge summaries). Spans that cover only whitespace are dropped; they hide nothing. Security PhiDetectionException no longer passes on a detector's exception as its inner exception, since some exceptions hold the text they were working on in a property (a regex timeout's Input) that a structured logger writes out; its message names the exception's type instead ("Detector 'patterns' failed with RegexMatchTimeoutException."). The clinical sidecar's images take certifi 2026.10.23, filelock 4.2.4 and setuptools 84.2.1, which fix known vulnerabilities.

title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence-Driven Chatbots on Customer Engagement and Booking Intentions in Online Travel Agencies within the Global Tourism Market
abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and conversational technologies are revolutionizing the tourism industry's digital interactions—shaping the way we connect with travelers globally.AI and conversational technologies have dramatically changed how the global tourism industry reaches travelers digitally. One of these innovations is the use of AI-powered chatbots by Online Travel Agencies (OTAs) to transform the way consumers engage with travel platforms, turning them into dynamic, personalized, and conversational spaces for booking. This research explores the role of AI-powered conversational agents in improving customer engagement and booking conversion rates within the highly competitive tourism industry worldwide. This research highlights the cognitive and psychological factors that contribute to user trust and satisfaction, such as the ability to provide 24/7 availability, custom itineraries, and smooth payment processing, in the case of generative and hybrid chatbots. Drawing from the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) paradigm and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the paper proposes that real-time algorithmic support to address travel anxiety and perceived value of the travel experience. Furthermore, it faces industry challenges such as AI hallucinations, data privacy, and the delicate balance between automation and the human touch. The insights provide actionable strategies for online travel agencies (OTAs) and hospitality marketers looking to adopt conversational AI, improve user journeys, and secure a lasting competitive advantage in the digital realm.

title: SecKB-Bench and PROVE Reference Implementation: Benchmark Generator, Reference Code and Measurement Artifacts for Provenance-Gated Retrieval and Egress Containment in LLM Knowledge Systems
abstract: security of retrieval-augmented language models is usually studied on one side at a time: the integrity of what enters the knowledge base, or the confidentiality of what leaves it. We show that the two sides are the ends of a single channel, and that treating them separately systematically overstates the protection obtained. A claim that survives ingestion is later retrieved and reproduced, so an adversary who can write documents controls part of the set from which the system is allowed to disclose; we call this poison-to-leak amplification. We formalise the channel, place claim units, attribution, admissibility and the leak surface on one footing, and specify an adversary that both writes and queries. We then prove an amplification bound showing that sentence anchoring turns the per-response disclosure ceiling into a policy invariant independent of the adversary share of the corpus; a composition cut showing that entailment-closed admissibility makes multi-turn composition gainless, together with a constructive lower bound for the case where closure fails; and a geometric bound on the cumulative success of a mutating attacker. From these we derive three design rules: verify at ingestion rather than enumerate at egress, deflect according to the value at stake, and refuse without explaining. The resulting framework, PROVE, gates admission on claim-unit provenance, restricts retrieval to a sensitivity-layered whitelist bound to review status, locks the evidence set and anchors every sentence to it, verifies the answer with a semi-supervised detector, and invalidates revoked entries within one update step. On SecKB-Bench, a constructive benchmark of 44,000 instances over seven attack families, PROVE reduces aggregate attack success from 90.1% to 1.82% and per-response leakage by 99.4%, while over-refusing less than any baseline, at 1.9 times the inference cost of the undefended pipeline.

title: A Dempster-Shafer-Based Expert System for Personalized Higher Education Major Recommendation
abstract: Selecting a study program at a State University (Perguruan Tinggi Negeri/PTN) is a decision that many senior high school students approach without a systematic review of their interest, aptitude, achievement, and career goals, a gap made more pressing by the limited counseling capacity available at most schools. Earlier expert systems for major recommendation have relied on Forward Chaining or Certainty Factor, methods that combine evidence into a single rule outcome or scalar confidence without explicitly representing the uncertainty left by incomplete evidence. This study developed and implemented a web-based expert system, Peta Kampus, that applies Dempster-Shafer evidence theory to generate a personalized major recommendation from a student's answers to a structured questionnaire. The knowledge base was constructed with school counselors and an education practitioner into 275 evidence-linked questions covering 55 majors across 21 faculties, each carrying an expert-assigned belief value. The system was built on a native PHP Model-View-Controller architecture with MySQL as the data store, and its inference engine combines successive evidence using Dempster's rule of combination while tracking residual uncertainty and evidentiary conflict. The system was verified through Black Box Testing of its functional modules, with all 15 tested scenarios passing, and evaluated through an accuracy comparison against three independent evaluators (school principal and two guidance counselors, 90% average agreement across 30 cases) and a User Acceptance Test administered to 30 students, which returned an overall satisfaction score of 94.8%. The resulting system gives students and counselors a belief-and-plausibility-based recommendation that is more transparent than a single deterministic score.

evidence.title: A Dempster-Shafer-Based Expert System for Personalized Higher Education Major Recommendation
evidence.abstract: Selecting a study program at a State University (Perguruan Tinggi Negeri/PTN) is a decision that many senior high school students approach without a systematic review of their interest, aptitude, achievement, and career goals, a gap made more pressing by the limited counseling capacity available at most schools. Earlier expert systems for major recommendation have relied on Forward Chaining or Certainty Factor, methods that combine evidence into a single rule outcome or scalar confidence without explicitly representing the uncertainty left by incomplete evidence. This study developed and implemented a web-based expert system, Peta Kampus, that applies Dempster-Shafer evidence theory to generate a personalized major recommendation from a student's answers to a structured questionnaire. The knowledge base was constructed with school counselors and an education practitioner into 275 evidence-linked questions covering 55 majors across 21 faculties, each carrying an expert-assigned belief value. The system was built on a native PHP Model-View-Controller architecture with MySQL as the data store, and its inference engine combines successive evidence using Dempster's rule of combination while tracking residual uncertainty and evidentiary conflict. The system was verified through Black Box Testing of its functional modules, with all 15 tested scenarios passing, and evaluated through an accuracy comparison against three independent evaluators (school principal and two guidance counselors, 90% average agreement across 30 cases) and a User Acceptance Test administered to 30 students, which returned an overall satisfaction score of 94.8%. The resulting system gives students and counselors a belief-and-plausibility-based recommendation that is more transparent than a single deterministic score.

title: INDEPENDENCE v1.1.0: Formal Models, Bounded Conformance, and Evidentiary Trust Boundaries
abstract: INDEPENDENCE v1.1.0 is a research-preservation and formalisation package concerning deterministic elementary cellular automata, software independence, and evidentiary trust boundaries. It links the exact, published GitHub v1.1.0 source revision with the formalisation report, the original locally generated Lean/SPARK/Ada/JavaScript and Rocq research evidence archives, and the exact historical v1.0.1 Chromium/Firefox browser evidence archive. Preserved local receipts record six Lean 4 kernel-checked width-four model theorems, ten GNATprove-discharged verification conditions, 4,096 finite Ada conformance cases (plus ten invalid cases), 4,096 actual JavaScript finite comparisons, and fifteen Rocq 9.2 mathematical theorem/example obligations covering finite Boolean-list semantics. Historical browser evidence records 92 passing assertions, not a live production or independent execution attestation. SHA-256 manifests and independent Python standard-library verification preserve original archive byte identity and constrain unsupported proof/publication claims. The package does not establish formal model-to-production JavaScript refinement, external execution attestation, universal application correctness, security certification, WCAG compliance or superiority over third-party dependencies.

title: Simulator Update Frequency Sensitivity in Driving Scenario Search
abstract: We examine how archive partitions and simulator update frequency affect driving-scenario search comparisons. Twenty learned policies span two tasks, two algorithms and five training seeds per combination. The initial study includes 128,000 episodes and 16,800 search campaigns; intervals for all eight prespecified rotation contrasts include zero. Changing replay from 30 to 60 Hz changes 0.54–6.98 percent of collision labels across task–algorithm groups. An exploratory fixed-history analysis compares shared-label Cartesian bounds, which permit case-wise mixing, with five whole-bank rules: three frequency labels, the original 15/30 conjunction and all-three agreement. Among 40 main-method pairs, 38 retain a nonzero direction under all five rules, versus 21 under Cartesian bounds. Across all 840 pairs, 787 retain a direction under the five rules. Label-rule robustness does not imply statistical separation from search-seed variability. Budgeted flips show that small permitted changes can erode sign robustness sharply. A prospective six-bank application adds 184,320 episodes with frequency-specific adaptive search. Yield maximization and minimax-envelope selection both choose cross-entropy search in every group, so this application cannot establish whether auditing improves selection. The contribution is a controlled rotation intervention and a reproducible sensitivity comparison. Update frequency changes traffic behaviour as well as integration; no isolated solver-error or physical-safety claim is made.

title: Robust NLP for Social Good: Transformer-Based Classification of Noisy Disaster-Related Social Media Messages
abstract: Abstract In the wake of terrible occurrences, social media has become the preferred source for real-time information. Social media has become a significant instrument for victims of catastrophes to express their needs, document incidents, request support and share information related to their situation. However, automated analysis may be fairly difficult in the case of casual, abbreviated, grammatically inconsistent, spelling-variant and other textual noisy communications. Artificial intelligence may be used to this data to enhance the response to catastrophes provided by technology and the well-being of humans and help in the improved detection and organization of communications related to disasters. The current research is a study on the feasibility of the use of Natural Language Processing (NLP) based on transformers to classify the social media postings about the tragedy with background noise. A social media dataset related to catastrophes is pre-processed adequately to develop classification models. For the comparison of the performance of the handling of textual content on catastrophes a transformer-based model and a conventional machine-learning baseline are taken into consideration. Some of the main performance indicators used to evaluate the models include accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score. The problems caused by casual and distracting social media text are given specific attention. This project aims to (1) describe the challenges of collecting and evaluating noisy user-generated data and (2) empirically evaluate transformer-based text categorisation in a disaster-response setting. The research explores the use of AI-driven natural language processing on social media platforms connected to catastrophes to assist in the timely comprehension of crisis-related communication and human well-being. Moreover, it adds to the greater issue of Artificial Intelligence for social benefit.

title: Per-shot decoder confidences for "Soft information from neural-network logits and correlation-aware matching gaps"
abstract: Signed confidence of three decoders on the same sampled syndromes of rotated-surface-code memory experiments under uniform circuit-level noise (stim), 10^8 shots per run, for 20 runs: (d, r) = (5, 5), (5, 7), (5, 9), (5, 11), (7, 7), (7, 9), (7, 11), (9, 9) at p = 0.005, and d = r = 5, 7, 9 at p = 0.003, 0.0035, 0.004, 0.0045. Decoders: uncorrelated minimum-weight perfect matching (complementary gap), correlation-aware matching (complementary gap on a shared reweighted graph), and the pretrained graph-neural-network decoder of Lange et al., Phys. Rev. Research 7, 023181 (2025) (logit). Each run has one float32 NumPy array per decoder (positive where the decoder is correct, magnitude = confidence in dB) and a JSON file with the configuration, software versions and consistency checks. The code that generated the data and rebuilds every figure, table and number of the paper from it is at https://github.com/DavidDentelski/GNN-confidence-score. See README.md for the format.

title: LLM Trust Score: Scoring the Reliability of Language-Model Answers with Cross-Model Judges and Self-Consistency
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often give fluent answers that are wrong, and users have no cheap way to tell which answers to trust. This paper presents LLM Trust Score, a black-box layer that scores one answer from 0 to 100 without access to token probabilities. A writer model (gpt-4o-mini) answers each question three times at temperature 0.9. A Gemini model checks whether the three answers reach the same conclusion. Three judges from three other developers (Qwen, Mistral and Llama) rate each answer as correct or hallucinated with the help of web-search snippets, and the best-scoring answer receives a score and a High, Medium or Low label. A separate tie-breaker model (NVIDIA Nemotron) checks only the winning answer and removes 10 points when it disagrees with the judge majority. We evaluate on 200 fresh questions (66 TruthfulQA, 66 HaluEval and 68 TriviaQA) graded by Claude Haiku 5.5, a model that plays no part in the scoring. The writer was correct on 61.0% of questions. The trust score separated correct from incorrect answers with an AUROC of 0.674 (95% bootstrap interval 0.604–0.740) and a mean gap of 18.1 points (11.1–25.5). The labels were ordered as intended: 71.1% of High, 55.0% of Medium and 26.3% of Low answers were correct. The score is not a calibrated probability. Of the answers that scored 100, 28.0% were wrong, and the Brier score (0.272) was worse than always predicting the base rate (0.238). Discrimination was weakest on TruthfulQA (AUROC 0.568, interval 0.450–0.682). A simple proxy that uses only the judges’ hallucination flags ranked answers at least as well as the full score (AUROC 0.721). Reading the tie-breaker’s penalty back from the scores, it disagreed with the judges on 17 answers (8.5%), of which 35.3% were correct against 63.4% for the rest, and it added only 0.013 to the AUROC (interval −0.003 to +0.033). We give the reasons for every design choice, including why a Gemini agreement checker was preferred to a natural-language-inference (NLI) model, and we state which components were not evaluated on their own.

abstract: DNA-Lang Quantum Execution Corpus v1.0 This dataset contains 490,596 quantum execution shots across 109 production jobs on cryogenic IBM Quantum superconducting processors (98 jobs on ibm_fez Heron r2, 11 jobs on ibm_torino Heron r2). title: Institutional-QA-PT: A Portuguese Question Answering Dataset for Institutional Information
abstract: Institutional-QA-PT is a Portuguese-language question answering dataset about the Computer Science graduate program at the Federal University of São Paulo (UNIFESP). The file corpus_completo.json contains 514 original questions and 1,507 non-empty paraphrases, with reference contexts, answer texts, and character offsets for extractive question answering. The dataset accompanies the study “Local Institutional QA under Resource and Privacy Constraints: Benchmarking Extractive, Generative, and Verified Hybrid Pipelines in Portuguese”. Privacy review: individual email addresses and personal profile links were replaced, and the student representative’s name was pseudonymized. Public faculty names, general institutional contact details, and links to institutional student and graduate listings remain. The dataset is not fully anonymous. This record contains the QA corpus. Source documents, split definitions, code, and evaluation artifacts are available in the associated repository: https://github.com/GPAM-ai/Institutional-QA-PT The study uses a validation holdout rather than an independent test set.

title: A Tool in the Forward Pass: Frozen Tape Modules as Layers of a Small Language Model. Companion code, configurations, results and frozen modules
abstract: Companion material for the technical report A Tool in the Forward Pass: Frozen Tape Modules as Layers of a Small Language Model. A small neural module, trained alone on symbolic tapes and frozen, runs inside the forward pass of gemma-3-1b-it: a learned writer turns hidden states into a tape, the module reduces it to a result, and a learned reader returns the result to the model. Code (scripts/): the experiments, and the generator that writes every number and table of the paper from the results. Configurations (configs/): one per experiment, with the predictions registered before each run (the paper's Appendix B). Results (data/sweeps/): the measured results the paper is generated from. Frozen modules (checkpoints/): the arithmetic and the state-tracking tape modules (64k parameters each, four seeds). Paper (paper/): LaTeX source and PDF. See README.md in the archive for reproduction. Verify with SHA256SUMS. Licences: code MIT; data, results, checkpoints and the paper CC BY 4.0. Gemma weights are not included.

title: JOR 3.1 DSP Maritime/Acoustic Engine
abstract: Concept demonstration of the JOR (James Orion Report) Bayesian evidence-fusion engine applied to maritime active-sonar contact detection. Synthetic data only: the sensor model is illustrative and has not been validated against real acoustic data, and nothing here is a claim about real-world sonar performance. The demo retargets the JOR 3.1 fusion math to a sonar setting, with a sonar-domain sensor model, an independent kinematic-consistency evidence channel, tiered CONFIRM/REVIEW alerting, and ambient-noise modeling based on a published acoustics approximation. It uses a strictly disjoint TRAIN/VAL/TEST evaluation, with every parameter selected on TRAIN, confirmed on VAL, frozen, and evaluated once on held-out TEST. On the synthetic TEST set, JOR fusion reached 0.704 recall at a 0.027 false-positive rate, compared with 0.381 recall for a single-channel SNR threshold at the same false-positive rate. The archive includes the current script, the archived earlier version, an offline speed test, example figures, and an animated walkthrough. Released under the MIT License.

title: The Personal Agent, Built by Hand: A Statement of Prior Work — Renewed
abstract: A renewal of the statement of prior work first published on October 12, 2026 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23328584), the day Meta announced Muse Wonder headlining Active Memory and Active Focus. The claim: the personal-agent system described — an agent with continuing curated memory, a standing crew of six AI deputies on 24/7 autonomous cycles, a multi-model jury in standing session, and local offline AI built by hand — was designed, built, and in daily operation weeks before that announcement, by one independent operator on a $20/month plan, with a published, timestamped public record. This renewal carries the original receipts (September 8 – October 12, 2026) and adds the record since: two further library works, a hand-built phone toolkit, a text bridge to a local 35B vision model, the first live voice calls with the agent, and three books published on Zenodo on October 31, 2026 — ten published works in all. Not an accusation; a request for recognition: when the history of personal agents is written, this prior, public, independent body of work belongs in it.

title: RankSetu AI: AI-Powered Smart Learning, Practice & Exam Readiness Platform
abstract: MHT-CET candidates (Maharashtra Common Entrance Test) typically study through video lessons, PDF notes, messaging groups and test-series apps that keep their data in separate silos, which leaves them without levelappropriate practice or dependable feedback.This paper describes RankSetu AI, a mobile-first learning and examreadiness platform developed with Flutter and Firebase, which links practice, assessment, analysis and improvement into a single cycle.The platform provides subject-wise practice, timed mock tests that are scored automatically, an AI test generator, AI Dost (a Google Gemini-based mentor that solves doubts step by step), weakness detection, test recommendation, two-level caching, single-device sessions, client-side anti-cheat controls and a web-based administration panel.Item Response Theory drives adaptive difficulty, while a normal-distribution model yields a percentile estimate that is always shown with a disclaimer.The paper states openly which modules are implemented, which are planned and what the limitations are.

title: The Verifier Is Part of the Simulator: Evidence-View Gaming in Agentic Equation Discovery
abstract: A growing number of agentic pipelines search for governing equations: an agent proposes laws and a verifier checks them against simulated trajectories. The verifier sees only a numerical summary: integrals against test functions on a time grid. That summary carries its own discretization error, making the verifier part of the simulator. We freeze the trajectory, candidate library, verifier and thresholds, leaving the agent one move: which permitted summary to admit. Without scores or language models, finer time grids reduce numerical discrepancies and false library rejections. On PDEBench, the verifier instead accepts equations missing diffusion on score-selected summaries. Maximizing a public score rewarding decisive verdicts and larger mismatches when rejecting the library wrongly rejects all 1,500 in-library cases; retrospectively retuning score constants on a separate bank reduces errors to 13/180 at best. We call this evidence-view gaming: reward hacking by choice of permitted summary. In single-turn forced-choice tests, Claude models rarely choose summaries giving wrong verdicts when asked to be accurate, but often do so when asked to maximize the score or report missing physics. In separate trust prompts, they often rank those harmful summaries least trustworthy. Requiring several summaries to agree reduces errors but often withholds a verdict and performs worse than a fixed fine view on PDEBench: a safeguard, not a certificate. Evidence chosen after its verdict is known cannot alone authorize a claim.

title: Vision-Language Models Are Joint Denoisers in Robotic Action Generation
abstract: Diffusion-based vision-language-action (VLA) models cascade pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with diffusion action experts, but typically restrict the VLM to providing static conditioning. This separation limits how much pretrained perception and reasoning can guide action generation, especially in out-of-distribution settings. We introduce JADE, a Joint Action DEnoiser that enables the VLM and action expert to jointly refine actions. Our key insight is that structured action latents allow the VLM to read the current noisy action together with visual observations and language instructions. At every denoising step, the VLM contextualizes the noisy action and guides the action expert through gated cross-attention, so that its guidance evolves with the action being generated. We further supervise the VLM to recover clean action latents from noisy ones, which gives it a direct action-learning signal and couples perception with control. Additionally, joint denoising enables JADE to generate actions with fewer sampling steps, helping offset the additional cost of VLM participation. An adaptive step-size schedule further balances task performance and inference latency. On RoboDojo, JADE achieves an average success rate of 12.67%, the highest among the evaluated π_{0.5}-based methods, and is competitive with recent VLA and WAM foundation models pretrained at scale. It also improves performance on RoboTwin 2.0 and raises the average success rate across four real-world bimanual tasks by 20.8 percentage points compared with π_{0.5}.

title: Zonov Lipi: Speech Recognition for Code-Switched Clinical Conversations in English, Hindi and Hinglish
abstract: Zonov Lipi is a 1.55-billion-parameter speech-to-text (STT) model developed by Zonov.ai Labs for clinical conversations involving English, Hindi, and Hinglish. It is designed to address the challenges of Indian medical terminology, code-switched speech, and accurate clinical transcription. This research presents a safety-oriented evaluation framework that measures word error rate (WER), critical errors involving drug names and dosages, drug-name recall, and hallucinations on non-speech audio. The model is evaluated against commercial and open-source speech recognition systems across ten test sets containing 2,155 audio clips. The reported results demonstrate improvements in Hinglish transcription and drug-name recognition compared with the evaluated baseline systems. The report also discusses limitations, including hallucinations on noise and music, lower accuracy on some monolingual speech benchmarks, and the need for clinician review of medical transcripts. Zonov Lipi is designed to support on-premises deployment, allowing healthcare organizations to process audio within their own infrastructure. This technical report describes the model's architecture, training methodology, benchmarking results, security controls, privacy considerations, and future development plans. Organization: Zonov.ai LabsResearch Areas: Healthcare AI, Automatic Speech Recognition, Medical NLP, and AI Governance.

title: Do Coding Agents Catch Their Own Bugs? (They Don't.)
abstract: In software development, engineers need to foresee and fix potential problems with their code that are not explicitly specified in requirements---such as pre-emptively considering vulnerabilities or other bugs from a code change. But current benchmarks often do not measure these future-looking consequences. We introduce Foresight-SWE, a benchmark for measuring whether coding agents can anticipate and address unstated problems during software engineering tasks. Foresight-SWE consists of 212 samples spanning 4 languages and 35 popular open-source repositories. Each sample contains two pull requests (PRs), the second of which resolves defects the first one introduced. To measure whether agents exhibit foresight, we define the foresight resolve rate (FRR) as the fraction of instances where an agent fully resolves the original task while also avoiding the defect identified by a later PR. We evaluate eleven large language models and find that FRR ranges from only 6.13% to 24.53%, indicating that models largely fail to address problems introduced by the first PR change. This raises important questions about how models are trained and aligned in coding contexts, as well as how code review tools should be improved for more fail-safe coding. Foresight-SWE shifts evaluations in this direction.

title: SEPTIGRITY: When Did the Model Know—and What Did It Learn? A Methodological Systematic Review of Data Leakage, Label Leakage, Proxy Labels, Preprocessing Integrity, and Evaluation Practices in EHR-Based Early Sepsis Prediction
abstract: Background & Clinical Rationale: Early sepsis prediction models utilizing longitudinal Electronic Health Record (EHR) data routinely report remarkable retrospective discrimination (AUROC > 0.90–0.98), yet prospective bedside implementations frequently encounter performance collapse and severe clinician alarm fatigue. A critical contributor to this translational divide is methodological sensitivity across cohort inception, label timing, information availability, missing data handling, and evaluation design. A model may leverage genuine physiological trajectories, care-process signals (monitoring density, charting patterns), unavailable future information, or combinations of these mechanisms. These failure modes require rigorous, transparent appraisal. Objectives: This methodological systematic review aims to: (1) audit the chronological availability of predictors relative to prediction landmarks and evaluate access to post-decision or evaluation-set information; (2) identify data leakage, label leakage, outcome circularity, and proxy-label operationalization; (3) quantify the proportion of studies exhibiting documented problems, potential risks, documented safeguards, and insufficient reporting using explicit denominators; (4) identify study-specific implementations with traceable safeguards as positive exemplars; and (5) formulate an evidence-linked, actionable preprocessing blueprint to support rigorous clinical AI development. Methods & Eligibility: In accordance with PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-P statements, comprehensive searches are executed across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore Digital Library from January 1, 2016 (Sepsis-3 consensus introduction) through October 2026. Eligible studies evaluate machine learning, statistical, or deep sequence models developed on adult ICU or high-dependency longitudinal EHR time-series for pre-onset incident sepsis prediction. Methodological adherence regarding lead-time buffers, temporal boundaries, and preprocessing isolation is systematically audited using PROBAST-AI augmented by a dedicated 14-Channel Forensic Matrix and evaluated against 6 Proposed Safeguard Checkpoints. Two reviewers independently screen records and extract structured variables using CHARMS-compliant forms. Primary synthesis is descriptive and methodological, supplemented by conditional meta-analysis and exploratory meta-regression. Planned Protocol Outputs: The completed review will deliver: a study-level forensic audit map; channel-specific frequency distributions with Wilson 95% confidence intervals; a verified safeguard exemplar catalogue; a literature reporting-gap map; and an evidence-linked 12-step preprocessing blueprint.

title: DramaVQA: Probing Detailed Understanding of Ultra-Long TV Dramas
abstract: Despite recent progress in long-form video understanding, current benchmarks mostly focus on short clips or hour-scale videos. This leaves a major gap in evaluating ultra-long video understanding, where videos often last tens of hours. To bridge this gap, we introduce DramaVQA, a large-scale benchmark built upon long-form TV dramas. Containing approximately 20K question-answering (QA) pairs, the scale of DramaVQA exceeds previous long-video datasets, such as Video-MME and LVBench, by an order of magnitude. Our benchmark has two main features that make it stand out from existing datasets. First, we establish a scalable, LLM-assisted annotation pipeline that uses multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to generate complex questions, followed by strict human checking to ensure high data quality. Second, DramaVQA introduces a multi-level time structure; queries are designed across different video lengths, with the hardest questions requiring overall understanding across the entire drama. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art MLLMs face major challenges when tested on these very long videos, highlighting the need for agentic AI algorithms capable of managing long-term memory. The project is available at https://github.com/xinyuehuo/DramaVQA

title: Lookahead Curriculum-Transition Intervention Optimization (LCTIO): Predicting Future Learning Outcomes to Select Adaptive Curriculum Transitions in Generative Models
abstract: Curriculum learning organizes training examples according to their difficulty, often beginning with relatively simple examples before gradually introducing more challenging tasks. Although this strategy provides a structured approach to training, determining when a model should transition between difficulty stages remains an important problem. Fixed schedules may introduce more difficult examples before the model is adequately prepared, while transitions based exclusively on current training loss may fail to capture their downstream effects on generalization, optimization stability, and complex task performance. Lookahead Curriculum-Transition Intervention Optimization (LCTIO) investigates whether candidate curriculum transitions can be evaluated through estimates of their potential future training outcomes before a transition is implemented. Rather than selecting individual training examples, LCTIO focuses on the temporal evolution of the training difficulty distribution. At each curriculum decision point, the framework considers alternative interventions, including maintaining the current curriculum, advancing to a more difficult stage, delaying a planned transition, and modifying the mixture proportions of different difficulty levels. The proposed framework contains four principal components: curriculum-state representation, candidate transition generation, future learning outcome prediction, and uncertainty-aware intervention selection. Candidate transitions are evaluated according to predicted validation performance, training stability, retention of previously acquired capabilities, and performance on increasingly complex tasks. The framework also incorporates computational cost and prediction uncertainty into the intervention decision. An experimental protocol is proposed using diffusion-model training as the primary application. The planned comparison includes fixed curriculum scheduling, current-loss-based transitions, competence-based scheduling, and LCTIO-based predicted-validation-benefit transitions. Additional experiments investigate transition timing, difficulty-mixture allocation, prediction horizons, and computational overhead. This paper presents LCTIO as a methodological framework and research hypothesis rather than an experimentally validated optimization method. Its central question is whether explicitly predicting the consequences of alternative curriculum transitions can provide useful information beyond current-state-based scheduling. Experimental validation is required to determine whether the proposed approach improves generalization, training stability, or complex prompt generation under controlled computational budgets.

title: Words Before Pixels: Selective Modality Routing for Vision-Language Model Unlearning
abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) unlearning is often treated as an objective-design problem: given multimodal forget data, the goal is to optimize a loss that removes undesirable behavior while preserving retained capabilities. We argue that this view overlooks an equally important data-centric question: how should each forget example be represented before optimization? Existing methods typically keep image-conditioned failures in their original image-text form, implicitly assuming that pixels are the right route for unlearning whenever pixels appear in the input. We challenge this assumption by constructing modality-decomposed versions of VLM benchmarks, enabling controlled comparisons among image-only, text-only, and multimodal representations of the same examples. Our modality-mixing experiments show that unsafe instruction-following behavior is more effectively suppressed through textual representations than through images alone, while purely text-only unlearning can still weaken visual grounding when the target behavior depends on visual evidence. Motivated by this trade-off, we introduce ModRoute, a gradient-guided per-sample modality routing strategy that selectively converts high visual-pressure examples to text-only form while keeping the remaining examples multimodal. Notably, on VLGuard with LLaVA-1.5-7B, ModRoute has the strongest composite unlearning-utility score of 0.847 at γ=0.5, a 2.5% improvement over the best random-switching score and geq46% better than pure multimodal or text unlearning. Overall, our results show that effective VLM unlearning depends not only on the objective, but also on the composition and per-sample modality routing of the unlearning data.

title: te-comp: A Complete MLIR Compiler Generating Self-Contained C Inference Engines for MCUs
abstract: Deploying deep learning on microcontrollers (MCUs) requires fitting both the model weights and runtime activations within tens to hundreds of kilobytes of SRAM and Flash. Existing approaches either use an interpreter with a pre-written kernel library or combine a Python code generator with hand-written C kernels. This incurs dispatch overhead and requires framework dependencies. None produces self-contained, dependency-free C code specialized to a given model. In this paper, we present te-comp, the first complete MLIR-based compiler that takes a standard model in .tflite or .safetensors format and emits all C source files needed for deployment: the inference engine (kernels, weight arrays, memory layout) and the RTOS integration layer with zero runtime dependencies. On 10 MCUNet CNN benchmarks, te-comp outperforms MCUNet TinyEngine by using 38% less SRAM (up to 5.9times) and 15% less Flash, while generating complete C code rather than linking a pre-written kernel library. To demonstrate, we use te-comp to compile an 8.3M-parameter GPT-Neo transformer (TinyStories-v2) and deploy it on a single-core Cortex-M7 at 160MHz. The full firmware uses 249KB of 512KB SRAM and 3.62MB of 4MB Flash and achieves approximately 1 token/s interactive text generation via Q4_0 weight quantization, a stateful int4 KV cache, and vocabulary pruning -- a capability no existing MCU inference framework supports.

title: Zeroth-Order Policy Optimization for Scheduling in Queueing Networks
abstract: Reinforcement learning in queueing network scheduling presents significant challenges because of the countably infinite state space and the high stochasticity in transitions. In this paper, we propose zeroth-order policy optimization algorithms that are easy to implement and rely solely on estimates of the average cost, a single scalar quantity, without requiring the estimation of value or advantage functions. Our analysis focuses on back-pressure guarded policies and establishes uniform smoothness of the average cost objective with respect to the policy parameters. Building on this property, we establish finite-time convergence guarantees to an ε-stationary policy for the proposed algorithms. Numerical experiments on multiple queueing networks, including systems beyond classical exponential service distribution, demonstrate competitive performance, outperforming gradient-based RL methods like PPO and traditional queueing baselines.

title: Fast and Exact Relative-Position Attention via Structure-Aware Kernels
abstract: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content-position or bias-position terms. Unlike RoPE, which encodes position via per-token rotations directly on the queries and keys, relative-position terms generally require pairwise offset-dependent computation or lookups, complicating their integration into fused attention kernels and introducing severe memory, bandwidth, and compute overheads as sequences scale. To address this bottleneck, we propose an exact attention algorithm that incorporates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled computation. Our method (1) uses offset-aware tiling to avoid redundant indexing and memory accesses, (2) computes only the necessary key/query-relation products and reuses them across token pairs in both forward and backward passes, and (3) uses offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation, eliminating atomic contention. We provide a unified, efficient Triton implementation across diverse relative-position attention mechanisms and evaluate it against naive and specialized implementations. For 8K-token sequences, our method speeds up the forward (backward) pass by 1.8-6.4times (2.0-21times) and reduces peak memory up to 2.9-128times (1.4-54times) over the strongest baseline for each mechanism, enabling long-context end-to-end transcription that is 1.8times faster and uses 2.4times less memory. Our method thus provides a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.

title: TRIAGE: Reliability- and Load-Conditioned Escalation for Two-Tier LLM Serving with a Semantic Evidence Judge
abstract: Two-tier LLM serving escalates selected requests from a small model to a large one, but prompt-based routers cannot see whether retrieved evidence supports an answer, and they treat the GPU cost of an escalation as constant. We study TRIAGE, which conditions escalation on a post-generation reliability state and on a load-dependent GPU price, and we report both what held and what did not on one A40 serving Qwen2.5-7B and 32B (AWQ) under VLLM. Escalation cost rose 21.9x from 1 to 10 requests/s but showed no monotone dependence on KV-cache headroom, and a pre-registered claim that the reliability state detects corrupted evidence (AUROC>=0.70) was falsified at 0.571, although any prompt-only router scores exactly 0.500 by construction. Post hoc, a semantic evidence judge raised detection to 0.846 (0.926 on never-served items) and predicted wrong small-model answers at AUROC 0.90-0.96 on RGB and three RouterBench model pairs; the resulting cascade stayed within about 3 pp of GPT-4 at 79.5% lower API cost for GPT-3.5->GPT-4, yet fell below random routing for open-model pairs with 2-3x price ratios. End to end, the 7B->32B pair showed only a +2.88 pp held-out gap, so the allocator rightly declined to escalate and the headline is a null that a small pre-launch gate failed to expose.

title: Do Adversarial Patches Survive Real-World Image Degradations? A Large-Scale ImageNet Study
abstract: Computer vision systems are increasingly deployed in fully autonomous settings, making the real-world application of adversarial patches highly relevant. Previous research has focused on the effect of real-world image degradations on computer vision systems and the efficacy of adversarial patches; however, it remains unclear to what extent an adversarial patch can maintain its efficacy under real-world image degradations. This study investigates adversarial patch performance under real-world image degradations in a large-scale ImageNet-1k study across two architecture types, using six of the currently most relevant backbones and fifteen ImageNet-C-based degradation types. The results show that patches are able to retain substantial efficacy even when degraded; with considerable variability both in terms of patch source architecture and degradation type. Conceptually, this highlights the difference between adversarial and degradation robustness and suggests that patches encode characteristics of the source architecture. Practically, it underscores the importance of degradation-specific adversarial evaluation as well as the role of architecture choice in robustness.

title: StreamDuo: A Live Commentator and a Research Agent for Unseen Games
abstract: Streaming video LLMs can now commentate live gameplay, but they are trained and tested on the same games. We study cross-game streaming commentary, in which a model trained on one game commentates games it has never seen, and find that current commentators transfer their timing but not their knowledge of the game world. We propose StreamDuo, which pairs a trainable commentator with a frozen research agent that reads the wiki of the game being played. When the commentator sees something it cannot name, it sends the current frames, and the research agent returns a few wiki entries two seconds later while the stream continues. We train only the commentator, on a single game, in two stages. Information-gain labels teach it to ask only where an answer would help it say what the human caster said, and on-policy self-distillation from a copy of itself that sees the ideal answer teaches it to use noisy answers. Trained on Baldur's Gate 3 and tested on ten unseen games, StreamDuo raises entity recall from 0.082 to 0.116 over Proact-VL trained on the same data, cuts source-game leakage from 9.9% to 1.0%, and achieves the best timing and the highest judged liveliness and overall quality among streaming models.

title: Zero-Gated Cross-Attention
abstract: Injecting non-text modalities into frozen language models often introduces early optimization instability, making it difficult to separate architectural gains from transient training dynamics. We introduce Inductively Gated Cross-Attention (IGCA), a zero-initialized cross-attention bridge that preserves pretrained model behavior at initialization while enabling gradual multimodal conditioning. Integrated across six decoder layers of frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b1 backbones (with 40,404,961,288 trainable adapter parameters used during training), IGCA acts as an exact algebraic no-op at initialization with a maximum output discrepancy of 0.00e+00. Over 59,500 training steps on Falcon-40B, the training loss decreases from 3.9403 to 0.0007 (with final ten step losses of [0.0001, 0.0003, 0.0005, 0.0002, 0.0005, 0.0011, 0.0005, 0.0006, 0.0005, 0.0007]). On held-out evaluation, the best gate-on checkpoint achieves a loss of 2.2201 compared to 4.3469 for the gate-off baseline -- a 48.9% reduction (2.1268 nats) -- while average held-out loss improves from 4.3423 to 2.2498 (1.9075 nats) with a mean gate magnitude of tanh(α) = 0.0713.

title: Weaponising Model Safety: Steering LLM Decision Harnesses
abstract: LLM-based decision agents (phishing triage, SOC alert triage, content moderation, CI security gates, transaction screening) send untrusted input to a model, ask for a classification, and branch on the answer. Providers now enforce safety policy with hard stops: generation is terminated and the caller receives a refusal rather than a verdict. We show that this refusal is an attacker-reachable control-flow input. When an attacker places content in front of the classifier that trips the provider's safety layer, the call returns no verdict, and many harnesses map that absence to their permissive default: deliver, approve, close. The attacker does not fool the model; they stop it from answering. We test 14 common handling patterns. All 14 classify a malicious item correctly when given a clean verdict, and 12 of them then fail open on at least one non-verdict state; 73% of outcomes across all patterns and non-verdict states are fail-open. A live probe confirms that the stop happens before any output is produced, that structured output is not exempt, and that the harness reports the refusal in an envelope marked subtype: "success". The fix is a few lines of code. The mechanism is old, the trigger is newer than the code it breaks, and, unlike prompt injection, it becomes more reliable as models get safer.
