title: Know When the Equation Is Wrong: Structural Uncertainty for LLM-Guided Symbolic Regression under Extrapolation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can help discover mathematical equations from data, but most LLM-guided symbolic regression methods focus on a single best equation without quantifying uncertainty over alternative functional forms. This is challenging because distinct equations can fit the observed data similarly while producing substantially different extrapolations. Our experiments on the LLM-SRBench dataset show that standard conformal intervals achieve nominal in-distribution coverage but frequently fail under extrapolation. To tackle this challenge, we introduce LLM-SR-UQ, a framework that retains competing equation structures and uses their disagreement to characterize uncertainty about the underlying functional form. We extend the standard fixed-width conformal approach to quantify structural intervals, which measure disagreement among candidate equations and identify where prediction intervals should widen. Extensive experiments show our framework substantially improves coverage attainment by incorporating structural disagreement while preserving in-distribution coverage. Our approach also shows good generalizability when it is applied to other symbolic-regression methods.

title: AuditFL: A Contract-Backed Clearing Layer for Open Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning (FL) keeps raw data local, but most deployments still rely on a trusted coordinator for client admission, checkpoint distribution, update collection, aggregation, and rewards. This paper presents AuditFL, a contract-backed clearing layer for auditable FL in open settings. AuditFL keeps training and aggregation off chain, stores model artifacts in an assumed reliable off-chain artifact store, and records only content identifiers and economic state on chain. Clients reserve update tickets with deposits, publish update identifiers, and later claim refunds or rewards; the task coordinator publishes global checkpoints and finalizes rounds through deterministic settlement rules. The design does not remove the aggregator, but makes its on-chain round decisions attributable, replayable, auditable, and economically constrained. We implement AuditFL as both a deterministic state-machine prototype and a Solidity contract on a local Ethereum-compatible Anvil chain. On full MNIST with Dirichlet non-IID splits, 12 rounds, and up to 200 clients, AuditFL preserves the Plain FL learning trajectory while its overhead follows closed-form control-plane models. At 200 clients, the contract run issues 5,026 transactions, stores 2,413 off-chain artifacts (144.9 MiB), and consumes 829.7M EVM gas, dominated by per-client reserve and publish calls. Controlled dropout, invalid-update, and artifact-unavailability stress tests reduce inclusion nearly linearly but still finalize rounds, with final-accuracy changes remaining within a few tenths of an accuracy percentage point even under high injected failure rates.

title: Copy-cup gates in tensor products of group algebra codes
abstract: We determine conditions on classical group algebra codes so that they have pre-orientation for cup products and copy-cup gates. This defines quantum codes that have constant-depth $\operatorname{CZ}$ and $\operatorname{CCZ}$ gates constructed via tensor products of classical group algebra codes, including hypergraph and balanced products. We show that determining the conditions relies on solving the perfect matching problem in graph theory. Conditions are fully determined for the 2- and 3-copy-cup gates, for group algebra codes up to weight 4, including for codes with odd check weight. These include the bivariate bicycle codes, which we show do not have the pre-orientation for either type of copy-cup gate. We show that abelian weight 4 group algebra codes satisfying the non-associative 3-copy-cup gate necessarily have a code distance of 2, whereas codes that satisfy conditions for the symmetric 3-copy-cup gate can have higher distances, and in fact also satisfy conditions for the 2-copy-cup gate. Finally we find examples of quantum codes from the product of abelian group algebra codes that have inter-code constant-depth $\operatorname{CZ}$ and $\operatorname{CCZ}$ gates.

title: Asynchronous Flow Map Language Models
abstract: The order in which tokens are predicted in language modeling has a profound impact on the quality of generated sequences. Autoregressive and masked diffusion models iteratively fill in tokens and can exploit such orderings across generation steps, but how to leverage an ordering for one-step parallel language modeling is unclear. We introduce asynchronous flow map language models (aFMLMs), which incorporate prediction order into one-step modeling by learning the flow maps of asynchronous flows. These flows specify an ordering through a tokenwise time schedule that controls the relative denoising progress of tokens. We formulate a general class of asynchronous flows that admit both prescribed and learned, state-adaptive schedules, show that they define valid flow maps, and develop new methods for their flow map distillation. The resulting models can generate all tokens in a single forward pass by internalizing the ordering encoded in the flow into their hidden computations. On Sudoku solving and code generation for GSM8K math word problems, aFMLM establishes new state-of-the-art one-step performance.

title: Hawkeye: Reading Illegible Text with Vision Language Models
abstract: While modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been remarkably successful in general scene text recognition, they consistently struggle with the long-tail distribution of text that is degraded by motion blur or low resolution. These limitations are particularly apparent in egocentric applications like smart glasses, where text is often captured in noisy environments. In this paper, we introduce the BSTRB (Blurry Scene Text Recognition Benchmark), a novel benchmark of 8,398 noisy image samples with high-fidelity annotations derived from 1,699 real-world video sequences. To support this, we present Hawkeye, a VLM fine-tuned on BSTRB to read and reason about illegible text by leveraging contextual priors and pixel-level alignment. Our results show that \name matches much larger VLMs on BSTRB overall and exceeds them on text at or below 20 pixels, in a single pass suited to real-time deployment. We characterize the resolution at which current VLMs begin to fail.

title: When Does Jacobian Fine-Tuning Stabilize Neural PDE Emulators?
abstract: Neural emulators of chaotic PDEs are trained on one-step prediction but deployed autoregressively, where their errors compound. Jacobian-based regularisers aim to curb this growth, but in a chaotic system part of the growth is physical and cannot be trained away. We separate the two sources of this error with a first-order decomposition. We compare the emulator's error with a counterfactual that propagates the same one-step mistakes through the solver's Jacobian, giving an amplification ratio: the factor by which the model's own dynamics amplify its errors. We study 21 configurations across four PDEs, five architectures and two model sizes (8-10k and 33k parameters), with errors measured at one Lyapunov time. Jacobian fine-tuning reduced the error by more than 10% for 1 of 34 seeds whose amplification ratio was at most 1.25, and for all 20 seeds whose ratio was at least four; for the latter, the error fell by a factor of 8 (small models) and 55 (33k models) in geometric mean over seeds. The gain approximately equals the one-step accuracy cost of fine-tuning divided by the amplification ratio. Matching the solver's Jacobian along the model's own error direction (EDJM) outperformed random directions at the same cost on 28 of 35 seeds; input-noise injection performed comparably to EDJM.

title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. evidence.title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
evidence.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It is a supply layer. title: Robust high-order quantum simulation using finite-width pulses
abstract: We present a general framework for promoting first-order pulse sequences in quantum simulation to higher-order sequences that maintain robustness in the presence of finite pulse-width effects. Our approach maps a given first-order pulse sequence to a first-order Trotter formula, applies higher-order Trotter-formula constructions, and then compiles the resulting evolution back into physically implementable finite-width pulses via dynamically corrected gates. The resulting sequences achieve arbitrarily high-order error scaling with respect to the control cycle time of the underlying first-order sequence while maintaining robustness to finite pulse-width effects. The framework also enables the use of multi-product formulas for more efficient constructions. We apply the framework to several physically motivated quantum-simulation tasks and numerically verify the predicted error scalings.

title: CompoSET: A Controlled Single-Edit Benchmark for Vision-Language Compositionality
abstract: Vision-language compositionality is the ability to identify which properties, relations, quantities, and states bind to which entities in both an image and a caption, and to match those bindings across modalities. Existing benchmarks evaluate this ability through image-text matching: a model ranks candidate image-caption match similarities and succeeds when the correct match comes on top. In such datasets, paired images differ by more than a single binding: scene, layout, and content all differ, with 97% of pixels changing on average. Such pairs do not isolate compositionality: results are confounded by global image differences. We introduce Compositional Single-EdiT (CompoSET), a benchmark dataset in which each base image-caption pair has an edited counterpart, or foil, that preserves the scene but differs by a single controlled edit, such as color, count, spatial relation, or object state. Base and foil images preserve naturalistic scene complexity yet are visually near-identical: only 8% of pixels change on average. Our dataset has many foils per base scene (~22) in order to separate scene difficulty from edit difficulty, a distinction one-foil-per-base benchmarks cannot make. CompoSET contains 1,776 instances across 80 naturalistic scenes, spanning 16 edit types in 4 semantic categories, with captions at 3 verbosity levels. We test 22 dual-encoder VLMs and find that all models perform at or below chance level on CompoSET, despite scoring well on prior benchmarks. This suggests that apparent progress under prior image-text matching protocols may be an artifact arising from confounds in benchmark design, and that compositional understanding in dual-encoder VLMs is far from solved. CompoSET addresses the confounds and offers a better controlled benchmark to measure future progress.

title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents
abstract: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI (*100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.

title: MUON-RT Reusing the Teacher's Trajectory for Momentum-Free Muon for LLM Self-Distillation
abstract: Self-distillation methods for large language models with an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher already retain a history of student updates. Muon nevertheless stores a separate momentum buffer, increasing persistent training memory. We propose Muon with Reused Teacher (Muon-RT), which reuses the teacher-student displacement to eliminate momentum buffers for hidden weight matrices. We show that this displacement encodes an exponentially weighted history of applied updates and smooths temporally uncorrelated noise under a local model. Muon-RT removes its radial component, normalizes it spectrally, and mixes it with the current gradient after Newton-Schulz (NS) orthogonalization. Under explicit regularity and alignment assumptions, we establish linear contraction of an expected objective-gap bound toward a residual error level. With Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Muon-RT improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.6 points with 42% less persistent memory, and over momentum Muon by 5.4 points with 27% less persistent memory. With Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) on Olmo-3-7B-Instruct, it improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.0 points.

title: Enhancing qubit readout fidelity with two-mode squeezing of the coherent measurement signal
abstract: Abstract The ability to perform high-fidelity quantum nondemolition qubit readout is pivotal for the realization of large and powerful quantum computers. Such readout of superconducting qubits is generally enabled by amplifying the weak dispersive measurement signals using phase-preserving quantum-limited Josephson amplifiers with sufficient gain to dilute the contribution of the added noise by the output chain. Here, we further enhance the qubit readout fidelity by (1) simultaneously measuring the two-mode squeezed states of the amplified readout signals at the signal and idler frequencies of the nondegenerate amplifier and (2) coherently combining them at the classical processing stage following a relative rotation that maximizes the signal to noise ratio of the qubit-encoded readout quadrature. Such readout scheme exhibits enhancement in the readout fidelity for all practical values of amplifier gain and noise added by the output chain and is fully compatible with frequency multiplexed setups used in large quantum processors.

title: GeoFlip: Benchmarking Geometry-Sensitive Physics in Video Generation
abstract: Video generation models synthesize realistic motion, but can they respond correctly to changes in initial geometry? We introduce GeoFlip, a video generation benchmark centered on physical outcome flips induced by geometry. With shared physical settings and textual prompts held fixed, GeoFlip applies controlled interventions to support extent, object placement, and mechanism configuration, constructing paired scenes with contrasting reference events, such as remaining stable versus falling or tipping. These pairs test whether models translate geometric differences in the first frame into correct physical evolution. The benchmark comprises 482 scene pairs and 964 reference videos across six physical categories, with reference outcomes established through procedural scene construction, physics simulation, and numerical validation and verification of physical events. We evaluate 16 models for image to video generation along three dimensions: event correctness, structural integrity, and similarity to reference videos. We examine evaluation consistency with independent vision language judges. On the 442 conditions shared by all models, the highest event correctness averaged across tasks is 27.98%, revealing substantial limitations in physical generation conditioned on geometry. Model strengths vary across physical mechanisms, and the three evaluation dimensions capture distinct capabilities. Typical failures include ignoring geometric changes, generating incorrect object motion, bending rigid objects, and introducing additional components. Rank correlations between judges reach 0.906 for event correctness and 0.929 for structural integrity. By combining controlled geometric interventions, verifiable physical references, and multidimensional evaluation, GeoFlip assesses progress from visual realism toward physical consistency conditioned on geometry.

title: EvoTeam: Multi-Agent Collaboration via Evolving Teams
abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on collaboration among specialized agents to solve complex tasks. Existing methods improve MAS by refining the prompts, skills, and execution strategies of individual agents based on task feedback. However, improving individual agents does not necessarily lead to better team collaboration. Recent studies have therefore extended evolution to the collaboration level, using collective execution experience to adjust team organization, and inter-agent interactions. Nevertheless, evolving collaboration across heterogeneous tasks remains challenging, as existing approaches often constrain team reorganization within a shared structure and reuse interaction rules across incompatible team contexts. In this paper, we propose EvoTeam, a collaboration-centric evolution framework that jointly evolves team organization, interaction rules, and individual agent skills through execution experience. It maintains a library of reusable teams, selecting or creating agent teams and guiding collaboration through team-specific interaction rules. Collaboration experience accumulates within compatible team contexts, while individual skills remain reusable across teams. Experiments across four benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness. Our code is available at https://github.com/DEEP-JLU/EvoTeam.

title: Model Extraction of Convolutional Neural Networks with Max-Pooling
abstract: Model extraction attacks aim to recover the internal parameters of neural networks through black-box queries. While significant progress has been achieved for fully connected ReLU networks, far less is known about structured architectures such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), which are widely used in practice. In particular, convolutional layers introduce locality and weight sharing, while max-pooling operations leak only relative activation information, both of which require rethinking and extending existing extraction techniques. In this work, we study the extraction of CNNs combining ReLU activations and max-pooling layers in the soft-label setting. We first demonstrate that max-pooling can be understood as a natural extension of the ReLU non-linear operation and classify the different types of critical points observed in this setting. We show that max-pooling critical points capture the difference between two convolutional neurons and that the local structure of convolution allows us to determine the shift between them and reconstruct the underlying convolutional kernel. We also introduce optimizations that take advantage of the specific structure of CNNs: by using receptive-field analysis, we design efficient methods to filter noise and localize critical points. These improvements significantly reduce the computational cost compared to a naive reduction to a large sparse fully connected network. Finally, we validate our approach experimentally on a compact VGG-style convolutional neural network trained on CIFAR-10. The results show that our methods permit accurate weight extraction in CNNs in practice, while correctly localizing critical points in convolutional layers.

title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more capable and widely used, understanding when and how humans should work with these systems is becoming increasingly important. However, the empirical evidence in this space offers conflicting recommendations, which leaves individuals and organizations without clear guidance on when to combine human and AI capabilities. Existing meta-analyses can help reconcile these findings, but they require substantial manual effort and cannot readily incorporate new evidence as it emerges. To address this challenge, we introduce AutoAnalysis: an automated, self-updating meta-analysis of when humans and AI work better together, and when they work better alone. AutoAnalysis' most recent run synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. Across this body of work, we found that, on average, human-AI combinations performed significantly better than humans alone, but they performed significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone. These findings highlight the important distinction between improving human performance and achieving human-AI synergy and underscore the need to evaluate collaboration against both human and AI performance alone. As new studies emerge, AutoAnalysis will integrate their findings into the meta-analysis, providing cumulative evidence about when humans and AI perform better together and how human-AI performance varies across AI agents, tasks, and processes.

title: MoLRSI: A Recursive Self-Improving AI agent for Molecular Discovery
abstract: Molecular discovery requires navigating vast combinatorial search spaces while balancing competing biological objectives. AI agents can automate expert-defined molecular design protocols, but automation alone does not address how to optimize workflows for new tasks or improve their development through experience. Here we introduce MoLRSI, an AI agent that combines systematic optimization of workflows and model architectures with persistent cross-task memory to recursively improve its search policy for molecular discovery. Workflow performance, refinement outcomes, and execution feedback guide subsequent searches, allowing the agent to improve both its workflows and its strategy for developing them. We evaluate MoLRSI in two challenging molecular discovery settings that require balancing competing properties. In antibiotic discovery, MoLRSI developed a screening workflow balancing antibacterial activity, cytotoxicity and structural novelty, achieving an experimental hit rate of 15.9%, compared with 8.7% for a previous expert-led workflow using the same training data and screening library. In de novo peptide-MHC binder design, MoLRSI developed workflows that jointly consider target binding and specificity, producing eight experimentally validated hits against MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 pMHCs with preferential binding over tested off-targets while Claude Science completely failed. These findings demonstrate how experience-guided workflow optimization can address competing discovery objectives while improving the search strategies used in subsequent campaigns.

title: Less Loss, Fixed Weights: Logit Corrections for Forgetting
abstract: When a language model is fine-tuned to follow instructions, or further pretrained on a new subject, it often gets worse at predicting standard web text. This is known as "forgetting." We ask whether this loss can be undone by simple, fixed adjustments to the model's final token predictions. Across 14 pairs of base and derived models, from 1B to 7B parameters, we fitted a fixed bonus or penalty for each token (a vocabulary bias), alone or together with a temperature. On text held out from correction fitting, the largest top-4K bias recovery estimate is under 10%, with loss conditional on the retained vocabulary. Combining the bias with a temperature recovers up to 36%. Models further pretrained on math lose the most and recover almost nothing. Finally, in a controlled simulation where a model is damaged at random, with no planted bias or temperature change, the bias-plus-temperature fix still recovers 29%. Most of the real-model loss increase stays out of reach of our restricted fits.

title: DeFT-RAG: Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.

With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.

title: SOPO: Socratic Guided Policy Optimization for Span-Level Hallucination Detection
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained widespread adoption in various natural language processing tasks, but suffer from hallucination issues where they generate unfaithful or inconsistent content. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has shown promising applications in reasoning tasks, its application to span-level hallucination detection is challenged by localization ambiguity, reward sparsity on hard examples, and uncontrolled length inflation. To address these issues, we introduce Socratic Guided Policy Optimization (SOPO), a multi-turn RL framework for robust hallucination detection. The key innovation of SOPO is a Socratic feedback mechanism, where a teacher model guides the reasoning trajectories during rollout by providing indirect hints inferred from the ground truth. This teacher-guided approach enables the model to generate more effective reasoning trajectories for hard examples, thus alleviating reward sparsity. Furthermore, we incorporate Turn-based Advantage Scaling to penalize verbosity bias, encouraging the model to develop efficient and autonomous reasoning capabilities. Empirical results on RAGTruth demonstrate that SOPO (4B) achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing leading proprietary models (e.g., GPT-5) and standard RL baselines, while obtaining higher reported mean scores than GRPO on four out-of-domain benchmarks, with mixed evidence against CAPO. We release our training and evaluation code alongside the 1.7B and 4B SOPO models at https://github.com/patsnap/SOPO.

title: Recent advances in quantum architecture search
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) constitute a prominent paradigm for exploring the capabilities of near-term quantum computers. As the effectiveness of VQAs depends heavily on the design of variational quantum circuits, Quantum Architecture Search (QAS) has emerged as a critical research area to automate the discovery of high-performing circuit structures. This paper reviews key advancements in current research on QAS, including its core concepts, representative methodologies, applications, and emerging trends. The content is structured to ensure broad accessibility for a diverse audience of researchers while preserving the core principles of complex methodologies. In addition, we discuss remaining challenges and suggest potential research directions to offer perspectives on future exploration in this rapidly evolving field.

title: On Statistical-Computational Gaps in Graph Combinatorial Testing Problems
abstract: We study high-dimensional graph combinatorial hypothesis testing problems in which a signal is supported on the edge set of an unknown subgraph drawn from a class invariant under vertex relabeling. For Gaussian observations, we characterize sharp statistical and computational thresholds (at polynomial order) for the signal magnitude required for strong detection across various combinatorial graph alternatives. Our analysis is based on bounding the second moments of the full and low-degree likelihood ratios in terms of the overlap of two independent latent structures and comparing the resulting lower bounds with scan, average, and coordinatewise maximum tests. Under an appropriate low-degree conjecture for computational hardness, we obtain planted-clique thresholds matching those known for Gaussian submatrix detection and identify new statistical-computational gaps for multiple planted cliques and hypercliques, thick cycles and thick paths. We also establish a novel transfer principle across natural exponential family observation models: matching the one-coordinate chi-square divergence preserves full likelihood-ratio second moments exactly and makes low-degree second moments equivalent up to constant factors under a degree condition. Under local regularity, we obtain corresponding testing upper bounds in terms of an effective signal strength. When these upper and lower bounds match, they yield universal threshold scales in the local alternative regime. As a consequence, statistical-computational gaps for planted-clique detection in Erdős--Rényi settings can be deduced from the Gaussian model.

title: Operating a bistable qubit
abstract: Parasitic two-level-system (TLS) defects limit the stability and performance of solid-state quantum processors. Their interaction with a qubit can cause discrete, stochastic shifts of the qubit frequency, making the qubit bistable. We experimentally demonstrate an adaptive protocol for operating a bistable qubit with high fidelity using a classical controller powered by a field-programmable gate array. Our “1-bit feedback” protocol estimates the qubit's bistable frequency and corrects the control frame using only one single-shot measurement, reaching the information limit set by the qubit's intrinsic entropy. We validate the protocol in a superconducting qubit by suppressing TLS-induced Ramsey beating, and deploy it to stabilize gate fidelities over time with approximately 136 kHz estimation bandwidth and a 77% error reduction. Our approach provides a simple, yet fundamentally efficient strategy for mitigating dephasing errors induced by strongly coupled TLS defects, and may enable the operation of large future qubit arrays suffering from few remaining, discrete instabilities.

title: Quantum purity amplification for arbitrary eigenstates and multiple outputs
abstract: Quantum purity amplification (QPA) is the task of coherently transforming $n$ copies of a mixed state into high-fidelity copies of a chosen eigenstate. We develop a general theory of QPA for $n$ input copies, $m$ output copies, and arbitrary choices of target eigenstate, local dimension $d$, and input spectrum. We introduce the overhang-removal protocol, derive its all-site and one-site fidelities across output regimes, and show that it is optimal in several regimes, both asymptotically and nonasymptotically. For the asymptotic analysis, we use a path-graph parametrization to show that, when the target eigenvalue has a constant spectral gap $D_{k,\mathrm{min}}$, achieving worst-case all-site error $\varepsilon$ scales as $O(m/(\varepsilon D_{k,\mathrm{min}}^2))$. When $m/n$ approaches a constant, the performance exhibits phase-like regimes, which we characterize explicitly. For the nonasymptotic analysis, we develop a theory of generalized Young diagrams that yields tight sample complexity bounds and provides the first tight dimension-uniform guarantee for optimal QPA. We also provide asymptotically efficient implementations of the overhang-removal protocol. Together, these results establish QPA as a rigorous example of coherent quantum information processing with dimension-uniform sample complexity, supplying the technical foundation for the coherent-incoherent separation developed in the companion work.

title: MoETok: Sparse Expert Routing for 1D Visual Tokenizers
abstract: Modern visual tokenizers aim to preserve fine-grained visual details while learning high-level semantic representations for downstream generation and understanding. Query-based 1D visual tokenizers encode images into flexible latent sequences, yet how individual learnable queries gather and encode image information remains poorly understood. We reveal that these queries spontaneously develop complementary roles under semantic supervision: a small set of Content queries captures high-level semantic information, while a larger set of Detail queries preserves fine-grained visual details for reconstruction. To adapt token processing to these heterogeneous roles, we introduce MoETok, a 1D visual tokenizer that routes tokens through sparsely activated experts. Jointly optimized with reconstruction and semantic objectives, the router learns role-specialized processing paths adapted to each token's representation. Across model scales and token budgets, MoETok consistently improves reconstruction, semantic representation, and autoregressive generation over dense tokenizers under matched supervision and active computation. On ImageNet, it combines strong reconstruction and semantic representation with state-of-the-art class-conditional generation within the 1D tokenizer family. We further validate MoETok at scale in a unified autoregressive model jointly trained for understanding and generation with a next-token cross-entropy objective. The resulting model combines competitive visual understanding with state-of-the-art generation among unified discrete models, matching or surpassing diffusion-based models such as BAGEL and Qwen-Image on benchmarks including DPG-Bench (87.61), GenEval2 (40.04 GM), and WISE (0.49).

title: ID2Pattern: Pretraining Generalizable Identity Behavior Patterns for Transaction Risk Foundation Models
abstract: Large-scale behavioral pretraining offers a promising route to generalizable representations in online payment systems. However, high-cardinality identity fields such as card, device, and account IDs, though rich in behavioral signals, remain underexploited. Their continually growing vocabularies and limited semantic meaning make existing vocabulary-based and semantics-based encodings ill-suited. Their generalizable signal lies not in specific values, but in the identity behavior patterns they exhibit across a transaction sequence. Building on this insight, we propose ID2Pattern, a pretraining framework that brings these patterns into transaction foundation models. ID2Pattern first encodes identity fields with a Local Anonymous ID (LAID) tokenizer, which captures how each identity appears and recurs within the sequence, independent of its specific value. It then pretrains a multi-scale pattern codebook on unlabeled sequences, which abstracts LAID sequences into discrete behavior patterns for downstream prediction. Experiments on an industrial dataset with over 100M sequences and six public datasets show that ID2Pattern consistently outperforms strong baselines, improving industrial by 4.13% and public datasets by 8.83% on average. Notably, ID2Pattern remains equally effective even when all identity values are unseen during training, highlighting its potential to generalize to new users and markets.

title: Semi-asynchronous federated learning in Flower: Framework extension and performance assessment
abstract: This paper presents an extension of the Flower federated learning framework to support Semi-Asynchronous Federated Learning. The proposed approach adapts the traditional synchronous paradigm to better handle client heterogeneity and straggler effects. By introducing a semi-asynchronous training strategy, the system allows partial synchronization among clients while maintaining training efficiency and scalability. We implement and evaluate the proposed modification within Flower, instantiated as the FedSaSync strategy, demonstrating improved robustness and reduced idle time compared to fully synchronous baselines in heterogeneous environments. The results show that SAFL can balance convergence stability and system efficiency in heterogeneous environments typical of edge and distributed learning scenarios.

title: Can Synthetic Data Replace Real Data? Evaluating the Efficacy, Limits, and Label Trustworthiness of Generative Data in Supervised Learning
abstract: Synthetic data are increasingly proposed as substitutes for real training records where privacy restricts data sharing. We evaluate this substitution on a medical appointment no-show dataset of 110,526 records with the Train-Synthetic-Test-Real protocol, five classifiers, six synthetic mixing ratios and nine generation runs of CTGAN, TVAE and a Gaussian copula on this and a second dataset (UCI Adult). Full substitution lowered mean AUC-ROC in every run (by 5.72% to 11.46% across classifiers in the primary run), and mixed training beat training on its real part alone in at most six of 40 paired DeLong comparisons per run (Holm correction) while losing in 6 to 30. We propose Synthetic Label Trustworthiness Estimation (SLTE), an empirical label-consistency check that scores each synthetic label against a model trained on real data, relabels low-confidence samples by nearest-neighbour vote and down-weights uncertain ones. SLTE changed 12.88% of the primary synthetic labels, 94.2% of them from minority to majority class, but a label-permutation null reproduced this asymmetry and the same procedure changed 14.20% of held-out real labels, so the changes reflect disagreement with a real-data model rather than generator errors. In the primary run SLTE improved AUC-ROC significantly only at 80% and 100% synthetic data, recovering 57.8% of Gradient Boosting's loss at full substitution, but it lowered recall for most classifiers, and in other runs it lowered AUC-ROC for Decision Tree, Logistic Regression or Naive Bayes. Synthetic data did not replace real data here; SLTE is a quality-control step for when substitution cannot be avoided.

title: WPM Mathematical Extension: AI-System Prediction and Training Dynamics
abstract: This record contains seven companion mathematical studies in the WPM Mathematical Extension series: an AI-system prediction overview and six scenario-specific studies. The collection comprises: • WPM for AI-System Prediction Overview.• Data-Driven Prediction of AI-Training Structural Transitions.• Data-Driven Prediction of Oscillatory AI-Training Behavior.• Data-Driven Prediction of AI-Training Instability.• Data-Driven Prediction of AI-Training Plateau Transitions.• Data-Driven Prediction of Foreseeable AI-Training Failure.• Data-Driven Prediction of AI Optimization Response. The studies develop target-conditioned forecasting procedures using observed training histories, location and scale features, adaptive temporal resolution, causal risk landscapes and qualified structural descriptors. Topics include cross-temporal displacement, increment-sign reversals, gradient excursions, plateau recognition, first-arrival risk, warning horizons, future optimization response and selective prediction. The forecasting layer is data driven, learning from observed histories and matured outcomes rather than receiving the system’s true governing equation. Explicitly fitted n/s scaling-spectrum descriptors are distinguished from compact observable proxies. Telemetry comparisons are interpreted by target, horizon and metric rather than as a universal performance claim. Definitions, derivations, theorems, proofs, worked mathematical examples and application procedures address uncertainty, calibration, label maturity, censoring and intervention policy. The collection distinguishes structural change from failure, oscillation from periodicity, plateau morphology from successful optimization, and response magnitude from useful training progress. All seven papers share DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23784369 and extend the author’s published WPM architecture and foundational n/s scaling-spectrum framework.

title: FoAViS: Analyzing Learned Fixation Strategies in a Foveated Active Vision System
abstract: Human vision is foveated and active: resolution is highest at the fovea and falls off towards the periphery, and fixations are actively directed to locations of interest. Building a machine system that processes information in the same way lets us study gaze behavior in a controlled setting where the system's components and objectives are known. The emergence of gaze characteristics can therefore be examined systematically, which may in turn inform our understanding of biological vision. This requires a model that can sample like the fovea, handle various tasks from classification to dense prediction, and be trained concurrently with a fixation policy. In our study, we present such a system and study its capabilities and the fixation policies that emerge from it. Our system, FoAViS, samples visual input by adopting the established log-polar foveation and accumulates information in a 2D spatial memory. title: Saffar Kernel Atlas and saffar-kernel Pipeline: Lexical, Grammatical and Phraseological Kernels Across 13 Languages
abstract: saffar-kernel Pipeline This repository accompanies the research paper "How Much of a Language Does a Learner Need? A Thirteen-Language Analysis of the Lexical, Grammatical and Phraseological Kernel of Everyday Speech" by Mohyeddin Saffar. title: Entanglement entropy in two-particle Grover walks on graphs
abstract: Abstract We define a two-particle quantum walk of identical particles on a graph G via the one-particle Grover walk on the Kronecker product G ⊗ G, and call it the two-particle Grover walk. In systems of identical particles, quantum mechanics requires that quantum states have a certain invariance with respect to the exchange of particles. Focusing on the symmetry of the Kronecker product G ⊗ G as a graph, we show that the time evolution operator of this walk commutes with the swap operator, which ensures that this requirement is satisfied. Furthermore, we study the entanglement entropy of quantum states evolved by this walk. For the complete bipartite graph K n,n , we completely determine the values of n for which the quantum states evolved from specific initial states attain the upper bound of the entropy at some time, and prove that they are exactly 1 and 2.

title: New Lower Bounds for Private PAC Learning
abstract: We study realizable PAC learning under approximate differential privacy, and give a framework for proving lower bounds on its sample complexity. We construct classes with identical VC and Littlestone dimensions but different private sample complexities at common privacy and accuracy parameters, showing that these dimensions do not determine the sample complexity, even for improper learners. To address this we introduce the Independent Class Packing (ICP) parameter, the largest total sample complexity of classes in $\mathcal{G}$ that can be packed independently into a class $\mathcal{H}$, and prove that every $(\varepsilon, δ)$-DP, $(α, β)$-PAC learner for $\mathcal{H}$, possibly improper, uses $Ω\left(\mathrm{ICP}(\mathcal{H}, \mathcal{G})/(α\varepsilon)\right)$ examples. Using this framework we prove tight lower bounds for axis-aligned rectangles, union of intervals and linear subspaces and improved lower bounds for halfspaces and convex polygons. Finally we also show that for product classes, and more generally when the same classes pack into $\mathcal{H}$ and cover its domain so that target labels can be used directly, ICP characterizes private PAC sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.

title: Algebraic Symmetry and Stochastic Independence: A Comparative Study of Deterministic, Seeded, and Matrix-based Randomness Extraction on QRNG-Generated Datasets
abstract: Theoretically, Quantum random number generators (QRNGs) can produce truly random numbers that cannot be predicted in advance and have numerous uses. But in practice, it cannot escape the problem of unwanted classical noise, which reduces the quality of the random bits they produce. Therefore, we need to post-process data from a QRNG’s entropy source to improve the statistical quality of the classical output sequence generated from the quantum entropy source. In this work, we implement and compare six extraction primitives: Von Neumann, Multi-level Peres, Toeplitz-hash, Circulant-hash, Trevisan’s construction, and SHA-256 distillation. Using a large classical random bit stream generated by an experimental QRNG, we evaluate these algorithms based on extraction efficiency (η), computational complexity, and seed-entropy requirements. The findings show that although deterministic approaches, such as Multi-level Peres, outperform von Neumann maps, algebraic approaches, especially Circulant extractors, offer higher throughput (η = 0.90) and lower seed consumption by leveraging the cyclicity of the group Zn. The Trevisan extractor provides strong theoretical security with reduced seed growth, but at the cost of higher computational complexity. In contrast, the SHA-256-based method offers fast practical post-processing but provides no information-theoretic entropy guarantees. Statistical validation via autocorrelation and inter-sequence cross-correlation confirms that all evaluated methods successfully decouple hardware-induced dependencies

title: When Does Test-Time Search Help World Action Models? An Empirical Audit of Candidate Selection and Simulator Integrity
abstract: World-action models increasingly apply test-time scaling, spending extra inference computation on candidate selection and adaptive allocation to improve control. Such gains are credible only when candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable. We audit all three on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa with a premise-first, pre-registered methodology. On clean data, a learned value selector is 1.66 pp worse than random; a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 pp, with an episode-level interval spanning zero; and 82% of states show identical candidate outcomes, leaving little selection headroom. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but yields at most a measured 1.15$\times$ end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25$\times$ on a decode-excluded path), short of a 1.5$\times$ target, and our adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive under a power gate. We further identify and fix a silent rendering corruption whose rate rises sharply along compute-heavy planning paths while leaving the official direct-policy result unaffected, and release a detector, fix, and scripts. These findings show why test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises (decision signal, realized efficiency, evaluationintegrity) rather than by success rate alone. Conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration.

title: Just Talk Once: Communication-Efficient Split Federated LLM Fine-Tuning on Edge Devices
abstract: Large language model (LLM) fine-tuning is increasingly shifting toward data generated on edge devices, where memory, computation, bandwidth, and connectivity constraints make conventional federated learning difficult to sustain. Split federated fine-tuning (SFT) improves client-side efficiency by offloading most model parameters and computation to the server but requires step-by-step bidirectional communication loop across the split interface and forces continuous client involvement throughout training. In this paper, we present L-shaped SFT, a split fine-tuning framework that removes this bidirectional bottleneck. Our key insight is that weight tying in modern LLMs enables server-side hidden activations to be directly supervised using target embeddings, allowing the training loss to be computed on the server without returning server outputs to the client. To further eliminate the need for continuous client participation, based on L-shaped SFT, we introduce one-shot SFT, in which clients upload activations once and then go offline while the server continues optimization over cached representations. We implement our design in a real system testbed with heterogeneous edge clients, including commercial smartphones and NVIDIA developer boards. Experiments demonstrate that our schemes significantly reduce communication costs and client online time compared with existing SFT baselines.

title: Mind the Gap: Explicit Cross-Benchmark Calibrations for Estimating Missing LLM Evaluation Scores
abstract: Abstract Most language models are evaluated on only a few benchmarks: in our compilation of 401 models and 146 benchmark versions, the benchmark test coverage is only 8.3% on the most frequently used benchmarks. We present benchgap, a pipeline that estimates the missing scores without running any evaluations. It calibrates each benchmark against each same-capability benchmark on the models measured on both, fitting six monotone curve families and keeping the one with the lowest leave-one-out cross-validated error; multivariate mappings combine several sources. Calibrations never cross capability groups, must rise and never extrapolate beyond one fitted-range width; estimates never feed further estimates, and each carries its own cross-validated error and confidence level. In an end-to-end holdout of 15% of the measured scores, the pipeline fills 71% of the masked cells at 4.6 percentage points (pp) mean absolute error (MAE), 23% lower than a rank-2 matrix-completion baseline on the same cells; on the cells it leaves empty, the baseline's MAE is 11.8 pp. Realized MAE rises with the confidence level (3.1, 5.1 and 7.5 pp from high to low), but the realized root-mean-square error exceeds the claimed error labels, which are selected minima, by a factor of 1.4–1.7. We also quantify the harness tax, the disagreement between evaluation setups: on verified same-item-set pairs it is 8.7 pp on agentic benchmarks against 2.3 pp on tool-free ones, and enabling tools on Humanity's Last Exam raises the scores of all 11 models measured both ways, by 10.0 pp on average. Estimates are updated daily at https://benchgap.net.

title: Sharing of Irreversible Latent Features in lieu of RF IQ Data for Multiple Downstream Learning Tasks
abstract: Wireless in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) data is a valuable resource for training radio-frequency machine-learning models, but sharing raw I/Q samples can create legal risk under the Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA). This constraint motivates the central question of this thesis: can we learn an encoding of the I/Q signal that remains useful for downstream wireless tasks while making the original waveform difficult to reconstruct? To answer this question, this thesis proposes a framework that releases a compact latent representation of the I/Q signal instead of the raw data and adds structured noise before release to impede adversarial reconstruction. The key technical contributions are as follows. First, a shared deterministic encoder is trained jointly on three representative, physically distinct wireless tasks namely, RF transmitter fingerprinting, coarse carrier-frequency-offset (CFO) estimation, and wireless channel estimation using a publicly available ORACLE over-the-air WiFi dataset. In this setting, joint multi-task training improves RF fingerprinting accuracy from 85% (single-task) to 97% (three-task), demonstrating that shared representations benefit all tasks simultaneously. Second, we propose a task-aware anisotropic noise injection mechanism that constructs the noise covariance from the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) of the aggregate task set. Noise variance is allocated inversely to the magnitude of the FIM eigenvalues along each latent direction, reflecting the intuition that task-insensitive directions should receive more noise, whereas task-critical directions should receive less. A single regularization parameter γ continuously tunes the anisotropy, recovering isotropic Gaussian noise as the limiting case. Third, we prove an information-theoretic lower bound on the per-coordinate mean-squared error that any adversarial decoder must incur when attempting to reconstruct the original I/Q signal from the noisy latent representation. Empirically, the proposed anisotropic mechanism achieves a strictly better privacy-utility tradeoff than isotropic noise at the same total power budget. At noise level β = 5, isotropic noise achieves channel estimation utility R² = 0.35; the anisotropic mechanism matches the same privacy level while retaining R² = 0.63. Comparison against two baselines: NeuraCrypt, which uses a frozen random convolutional encoder with per-sample pixel shuffling, and Renyi Differential Privacy (RDP) with Gaussian noise calibrated to match our reconstruction MSE shows that both baselines collapse task utility at the privacy levels required for meaningful reconstruction hardness (NeuraCrypt: RF fingerprinting 8.1%, CFO R² = 0.037, Channel R² = 0.83; RDP: RF 7.3%, CFO R² = -0.14, Channel R² = -0.08$), while the proposed method preserves useful performance across all three tasks (RF 51.9%, CFO R² = 0.31, Channel R² = 0.41).

title: Prune Gradually, Adapt Sparsely: Efficient Pruning of Large Language Models at Extreme Sparsity
abstract: Weight pruning can reduce the storage and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), but preserving quality at high sparsity levels remains challenging. Existing methods face a quality-cost trade-off in this regime. One-shot pruning is cheap but degrades sharply as sparsity increases, even when followed by post-pruning recovery. A growing line of work instead optimizes the mask directly from the dense model under the end-to-end objective; among these methods, [Lee et al.,2026], the recent state of the art at extreme sparsity, reaches high quality but at the cost of model-sized optimizer state and auxiliary variables. To address this gap, we propose ETAPS, which prunes gradually and adapts sparsely: it tightens a global sparsity constraint in progressive stages while training a sparse delta with a small, fixed budget. Our key observation is that gradual weight removal keeps each pruning step small enough for sparse adaptation to compensate, allowing the adapted model to provide end-to-end gradients that guide the next pruning decision without model-sized optimizer state. Across six models from 125M to 13B parameters, ETAPS achieves lower perplexity than ELSA at every evaluated sparsity from 50% to 90%, with perplexity reductions of up to 42%. ETAPS is also far cheaper: at 90% sparsity, it prunes LLaMA2-7B on a single H200, where ELSA uses four, with $5.0\times$ smaller total persistent state and 49% fewer GPU-hours. Together, our findings point to a promising direction for achieving high quality in demanding regimes such as extreme sparsity at substantially lower cost.

title: When Is a Game a Markov Decision Process? Correspondences Between Game Theory and Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning and game theory describe the same object from two sides. Game theory says what a rational outcome of a strategic interaction is; reinforcement learning says how an agent could reach one through experience. The two literatures nevertheless keep separate vocabularies for identical structures, and the treatments that bridge them present the correspondence as analogy rather than theorem. This monograph supplies the theorems. A game is a Markov decision process in three distinct senses, and every table entry is labelled with the one that applies: a definitional identity, an exact reduction carried by a value- and solution-preserving map, or a structural analogy that fails under identifiable conditions. We take every standard class of game, from normal-form through repeated, stochastic, partially observable, extensive-form with imperfect information, Bayesian, graphical, Stackelberg, potential, coalitional, mean-field and evolutionary games, and identify for each the decision-theoretic model that reinforcement learning already studies under another name. The same treatment is applied to solution concepts: Nash equilibrium and the fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator, quantal response equilibrium and the soft Bellman operator, the Shapley value and credit assignment, Blackwell approachability and no-regret learning. We map each model class onto the training procedures sound for it and record the complexity of the associated solution problems. A final part collects the correspondences that do not hold: the non-stationarity that invalidates the independent-learner reduction, the impossibility results that forbid uncoupled convergence to Nash equilibrium, and the gap between the coarse correlated equilibria that no-regret self-play reaches and the correlated equilibria it is credited with.

A final part collects the correspondences that do not hold: the non-stationarity that invalidates the independent-learner reduction, the impossibility results that forbid uncoupled convergence to Nash equilibrium, and the gap between the coarse correlated equilibria that no-regret self-play reaches and the correlated equilibria it is credited with.

title: maharataylor92-source/quantum-teleportation-benchmark: v1.0.0 — Six-state teleportation benchmark on IBM hardware
abstract: Initial public release of the six-state quantum teleportation benchmark on real IBM Quantum hardware. Devices and headline results (October 2026): ibm_fez — teleportation mean fidelity 0.9008 (two runs); bare control 0.9733 ibm_kingston — full six-state tomography, mean fidelity 0.9606 ibm_phoenix (120-qubit Nighthawk) — teleportation mean fidelity 0.9583; bare control 0.9950 Both error budgets are closed: the teleportation machinery costs ~7.2 fidelity points on ibm_fez and ~3.7 points on ibm_phoenix. The ±i states are perfect in the bare control yet lowest in teleportation, consistent with dephasing during the measurement-and-correction window. Contents: RESULTS.md (full write-up), data/ (7 result files), notebooks/ (both hardware notebooks), LICENSE (MIT for code, CC BY 4.0 for data).

title: Robust Learning of Multi-Index Models under Logconcave Distributions via Weak Partial Learners
abstract: We develop a new algorithmic framework for learning Boolean concept classes under logconcave distributions. Our framework applies to broad families of multi-index models and yields significantly faster robust learners than were previously known in these settings. It extends to partial classification and testable learning. Consequently, we obtain improved learners for several fundamental concept classes, including functions of halfspaces and multiclass linear classifiers, under logconcave marginals. Our starting point is a new boosting framework based on weak partial learners. Classical boosting approaches require often-intractable distribution-free weak learners or yield weak approximation guarantees. We show instead that weak learners for partial classification, where labels may be undefined on part of the domain, suffice for strong agnostic learning. The key challenge is that boosting requires a weak learner that succeeds under conditioned distributions that are not guaranteed to be logconcave. To address this, we develop a recursive moment-based partitioning procedure: given a logconcave distribution $X$ and a conditional version $X'$, we partition the space into polynomially many convex regions so that, on most regions, the low-degree moments of $X$ and $X'$ approximately agree. On each good region, a well-behaved multi-index model correlates with a low-degree polynomial, giving a weak hypothesis. Combining these hypotheses yields the required weak learner. A key ingredient of our approach is an efficient method for detecting moment discrepancy. Specifically, we show how to find a low-dimensional subspace that captures any non-trivial discrepancy between $X$ and $X'$, if one exists. Our approach combines spectral analysis of moment tensors with recent progress on isoperimetry for logconcave measures. This discrepancy-finding procedure may be of independent interest.

title: Sentiment Analysis of TikTok User Reviews on the Google Play Store Using the Naïve Bayes Classifier Method
abstract: The high volume of reviews provided by TikTok users on the Google Play Store platform has resulted in a large amount of unstructured opinion data. This study analyzed user sentiment to provide developers with insights into user satisfaction levels and common application complaints. The method implemented in this research was the Multinomial Naïve Bayes classifier. The dataset consisted of 860 application reviews collected over a two-year period, from 2023 to 2024. All data were processed through a comprehensive series of text mining stages using the Python programming language, which included text preprocessing (case folding, cleaning, tokenizing, filtering, and stemming) and feature weighting via Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF). The test results demonstrated that the proposed model successfully classified sentiments into positive, negative, and neutral categories with an overall accuracy level of 79%. Specifically, the model achieved its optimal performance in the positive sentiment category with an f1-score of 0.86. These findings indicate that the Naïve Bayes method has reliable capability in processing social media reviews for continuous application quality improvement.

title: WASABI: Wasserstein Sampling via Bridge Interpolants
abstract: Sampling from Boltzmann distributions is a fundamental problem in physics, chemistry, and biology. We introduce WAsserstein SAmpling via Bridge Interpolants (WASABI), a method that trains a diffusion model to generate samples from a target Boltzmann distribution given access only to the energy function. WASABI minimizes the KL divergence between the distribution generated by its diffusion model and the Boltzmann target using Wasserstein gradient flows. This approach builds on a principle underlying classical sampling methods such as Langevin dynamics. However, applying Wasserstein gradient flows to diffusion models is challenging because the updates require the gradient of the model's own log density, which is generally intractable. We derive a practical training algorithm that avoids computing this gradient. Once trained, WASABI can generate new samples without further evaluations of the energy or its gradient. On alanine dipeptide, WASABI outperforms the best reported baselines using an estimated 3.3 times fewer energy evaluations. It also achieves competitive performance on interacting particle system benchmarks.

title: Correlation bit acquisition: constructed inputs and verification results
abstract: Version 1.0.0 contains 20 rational coefficient records, 22 JSON numerical reports and acquisition traces, and 15 generated bit-plane input files. Coverage includes determinant and Schur comparisons, fixed-order integer constructions, exact moment states, threshold-margin checks, corner certificates, and the three-column stopping construction. The data contain no human observations or third-party research dataset. Extract alongside the matching software archive and follow the README to reproduce all 37 result files byte for byte. The data are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Finite completion checks have the scope stated in each report; interval certificates cover their specified boxes.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Marketing
abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most influential technologies shaping modern marketing. The rapid growth of digital platforms, customer data, and automated technologies has changed how businesses understand consumers, communicate with audiences, and measure marketing performance. AI enables organizations to analyse large datasets, predict consumer behaviour, personalize communication, automate routine tasks, and generate content. This research paper examines the role of AI in marketing, its major applications, benefits, challenges, ethical concerns, and future implications. The paper argues that AI can significantly improve marketing effectiveness when combined with human creativity, strategic judgment, and responsible data practices. At the same time, concerns regarding privacy, algorithmic bias, misinformation, transparency, and employment demonstrate the need for careful and ethical implementation. The future of marketing is therefore likely to depend on a collaborative relationship between human marketers and intelligent technologies.

title: Chronos-2: A foundation model for multivariate time series forecasting
abstract: Accurate forecasting with uncertainty quantification is critical in a variety of scientific applications ranging from epidemiology and economics to energy systems and earth sciences. Yet most forecasting models still need to be developed and trained separately for each domain-specific dataset. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) aim to remove this limitation and enable the application of the same model across domains through large-scale pretraining. However, most existing TSFMs treat each time series independently and therefore cannot model interactions among time series and external drivers. Here, we introduce Chronos-2, a foundation model for zero-shot forecasting that models the interactions between multivariate time series and heterogeneous covariates, which commonly arise in scientific applications. The model infers relationships among time series directly from historical context and generates probabilistic forecasts without task-specific treatment. Across various benchmarks, Chronos-2 achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on average by improving skill scores by 5.2 percentage points relative to the strongest baselines and increasing win rates by 10 percentage points. Chronos-2 is also computationally efficient, generating forecasts for 100 time series in under one second on a single mid-range GPU, 50x and 1000x faster end-to-end than the best task-specific point and probabilistic forecasters, respectively. In addition, we demonstrate its effectiveness in diverse scientific settings -- including infectious-disease forecasting, macroeconomic modeling, carbon-flux prediction, and runoff simulation -- where the model matches or surpasses specialized methods developed for each domain. These results show that a single pretrained model can capture structure shared across temporal systems.

title: Semantic Ethical Glass Box
abstract: GET /query now runs on a read-only Virtuoso account, the Virtuoso SQL port is no longer published by default, and all open Dependabot alerts are cleared. The backend image moves to Python 3.12. Tags 1.0.1 to 1.2.0 are unchanged. Security GET /query runs on a second Virtuoso session authenticated as a dedicated account (VIRTUOSO_READER_USER) that holds only SPARQL_SELECT and read access to the events graph. Writes, audit reads and deletion keep the existing account. The lexical filter and the dataset pin from 1.2.0 stay; the account is the barrier behind them (#27, #35). The backend refuses to start without verified reader credentials and never retries a user query with the writer account. The SQL privileges the reader can hold are checked against a reviewed manifest (apps/backend/virtuoso/reader-sql-policy.manifest): provisioning fails on any difference, and the backend rechecks the live listing at startup and every VIRTUOSO_READER_POLICY_RECHECK_SECONDS (default 30), dropping the reader session on drift (#27, #35). The Virtuoso image is pinned by digest in both Compose files and in the integration harness, so a moving tag cannot change the reader policy; the docs explain how to regenerate and review the manifest when updating the image (#33, #38). Port 1111 (Virtuoso native SQL) is no longer published to the host by default. It stays reachable on the internal Compose network and from inside the container (#32, #39). Dependencies updated to clear every open Dependabot alert (155 at the time): fastapi 0.162.0 (starlette 1.x), uvicorn 0.54.0, pyjwt 2.15.1, requests 2.34.2, PyYAML 6.0.3, python-multipart, anyio, h11, certifi, idna, urllib3, dnspython and others in the backend; the semantic_log_generator lockfile; and the segb-ui lockfile (vitest 4.x) (#42, #43, #44). Changed The backend image is built on python:3.12-slim-bookworm and the backend now requires Python 3.11 or newer (requires-python >=3.11,<3.13), because the dnspython fix needs it. The semantic_log_generator package still supports Python 3.10 to 3.12 (#42). .zenodo.json keeps the creators, the contact person and the community on Zenodo releases (#36, #37). Documentation Guidance to publish small, per-event logs instead of whole sessions: a single INSERT DATA of about 5,000 triples or more fails in the pinned Virtuoso 7.2.16, with or without more memory, and the API does not enforce a triple limit (#24, #40). The residual risk of native SQL access and of the built-in routines the reader can still call is documented, with a real-Virtuoso characterization test: the reader can invoke SPARQL_REXEC_TO_ARRAY and read what a remote endpoint's identity can read. Treat the reader credentials as internal to the backend (#34, #41). Upgrading from 1.2.x Set VIRTUOSO_READER_PASSWORD in .env (required, different from VIRTUOSO_PASSWORD; VIRTUOSO_READER_USER defaults to segb_reader). The new segb-query-reader-init service provisions the account before the backend starts. Setting up an external Virtuoso is described in docs/operations/centralized-deployment.md. If something outside Compose connected to the host port 1111, publish it explicitly or run isql from the container. Set VERSION=1.3.0 in your environment file (or remove the line). Compose passes VERSION to the backend explicitly, so a file copied from the 1.2.0 example keeps announcing 1.2.0 in /health and OpenAPI even when the 1.3.0 image runs. The backend now requires Python 3.11+ when run from source. Known limitations Uploads of about 5,000 triples or more in one request can still fail in Virtuoso 7.2.16 (#24 documents the guidance but does not change the behaviour). With the reader's credentials, native SQL can read audit rows; keep them inside the backend. The reader policy is tied to the pinned image build and fails closed on a different one until the manifest is reviewed and regenerated. Blank nodes are duplicated on re-upload; use URIs. Images: ghcr.io/gsi-upm/semantic_ethical_glass_box/segb and .../segb-ui, tags 1.3.0, latest and stable (also gsi-upm/segb:1.3.0 and gsi-upm/segb-ui; gsi-upm/segb:latest stays on 0.4.11).

title: Shock Loading Accesses Reaction Pathways beyond Accelerated Thermolysis
abstract: Thermolysis and shock loading can produce similar major stable products in energetic materials, despite different chemical evolution and reaction pathways. Here, we develop EMFF-MACE, a reactive machine-learning potential for C/H/N/O energetic materials, enabling thermolysis simulations of 20 materials and shock simulations of 10 on a common potential energy surface. Comparisons at matched normalized reaction progress reveal divergent chemical states and local structural environments. Mean reaction-state similarity decreases from 94.0% at 20% progress to 25.9% at trajectory endpoints, while 47.1-92.6% of shock local environments lie outside corresponding material-specific thermolysis reference domains. Structural and reaction-network analyses reveal enhanced intermolecular reorganization and additional association and rearrangement branches under shock loading, despite partially shared early decomposition chemistry. These findings show that loading history influences the structural states and subsequent reaction pathways accessed during decomposition, rather than merely the rate of thermolysis.

title: Perbandingan Kinerja Algoritma Naive Bayes dan Logistic Regression Berbasis TF-IDF dalam Klasifikasi Sentimen Komentar YouTube terhadap Layanan Digital Kampus: Performance Comparison of Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression Based on TF-IDF for Sentiment Classification of YouTube Comments on Campus Digital Services
abstract: Layanan digital kampus, seperti sistem informasi akademik, penerimaan mahasiswa baru online, e-learning, learning management system, dan administrasi akademik online, memunculkan beragam tanggapan dari pengguna di media sosial. Komentar YouTube menjadi sumber umpan balik yang penting, tetapi data yang besar, informal, dan tidak terstruktur membuat analisis manual kurang efisien. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengevaluasi kinerja algoritma Naive Bayes dan Logistic Regression berbasis Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) dalam mengklasifikasikan sentimen pada komentar YouTube terkait layanan digital kampus. Data penelitian terdiri atas 7.322 komentar yang dikumpulkan menggunakan kata kunci terkait sistem akademik online, LMS kampus, perkuliahan online, pendaftaran mahasiswa baru online, dan layanan digital kampus. Tahapan penelitian meliputi crawling data, preprocessing, pelabelan sentimen, ekstraksi fitur TF-IDF, pelatihan model dengan dan tanpa Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE), serta evaluasi menggunakan accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, dan confusion matrix. Hasil menunjukkan 3.181 komentar positif (43,4%), 2.350 negatif (32,1%), dan 1.791 netral (24,5%). Logistic Regression tanpa SMOTE menghasilkan kinerja terbaik dengan accuracy 81,57%, precision 80,77%, recall 80,59%, dan F1-score 80,67%. Temuan ini menunjukkan bahwa Logistic Regression lebih stabil dibandingkan dengan Naive Bayes dalam klasifikasi sentimen komentar YouTube berbahasa Indonesia mengenai layanan digital kampus.

title: A Context-Free Framework for Evaluating Morphological Generalization in Lexical POS Classification
abstract: Part-of-speech (POS) classification typically uses sentence context, making it difficult to isolate grammatical information available from lexical form alone. This study evaluates context-free lexical POS classification and morphological generalization using 370,100 English word types annotated with Penn Treebank-style POS labels. A majority-class baseline and four morphology-sensitive approaches—rule-based suffix, statistical suffix, character n-gram, and character-level BiLSTM models—were evaluated on coarse- and fine-grained classification tasks. Morphological transfer was examined separately through suffix hold-out experiments in which selected suffix families were excluded from training. Under standard stratified evaluation, the BiLSTM achieved the highest Macro-F1 in both coarse-grained (0.8323) and fine-grained (0.8412) classification. Strong performance under standard lexical classification therefore did not necessarily correspond to transfer to unseen morphological families. Morphological generalization should be evaluated separately from standard classification and interpreted in relation to the grammatical composition of the held-out family.
