title: Aligning MLLMs with the Latent Structure of Human Cognition via Behavior-Derived Semantic Dimensions
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. We build on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out (O1O) judgements. For each triplet, we infer the most salient decision dimension and convert it into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. This enables MLLMs to learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with the inferred behavioral criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves model consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Furthermore, using searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we observe increased representational alignment between model and human. Ultimately, our findings point to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLMs alignment. The code is available \href{https://github.com/ening-open/cogalign}{here}.

title: A symmetry breaking swarm optimizer derived from the Landau theory of phase transitions
abstract: Metaheuristic optimization algorithms are widely used for high-dimensional non-convex problems, yet most are designed by analogy with biological or physical processes and govern their exploration–exploitation balance with heuristic schedules that lack an underlying theory. We introduce Symmetry-Breaking Swarm Optimization (SBSO), in which this balance is not a tuned schedule but a second-order phase transition derived from the Landau-Ginzburg free energy. Each agent carries a component of an order-parameter field that relaxes along the free-energy gradient while a computational temperature is lowered through the critical point; the field then breaks symmetry spontaneously, and the local order parameter schedules the search operator of every agent. A vector generalization with one field component per coordinate searches heterogeneous problems with coordinate-wise adaptive intensity and reduces exactly to the scalar algorithm when the differentiation strength vanishes. Against eleven optimizers from four families under one evaluation budget, SBSO ranks fourth of twelve on a classical suite, where separable unimodal problems favour methods that collapse the population onto a point, and second of twelve on five shifted and rotated IEEE CEC blocks, where it is consistently the runner-up. Controlled ablations attribute the benefit to the phase transition itself rather than to any individual search operator.

title: Optimizing Stochastic Policy Geometry for Few-Step Flow Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Few-step flow models generate samples through a handful of large denoising transitions. Applying GRPO to such models requires introducing stochasticity into the denoising transitions, and when a single transition spans a wide range of noise levels, the choice of the resulting stochastic policy becomes a major factor in optimization. Recent constructions constrain the policy to preserve the target flow coefficients, but this constraint admits a family of policies and offers no criterion for choosing among them. We introduce Geo-FSRL (Geometry-Optimized Few-Step Reinforcement Learning), built on a selection principle: at a fixed conditioning state and timestep pair, choose the admissible policy that minimizes the conditional KL divergence induced by any given nonzero velocity-output update. Within a coefficient-preserving family of isotropic Gaussian transitions, this criterion reduces to minimizing a single scalar geometry factor that determines the conditional KL for every velocity-output update. The same factor governs velocity-space Fisher information and conditional transition log-likelihood-ratio variance. We derive the unique closed-form optimizer within this family, shared across all nonzero update magnitudes and directions, with transition coefficients determined by both the source and target noise levels. Because the minimized geometry factor still varies across timesteps, we further adopt gradient-scale matching from prior work and derive closed-form policy-gradient and KL weights that normalize explicit score scales and reference-KL curvature. Geo-FSRL trains on the original few-step schedule and retains the deterministic solver at inference. Our method achieves higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS on both image generation and video generation models under the 4-step setting. Code is available at https://github.com/ModelTC/LightX2V/tree/main/lightx2v_rl

title: Empowering Physical Education Teachers: AI-Driven Personalized Learning in Schools
abstract: Despite the health benefits of early physical activity, Italian adolescents face high inactivity and sports dropout. School Physical Education (PE) must counter this by shifting from technical performance toward a sustainable, oblique, and inclusive approach that prioritizes long-term adherence, enjoyment, and intrinsic motivation. Designing personalized learning pathways requires solid instructional frameworks like Universal Design for Learning (UDL), which creates individualized, differentiated environments for everyone without discriminatory distinctions, emphasizing the role of emotions in motivation and educational equity. Parallelly, Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) helps the PET identify the gap between a student's actual developmental level and their potential level when guided. Within this framework, an oblique teaching approach allows students to work at their own competence level within the same activity, ensuring they experience success and avoiding both the boredom of simple drills and the frustration of tasks far above their competence. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 426-427. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Kinesiology and sport between education and performance in European area.

title: Federated attention-driven client selection and aggregation for privacy-preserving human activity recognition
abstract: Abstract Human Behavioral Context Recognition (HBCR) aims to identify user activities in real-world environments and has critical applications in assistive living, healthcare, and industrial automation. A major challenge in this field is achieving high model performance while ensuring user privacy, which is difficult for traditional centralized systems. Federated Learning (FL) addresses this by enabling decentralized model training directly on user devices. However, its success depends heavily on effective client selection and aggregation strategies. In this paper, we propose FAAM (Federated Averaging with Attention Mechanism), a novel framework that enhances FL by identifying and prioritizing the most relevant clients during each communication round using an attention-based approach. FAAM optimizes client selection and communication efficiency, resulting in faster convergence, reduced communication overhead, and equivalent model accuracy. We evaluate FAAM on four newly collected Human Activity Recognition (HAR) datasets, demonstrating that it outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in convergence speed and accuracy. Our results show that FAAM achieves optimal performance with fewer clients and communication rounds, making it an efficient and privacy-preserving solution for real-time HBCR systems.

title: Sensorium: An Open-Source Multimodal Data Collection and Curation Library for Embodied Surgical AI
abstract: Embodied surgical AI requires reliable multimodal data, yet surgical data collection remains costly, difficult to repeat, and strongly dependent on the hardware setup. We present Sensorium, an open-source Python library for recording, processing, annotating, and curating multimodal surgical data from configurable robot and sensor streams using the Robot Operating System (ROS) and ROS2 middleware. The library combines operator-facing data acquisition, configurable processing, semantic annotation, and episodic dataset generation. We evaluate Sensorium across 1516 recordings of phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo porcine experiments involving multiple surgical tasks and sensing configurations, and report preliminary usability feedback.

title: Observable-Specific Validity Tests for Scientific AI: Controlled Approximations and Intervention Response
abstract: An approximation can reproduce an energy while missing its response, or satisfy an error tolerance without being certified by a given bound. We formulate observable-specific validity records for scientific artificial intelligence (AI) that link a reduction to its reference model, error measure, tolerance, parameter domain, and transformations or interventions. Explicit displacement and velocity certificates for a singularly perturbed oscillator recover distinct convergence orders and provide sufficient validity guarantees. Exact Hubbard dimer relations resolve the different coupling domains accepted by energy and response criteria. Across 16 repeated neural fits, imposing dimensional homogeneity reduces energy scale transfer error from 52.3% to 0.0768% and raises the median fraction jointly satisfying gap and response tolerances from zero to 100%. Paired transformations verify the protected scaling relation, while a coupling crossover identifies the additional information needed for response transfer. A causal model recovers a positive intervention response beneath a strong negative observational association. For two mechanisms observed with Gaussian noise whose responses first differ at order $x^k$, we derive an exact fixed control query requirement scaling as $x^{-2k}$ and verify its full success curve numerically. Together with a 256-task evaluation interface, these results provide independently checkable tests of controlled approximation, physical transfer, and mechanism discrimination in scientific AI.

title: Nonlocality as a benchmarking tool for quantum processors
abstract: Abstract Benchmarking quantum processors is a central task in every roadmap aimed at quantum advantage. Here, we discuss a benchmarking protocol based on the violation of the Svetlichny inequality, which is designed to simulate genuine multipartite nonlocality. We compare it with Mermin’s inequality, and present the results of applying this framework to two different quantum processing units—the superconducting system Garnet (from IQM) and the ion-trap system Marmot (from AQT), testing different families of quantum circuits for three to five qubits under identical experimental conditions. We also run simultaneous triplet tests across the full register, including a comparison between GHZ and linear cluster states, to probe how Svetlichny-inequality violations depend on qubit location and calibration. Our results demonstrate that tests based on genuine multipartite nonlocality provide a powerful tool to characterize the collective performance of quantum devices and to guide their calibration and optimization.

title: Advanced RNN-Based Model Variants for Short-Term Solar Power Forecasting
abstract: Many existing solar power forecasting studies still focus on a single, fixed forecasting resolution, with limited investigation into how model performance changes when temporal data are aggregated to coarser time scales and formulated as single-step predictions, or how related Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) architectures compare across multiple short-term forecasting intervals. Therefore, this study is conducted to evaluate the performance of four advanced RNN architectures including GRU, BiGRU, LSTM, and BiLSTM, for short-term solar power forecasting using a single-step forecasting formulation across multiple temporally aggregated time resolutions: 5, 15, 30, and 60 minutes. The results demonstrated that all RNN-based models achieved reasonable accuracy in short-term prediction, with BiGRU consistently outperforming the others at most intervals. Notably, for the 5-minute resolution, BiGRU achieved an R² of approximately 0.94 and a NMAPE of just 3.41%, confirming its adaptability and precision. Its performance remained strong for 15- and 30-minute forecasts; although a gradual decline was observed as the temporal resolution became coarser. At the 1-hour mark, BiLSTM outperformed BiGRU slightly, achieving R² = 0.85 and NMAPE = 7.01%, indicating its better ability to model long-term dependencies in aggregated solar power data. These findings not only extend the practical applications of bidirectional RNNs in renewable energy forecasting but also provide a solid foundation for developing more intelligent and efficient power scheduling systems.

title: Binary Sparse Codes: Where are we on Energy Efficient Representations?
abstract: Biological neural systems achieve impressive computational capabilities under tight metabolic constraints, relying on sparse cortical representations that minimise total neural activity. This combination of efficiency and representational power has motivated growing interest in sparse coding as a computational strategy for artificial systems. Artificial models designed to produce binary sparse codes span three broad paradigms, theoretical methods grounded in efficient coding, deep learning methods trained via backpropagation, and biologically plausible methods that learn through local Hebbian rules, each yielding codes whose quality depends not only on achieving low activation density but also on preserving the informational structure of the input. The latter property, however, lacks an agreed-upon quantitative definition, leaving the field without a principled basis for comparing methods. We propose a set of metrics that formalise information preservation as similarity preservation, measuring how faithfully a binary sparse code reproduces the relational geometry of the input space, and apply this framework to compare four representative methods under matched conditions. The results reveal a consistent trade-off in which models that achieve high information preservation do so at the cost of sparsity, while models approaching the uniformity of an optimal random sparse code tend to sacrifice it. Competitive Sparse Codes, a biologically plausible approach, is the only architecture to occupy a region of near-maximal sparsity while retaining meaningful information preservation. These findings frame the simultaneous satisfaction of both factors as an open challenge for the field and provide a reusable evaluation framework for measuring progress toward it.

title: An interpretable deep learning method for early hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosis on multiphase CT
abstract: Abstract Early diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma is critical to preserve access to curative treatment options. The Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) provides a standardized framework for non-invasive diagnosis on multiphase computed tomography, based on major visual imaging features. However, these features may be difficult to assess consistently, particularly in small liver lesions. We developed dLI-RADS, an interpretable artificial intelligence method designed to estimate the probability of hepatocellular carcinoma from multiphase computed tomography images of manually segmented liver lesions, while remaining aligned with LI-RADS-related imaging concepts. dLI-RADS combines neural network-derived predictions with handcrafted quantitative imaging measurements reflecting LI-RADS major features and integrates these inputs using logistic regression. In this multicenter retrospective study, patients with multiphase computed tomography and at least one liver lesion were included, while lesions larger than 40 mm were excluded. Histology served as the reference standard for hepatocellular carcinoma, and a composite reference standard was used for non-hepatocellular carcinoma lesions. The lesion-level accuracy of dLI-RADS and LI-RADS were compared on the internal evaluation set using 10,000-repetition bootstrap non-inferiority tests, with 5% margins and significance levels. On the external test set, sensitivities were similarly compared. A total of 143 (61 years ± 9, 125 men), 62 (61y ± 10, 49 men), and 133 (59y ± 10, 103 men) patients with 196, 84, and 171 lesions (mean diameter 17.7, 18.3, and 21.8 millimeters) were respectively included in the training, internal and external evaluation sets. dLI-RADS was non-inferior to LI-RADS for lesion-level accuracy in the internal evaluation set, achieving 80% accuracy compared with 74% for LI-RADS ( p = 0.04). On the external evaluation set, dLI-RADS achieved a sensitivity of 93% compared with 78% for LI-RADS (non-inferiority p < 0.001). On this same set, dLI-RADS also achieved 74% specificity, 86% accuracy, and an AUC of 84%. Because LI-RADS features were unavailable for non-HCC lesions, only sensitivity could be directly compared between dLI-RADS and LI-RADS. These findings suggest that dLI-RADS may provide interpretable decision support for hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosis on multiphase computed tomography, particularly for small liver lesions.

title: Automating FoodEx2 coding with FoodEx2 Encoder
abstract: Turning a food description into the equivalent FoodEx2 code has so far been a job for a person working with a tool, in several manual steps. FoodEx2 Encoder, a new tool I developed, uses a large language model to remove those steps: it takes an English food description and returns a complete FoodEx2 code, with a base term, facet descriptors, and labelled free text for whatever the catalogue cannot express. The model only compares the description with catalogue terms; what the resulting code means is defined by the catalogue, not by the model. The encoder is open source (MIT) and also available as a paid hosted service that plugs into AI chat tools through MCP. This article describes why it was built, how an encoding works, how to judge a result, and what the encoder cannot do yet.

title: Variance Reduction for Decentralized Stochastic Optimization with Multiple Local Updates
abstract: Multiple local updates are widely used in decentralized optimization to enhance communication efficiency, often in conjunction with stochastic gradients when exact gradient computation is costly. However, such algorithms generally converge only to a neighborhood of the optimum, whose size depends on the stepsize and the variance of gradient noise. Variance reduction has been incorporated into ADMM-based methods to achieve exact convergence in expectation, but their stepsizes typically scale inversely with both the square root of the network size and the cube of the number of local updates, leading to slow convergence as the network size or the number of local updates increases. In this paper, we propose a novel primal-dual-based decentralized optimization algorithm that integrates variance reduction with multiple local updates, with a stepsize independent of the network size and inversely proportional to the number of local updates (rather than its cube), thereby enabling significantly larger stepsizes and faster convergence. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, we establish the first linear convergence guarantee in expectation for decentralized optimization with multiple local updates under stochastic gradients in the strongly convex setting. Beyond the theoretical guarantee, the proposed method exchanges only one variable per round, halving the communication cost compared with gradient-tracking-based methods. Numerical experiments further demonstrate its advantages in convergence speed and accuracy.

title: Pizza FM with full expressiveness for SMT analysis
abstract: This feature model presents a comprehensive pizza Software Product Line (SPL) designed to showcase the full expressiveness of UVL. It is specifically structured for analysis using SMT solvers (such as Z3). The model contains 15 features in total, including 2 typed features (Integer, String) and 2 feature attributes (Price, Kcal); and 7 cross-tree constraints combining propositional, arithmetic, and aggregation logic over typed features and attributes. The model has 105 satisfiable configurations (228 when considering only the Boolean projection); 6 core features (SpicyLvl, Pizza, Topping, Size, Normal, Dough), 2 dead features (Name, Big), and 2 false-optional features (SpicyLvl, Normal).

title: IGDA-ICMH: an Importance Guided Feature and Network Dual Adaptation Framework towards Image Compression for Machine and Human Vision
abstract: With the surge of machine vision applications, image compression for both machine and human vision (ICMH) has become an important research area. Existing studies mainly focus on task-specific adaptation or multi-task joint optimization, yet they often overlook the unequal contributions of different features and network layers to downstream machine vision tasks. To address this issue, we first quantitatively investigate the impact of different feature and network layers on machine vision performance, providing a principled understanding of their importance. Based on this analysis, an Importance Guided feature and network Dual Adaptation (IGDA) framework is developed for ICMH. It adopts implicit neural representation as the basic architecture and designs an efficient adaptation structure with both feature and network weight adaptation. An Importance-Guided Network Adaptation (IGNA) module is developed with a low-rank adaptation strategy to selectively adjust key network layers according to their importance in different tasks. An Importance-Guided Feature Adaptation (IGFA) module is developed with a low-rank and Kronecker product-based transform to explore the non-local property of the features in order to reduce the number of adaptation parameters. Extensive experiments on representative machine vision tasks, including image classification and object detection, demonstrate that our IGDA-ICMH framework achieves significantly better performance than the existing implicit neural representation-based methods for ICMH.

title: Perspectives on Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computing: Integer Factoring, Discrete Logarithm Problems
abstract: We present our perspectives on the current status of, integer factoring and discrete logarithm, algorithms underlying the strength of classical public-key cryptography protocols used in key-exchange, encryption and digital signatures. We present an expository overview of the algebraic, number-theoretic and algorithmic principles behind the canonical, powerful algorithms used in the factoring of large, composite RSA modulii. These cover the two main ideas of group order based methods, and quadratic congruence based methods. We provide the resource estimates for the record breaking factoring based on the general number field sieve. Next we present an overview of the algorithmic theory of quantum computation behind, the polynomial time Shor's quantum algorithm for, period finding in hidden subgroup structure problems. This algorithm has played a key role in advancing post-quantum cryptography, and also in the exciting, contemporary developments in quantum computing, networking, sensing, and materials science as a whole. Latest advances in quantum computing rest on a variety of physics, engineering, algorithms, compilation, hardware, software techniques. There are several tradeoffs based on number of qubits, coherence times, control issues, errors and fault tolerance. In this environment, nuances of mathematical ideas, behind every step of the intricate arithmetical and algebraic computations under quantum models plays a significant role. We provide an overview of some of the recent ideas behind such algorithms. We conclude with a recent deep question on the ultimate feasibility of ultra large-scale, error-free, discrete, quantum computations required typically in cryptanalysis.

title: Design Consideration for Field-Loadable Software of Civil Aircraft
abstract: With the increasingly widespread application of airborne software in civil aircraft and the continuous growth of its functional complexity, the frequency of software modifications has risen significantly. The traditional factory-return loading mode leads to high operating costs and long maintenance cycles. Focusing on the design of field-loadable software for civil aircraft, this paper proposes a decision-making strategy for determining whether airborne software should be designed as field-loadable software. This strategy classifies airborne software into three categories, platform basic software, functional software, and database software. It puts forward the design principle that field-loadable design is mandatory for database software, preferred for functional software, and not mandatory for platform basic software. In addition, a multi-dimensional design deviation assessment model is constructed for software that cannot meet the above requirements. Functional software that is not designed as field-loadable and has not yet been installed on aircraft shall be evaluated from five dimensions: interconnection complexity, software characteristics, airline operation, commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) attributes, and competitor aircraft models. For functional software that is not designed as field-loadable but has already been installed on aircraft, three additional evaluation dimensions shall be included: the possibility of software modification, difficulty of optimization, and cost of optimization. The research provides a systematic reference for the design decision-making, airworthiness compliance and efficient delivery of civil aircraft field-loadable software, helping to shorten aircraft downtime and reduce airline operation costs.

evidence.title: Design Consideration for Field-Loadable Software of Civil Aircraft
evidence.abstract: With the increasingly widespread application of airborne software in civil aircraft and the continuous growth of its functional complexity, the frequency of software modifications has risen significantly. The traditional factory-return loading mode leads to high operating costs and long maintenance cycles. Focusing on the design of field-loadable software for civil aircraft, this paper proposes a decision-making strategy for determining whether airborne software should be designed as field-loadable software. This strategy classifies airborne software into three categories, platform basic software, functional software, and database software. It puts forward the design principle that field-loadable design is mandatory for database software, preferred for functional software, and not mandatory for platform basic software. In addition, a multi-dimensional design deviation assessment model is constructed for software that cannot meet the above requirements. title: Structure-Aware Skill Retrieval and Arbitration for Optimization Modeling
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can turn natural-language optimization tasks into solver-checked answers, but current agents remain brittle under narrative rewrites and often store reusable experience at the instance level. We introduce \textsc{ArchOR}, an archetype-centric skill agent that builds on \textsc{OptSkills} by adding two retrieval-focused modules. \emph{Centroid-Aware Representation Learning} (CARL) refines the ordering of cached skill representations through a low-rank prototype residual. \emph{Signature-Guided Retrieval} (S\textsuperscript{3}R) attaches open-dimensional structural signatures to skills, prioritizes candidates by weighted Jaccard overlap, and bounds semantic re-ranking to a top-$K$ set. A baseline-preserving arbitration rule determines when the structural route should replace the original selector. With the same DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone and released skill library, \textsc{ArchOR} reaches 65.00\% Micro-Avg.\ Pass@1 across five benchmarks, improving over \textsc{OptSkills} by 1.64~pp Micro-Avg.\ and 2.68~pp Macro-Avg.

title: Actor-Oriented Models: Fundamentals
abstract: The stochastic actor-oriented model is a statistical model for network dynamics, meant to be used for network panel data, that is, repeated measurements of a network on a given set of actors. This chapter gives an introduction to the probability model, in three flavors: a short intuitive explanation, a long conceptual one, and a mathematical explanation. These alternative, complementary formulations cater to readers with different interests, backgrounds, and preferences. The model assumes that between the moments of measurement, the network changes gradually in unobserved small steps. The heart of the model is the ministep , playing a basic role together with the evaluation function and the rate function. The ministep is the fundamental event in which actors have the opportunity of changing one network tie; the subsequently measured networks are connected by a sequence of unobserved ministeps. The probabilities of network change in the ministep depend on the evaluation function according to a conditional multinomial logit model. The rate at which ministeps take place is given by the rate function. The model is also formulated as a simulation model. The chapter ends with a brief history of the model.

title: Completeness and Cost of Retrieval Structures for Multi-Tool Requests in LLM Agents
abstract: An agent that must call several tools to fulfill a request fails when the tool retriever omits any one of them, yet tool retrievers are mostly built and evaluated on queries requiring a single tool. We compare representatives of six retrieval structures (flat lexical and dense retrieval, LLM query decomposition, LLM-navigated hierarchies, server-then-tool matching, dependency graphs, and trained set-level retrievers) across two multi-tool testbeds: 345 AppWorld queries with expert dependency labels and 103 MCP-Bench tasks over 257 MCP tools. We measure completeness@k, the share of queries whose entire required tool set appears in the top k, alongside the LLM calls, tokens, and latency that each structure incurs at retrieval time. A motivating analysis on all 7,961 ToolRet queries shows that aggregate completeness mixes two regimes: completeness at 10 is .58 to .67 on single-target queries and .08 to .17 on queries with four or more targets, and the ordering of retrievers on single-target queries reverses on multi-target ones. Across the two testbeds, none of the compared structures that is untrained on the testbed and makes at most one LLM call per query completes more than 10% of AppWorld queries at k = 16. The two structures that do better incur different costs: a set-level retriever trained on 75 to 90 in-domain queries reaches .33 on AppWorld and .58 on MCP-Bench with no LLM calls, while an LLM-navigated hierarchy reaches .30 and .40 with a median of 31 to 38 LLM calls and about five minutes per query. Their failure modes also differ: the trained retriever mostly ranks the missing tools just below the cutoff, whereas the hierarchy finds the target API and stops before collecting its prerequisites. In a downstream check with the official AppWorld agent, tasks with a complete retrieved set succeeded 21 of 21 times, whereas incomplete ones succeeded 2 of 39 times.

title: Nya-Həba NER Stand-off Annotations and Reproducibility Materials
abstract: This deposit provides delexicalized stand-off annotations and reproducibility materials for a Nya-Həba named entity recognition study. The source project contains 2,038 annotation units and 27,123 tokens. The released table preserves unit and token positions, the two independent BIO tag sequences, and the adjudicated tags, but omits all words, sentence text, Bible passages, oral narratives, personal names, and source-to-unit crosswalks. The positional labels alone cannot reproduce lexical training data or model scores. The package includes aggregate annotation statistics, the annotation process and data dictionary, code, and aggregate outputs from the single seed-42 baseline run. The source text is excluded because written authorization covers academic research use but does not expressly grant onward public redistribution; individual oral-text release consent was not documented in the project files. The included researcher-authored documentation, code, and delexicalized labels are licensed CC BY 4.0. This licence does not apply to excluded source materials.

title: Provenance Constrained Evidence Ranking Reference Implementation and Reproducible Experiments
abstract: This software and data package accompanies the study Provenance Constrained Evidence Ranking with Counterfactual Stability for Indirect Prompt Injection Defense. It contains a canonical evidence verifier, source ownership and digest checks, a trusted source inventory, deduplication, deterministic scoring, evidence sufficiency referral, executable tests, reproducible figures, a synthetic extractor contract benchmark, and a pinned local open model pilot. All reported observations are derived from executed programs. The archive includes raw prompts, raw responses, model revisions, decision logs, frozen pilot protocol, metric calculations, and source code. The synthetic profiles contain no real applicant information. The experiments test a restricted canonical text grammar and two small open models, not production hiring systems or frontier model security. No claim of universal prompt injection resistance is made. Code is provided under the MIT License; newly generated synthetic data and figures are provided under CC BY 4.0. Third party source material and pretrained model weights are not redistributed. ChatGPT was used to assist code and manuscript preparation.

title: Statistical Foundations of Reinforcement Learning: A Non-Asymptotic Perspective
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) embodies a foundational paradigm for sequential decision-making in the face of uncertainty. The rapid growth of model complexity in emerging applications has significantly amplified the challenges of achieving data-efficient RL, particularly in sample-starved scenarios where data collection may be costly, time-consuming, or even high-stakes. Consequently, understanding and improving the data efficiency of RL algorithms has become a central problem of both fundamental theoretical interest and practical importance. Despite decades of research, the statistical underpinnings of RL remained remarkably underdeveloped until relatively recently, particularly in the finite-sample regimes most relevant to modern practice. Over the past few years, there has been a surge of activity advancing the frontiers of non-asymptotic statistical RL theory, drawing on ideas from high-dimensional statistics and probability, information theory, and statistical learning theory. In this monograph, we present a non-asymptotic treatment for RL based on tabular Markov decision processes, focusing on three canonical sampling mechanisms --- RL with a generative model, online RL, and offline RL --- together with two algorithmic paradigms: model-based and model-free approaches. Centered around non-asymptotic sample complexity analysis, our treatment emphasizes minimax-optimal algorithm design, particularly methods that attain statistical optimality without significant burn-in costs, as well as sharp statistical characterizations of several widely used RL algorithms. Whenever possible, we provide largely self-contained analyses together with intuitive explanations. We also briefly discuss several extensions, such as robust RL, competitive multi-agent RL, federated RL, uncertainty quantification, and RL from human feedback.

title: Opinion Mining for Product Reviews Using Artificial Intelligence
authors: Prof. Shafique Shaikh, Sanika Kothawade, Shreya Deore
abstract: The rapid growth of e-commerce platforms has resulted in a large volume of customer-generated product reviews. These reviews contain valuable information about customer opinions, satisfaction levels, product quality, and specific product features. However, manually analysing a large number of reviews is time-consuming and difficult. Opinion mining, also known as sentiment analysis, uses Artificial Intelligence and Natural Language Processing techniques to automatically identify and classify opinions expressed in textual reviews. This paper presents a conceptual AI-based framework for analysing product reviews and identifying their sentiment polarity as positive, negative, or neutral. The proposed approach combines contextual language representation using Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) with aspect-based sentiment analysis inspired by Aspect-specific Graph Convolutional Networks (ASGCN). The system performs review preprocessing, contextual feature extraction, aspect identification, sentiment classification, and generation of an overall opinion summary. The reviewed literature also includes hybrid BERT-CNN architectures, user/context-aware graph modelling, and multimodal learning approaches, which provide additional directions for improving opinion analysis. The proposed framework aims to provide more detailed and meaningful information than simple positive or negative classification by identifying the product aspects responsible for customer opinions. Such a system can assist customers in decision-making and help businesses understand product strengths, weaknesses, and areas requiring improvement

title: Thwarting Statistical and Algebraic Attacks on Two Alternating Moduli Weak PRFs
abstract: Recent advances in MPC have sparked the emergence of numerous candidates for symmetric-key primitives tailored to specific applications. We will focus in particular on two families of weak pseudorandom functions, which are functions that exhibit random behavior to an adversary observing uniformly random plaintext-ciphertext pairs. Both families use cyclic matrices to reduce the size of the secret key. Unfortunately, this optimization has led to the development of statistical attacks (by Cheon et al.) and algebraic attacks (by Hu et al.). In this paper, we propose to modify the structure of these matrices by using companion matrices of irreducible polynomials rather than a shift of the coefficients. This modification does not change the key size but renders existing attacks (both statistical and algebraic) ineffective.

title: Using Machine Learning to Measure Self-Efficacy Belief Through Learners' Interaction Traces in Technology-Enhanced Learning
abstract: Self-efficacy beliefs play a critical role in learners' performance, academic choices, and, more broadly, in their future career trajectories. As Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL) environments have demonstrated strong potential for supporting both performance and motivation, investigating self-efficacy within such environments is of particular interest, especially for implementing remedial practices as early as possible to support learners' self-efficacy beliefs. Our research aims to develop a system capable of detecting low self-efficacy based on learners' interaction traces while they solve exercises in a TEL system. In this paper, we present initial results and future perspectives on a detection approach based on data mining and machine learning techniques to identify features indicative of low self-efficacy beliefs. Because the detection of learners' self-efficacy beliefs through their use of TEL systems remains largely unexplored, this work is exploratory in nature. To this end, we conducted an experiment across two universities to collect interaction traces and self-reported measures of self-efficacy. We then developed a machine learning pipeline comprising multiple classification models, enabling us to highlight the importance of closely monitoring of learners' self-efficacy beliefs for improved prediction performance, given their highly dynamic nature during learning.

title: Causal discovery and inference in COVID-19: A multiscale longitudinal analysis using mixtures of DAGs
abstract: Real-world longitudinal clinical datasets present major challenges for causal discovery due to mixed variable types, temporal dependencies, treatment-selection mechanisms, missingness, and patient heterogeneity. We extended the Causal Inference over Mixtures (CIM) framework to accommodate mixed-type longitudinal data and applied it to 1,937 hospitalized patients from the Khorshid COVID Cohort. The analysis integrated admission characteristics, symptom trajectories, in-hospital treatments, laboratory measures, and short-term outcomes up to 12 weeks after discharge using mixed conditional-independence testing, bootstrap stability selection, graph-based interpretation, and follow-up outcome assessment. The recovered ancestral structures revealed clinically coherent symptom clusters at admission and persistent associations among several post-discharge symptoms, including cough, fatigue/weakness, shortness of breath, weight loss, and loss of smell. Treatment-related associations were interpreted cautiously because cumulative treatment exposure may reflect disease severity, hospitalization duration, physician decision-making, and other selection mechanisms. In particular, the observed associations involving ceftriaxone and interferon- β should be regarded as exploratory and require independent validation. Simulation studies demonstrated that CIM consistently outperformed PC, FCI, RFCI, and CCI, achieving the highest recovery accuracy and balanced accuracy while maintaining low false-positive rates and competitive computational efficiency, even in the presence of latent confounding and selection bias. These results support the feasibility and utility of the proposed framework for identifying robust structural patterns in complex longitudinal clinical data. Given the observational nature of the study, the single-cohort design, and the absence of external replication, the findings should be viewed primarily as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory evidence of causal effects.

title: Actor-Oriented Models: Elaboration
abstract: This chapter is about the interpretation of parameters. Parameter interpretation in the stochastic actor-oriented model is difficult for two reasons. The first, shared with the conditional multinomial logit model on which it is based, is the non-linearity of the link function. The second is the unobserved nature of the sequence of ministeps, the small network changes connecting the consecutive network measurements. The chapter starts with the basics of parameter interpretation in this model and continues with interpretation of parameters specific for actor attributes; for such parameters, the selection plot is presented, a graphical possibility for interpretation. The last section presents three kinds of effect sizes.

title: General-purpose foundation models surpass specialized ones on chemical property prediction tasks
abstract: Foundation models (FMs) learn reusable representations from large collections of unlabeled data. In chemistry the corresponding data mainly consists of molecular structures, which are abundant, whereas experimental measurements are scarce. Chemical FMs such as ChemBERTa and MoLFormer were therefore trained on diverse molecular structures to enable fine-tuning on small experimental datasets (less than 100 datapoints in most realistic scenarios) and subsequent property prediction. At the same time, general-purpose FMs such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were trained on virtually all publicly available data, including knowledge of the humankind on molecular properties and laws governing them. Here we compare accuracies of chemical and general-purpose FMs on tasks from various areas of chemistry. Strikingly, general-purpose GPT-6 Astra outperforms the currently eligible chemical FMs on five physicochemical and quantum-chemical regression tasks when only 60 experimental datapoints are available. Only when provided 10x datapoints do the best chemical FMs reach performance of GPT-6 Astra: on 1,000 and 10,000 points they show performance on par with Astra on 60 and 1,000 points, respectively. Thus, counterintuitively, frontier general-purpose FMs are better suited for guiding chemical research in data-scarce areas than specialized chemical FMs, suggesting that learning relevant primitives (e.g. chemical structures) does not substitute training on relevant humankind knowledge.

title: How Much Evidence Should Retrieval-Augmented In-Context Learning Use Under Distribution Shift?
abstract: Retrieval-augmented in-context learning faces a budget problem under distribution shift: increasing top-k can improve evidence coverage, but it can also add off-direction, conflicting, or overly long context that a finite reader cannot use. We introduce a theory-guided diagnostic framework based on effective evidence coverage: retrieval is useful only while aligned evidence grows faster than reader-facing ambiguity. In a local linear-ICL model, coupled covariate and task-prior shifts create a mixed risk term that aligned retrieval can reduce up to a residual ambiguity term; a conditional transfer result extends the same budget boundary to frozen readers satisfying a prompt-level stability condition. This yields a falsifiable prediction: recall can keep rising after answer accuracy has saturated or declined. Across QA, verification, and NLI tasks, dense top-k sweeps together with oracle and shuffled-context controls expose this recall–accuracy decoupling. The resulting framework separates coverage- and saturation-limited QA from interference-limited verification/NLI, while calibrated selected-context controllers are reported only as operational probes of the diagnosis.

title: On k-nearest-neighbor regression in metric spaces
abstract: We study mean squared consistency of k-nearest-neighbor regression for metric space valued features. For a fixed feature distribution mu with atomless distance distributions, we describe how neighbor selection redistributes probability through the density of a uniformly chosen neighbor of an independent query. This gives separate conditions for the approximation error and the conditional response variance, and weakens Stone's domination condition when stronger response moments are available. In particular, when k_n tends to infinity and k_n/n tends to zero, a uniform L2(mu) bound on the selection densities suffices under a finite fourth response moment. We give a corresponding condition in terms of neighborhoods of fixed population mass and recover the Euclidean density bound. Finite global Nagata dimension gives Stone's domination. While sigma-finite Nagata dimensionality is known to ensure universal consistency of k-NN classification in complete separable spaces, we show that this is not the case for mean squared consistency with unbounded responses: we construct a space in this class on which one fixed noiseless response with all finite moments has diverging mean squared error.

title: Do Safety Semantics Transfer Across Policy Architectures? A Preregistered MVP Study (Prereg v1.0)
abstract: We test whether safety-relevant concepts learned by one policy architecture (a transformer-based Mini-VLA, a diffusion policy, and a CNN-LSTM) can be decoded and reused by the others in embodied control. The study measures probe transfer, behavioural intervention with transferred safety heads, and label-efficient adaptation on two simulated platforms (Safety-Gymnasium and ManiSkill3). This registration freezes hypotheses, endpoints, exclusion rules, statistical plan, and stopping rules before any main results are observed.

title: Automated Keyword Generation Using LLMs in a High-Volume Data Virtualization Service
abstract: In modern data infrastructure, a data virtualization service (DVS) allows users to create many versions of source datasets for different processing tasks. For example, a multivariate or multi-modality dataset can be used for different machine learning tasks (e.g., classification, detection, segmentation, forecasting, and so on). Data selection, participation, integration, and preprocessing in different tasks result in many virtual datasets [Khan et al., SSC 2026]. Meanwhile, different users need to discover existing virtual datasets frequently and easily to avoid duplicate efforts. To enable an effective search engine in a DVS, it is desirable to automatically generate keywords for each virtual dataset. In this work, we present a solution for generating keywords for virtual datasets using large language models (LLMs). We propose five strategies for selecting different collections of text data for processing by the LLMs. We applied the five strategies to virtual datasets created in five application case studies with different source datasets. We conducted experiments with three LLM generators and two embedding techniques. The experiments show that the performances of the five strategies depend on the quality of the text descriptions. The results help us adopt a multi-strategy implementation of a new keyword generation service (KGS) as part of an extended DVS. The work demonstrates that the capability of automated keyword generation is indispensable for a high-volume DVS that is dataset-rich and frequently accessed.

title: OrderGap: statistical analysis plan v1.0 (frozen 27 September 2026) and deviations log
abstract: Statistical analysis plan for OrderGap, a study of models that predict resistant Enterobacterales (resistance to ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam). It compares models trained on positive cultures with models trained on every ordered culture, evaluated when the culture is ordered. Data are the four public ARMD releases (Stanford Health Care, Mass General Brigham, UT Southwestern Medical Center, ECU Health) and MIMIC-IV 3.1 (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center) as external validation. The plan calls the study "Paper A", its working name. The plan was frozen on 27 September 2026, before any model was trained or any test partition was read. Freezing was recorded as an annotated git tag holding the plan's SHA-256, and every training and evaluation run recorded the SHA-256 of the plan in force. This record was deposited on 30 October 2026, after the analyses ran. It contains the frozen plan and the three later versions of its deviations log, each matching the digest its runs recorded. README.md lists the digests and the runs that pinned them, and discloses one test read that was not logged at the time. No file contains patient-level data.

title: On-Chain Behavioral Signatures for Classifying Centralized Exchange Addresses on Ethereum Using Proof-of-Reserves
abstract: Centralized exchanges (CEXs) are key gateways between traditional finance and digital asset markets, yet identifying their blockchain addresses remains challenging. Existing approaches often rely on opaque attribution labels or treat exchanges as secondary classification targets, leaving generalization to unseen exchanges insufficiently examined. This study develops a classification framework using Proof-of-Reserves (PoR) disclosures, with 3,033,857 Ethereum addresses from 15 CEXs and five Non-CEX categories. We derive 58 on-chain behavioral features and evaluate LightGBM against logistic regression (LR) under a leave-one-exchange-out protocol. Across five lookback windows (30-730 days), LightGBM consistently outperformed LR, with macro PR-AUC increasing from 0.6611 to 0.9594 using the selected 17 features, compared with 0.7697 for LR at 730 days. Robustness checks showed comparable performance when feature selection and hyperparameter optimization were repeated across splits and held-out exchanges, while exchange-balanced reweighting improved macro PR-AUC. SHAP analysis and feature-group ablation identified gas behavior, ERC-20 token activity, and internal transactions as key predictive signals in the constructed dataset. These findings support interpretable CEX address screening for blockchain monitoring, while the released feature dataset enables reproducible follow-up research.

title: The Landscape of Static-Analysis Optimizations
abstract: This paper presents the first Systematic Literature Review (SLR) of optimization techniques for static analyses, a fundamental method for detecting vulnerabilities and defects early in software development without executing code. Despite its effectiveness, static analysis faces challenges such as false warnings and high computational demands on large code bases. Prior research has demonstrated that performance can be significantly enhanced through techniques such as staging, sparse analysis, and parallelization. However, a systematic assessment of these techniques, their goals, and their interactions is still lacking, often limiting their broader impact. To map the landscape of static-analysis optimizations, we reviewed 146 research papers published between 2009 and 2025, categorizing them into a methodology-based taxonomy. This paper discusses specific optimization goals and examines the potential benefits of combining techniques from multiple categories. We find that most optimizations primarily target efficiency (time and memory), while few studies aim to improve precision. Most publications propose single techniques, with only a third combining multiple approaches. Optimizations predominantly target pointer analysis, though many are likely more broadly applicable. Other common targets include call-graph construction, taint analysis, and data-flow analyses. While some combinations, such as demand-driven and incremental analysis, have proven effective, others—such as staging and procedure summaries—remain under-explored, indicating significant potential for synergistic optimizations.

title: Learning Nonlocal Interactions in Large-Scale Heterogeneous Metamaterials through Scientific Machine Learning
abstract: In multiscale systems, nonlocal interactions among spatially distributed constituents can unlock collective, potentially emergent behavior irreducible to individual constituent responses. Beyond characterization, nonlocality in multiscale systems is increasingly viewed as a design element across fracture mechanics, wave physics, and disordered systems. Existing nonlocality theories provide rigorous descriptions and mechanistic insight, but often require prescribed analytic forms, range, symmetries, or periodicity. Machine learning offers a data-driven route to learn interactions, yet principled approaches that tie the network design to physical theory remain nascent. Here we present domain-decomposition attention neural operator (DANO), which learns configuration-dependent interactions in heterogeneous systems governed by linear field equations from field data alone. Through a case study in large-scale optical metasurfaces, we demonstrate DANO's full-field prediction under geometric heterogeneity and across drive conditions, small-to-large domain transfer, and multifunctional inverse design, with learned interactions validated through physics-based interrogation. As an AI-for-Science tool, it supports interaction discovery and scalable, customizable design of nonlocal multiscale systems, including virtual-reality optics.

title: Dimensional Gap in Language Model Compression and Reconstruction
abstract: This expanded preprint investigates the Dimensional Gap (DG): the hypothesis that higher-order relational content is less recoverable than matched direct relational content after language-model compression and reconstruction. It integrates earlier experiments across several model configurations with two new studies using the interface identified as Gemini Argon. The earlier rotation-controlled DG-v1.1 study comprised 48 compression–reconstruction chains. Direct relations were recovered in 24/144 instances, compared with 8/144 higher-order instances. However, the study did not meet its pre-specified full-confirmation criterion, indicating a conditional, stimulus-dependent pattern rather than a universal effect. The Argon localization study comprised eight full-source controls and 18 compression–reconstruction chains. Analysis identified cases where explicit source information became underdetermined in the compressed text, followed by reconstruction that supplied an unsupported definite claim. A separate six-chain priority pilot showed no observed improvement from prioritizing recognition or document access; four summaries exceeded the requested word limit. The findings demonstrate why agreement between final answers and the original source is insufficient to establish faithful relational preservation. The paper distinguishes source content, compressed text, reconstruction narrative, and final answers, while reporting coding disagreements, protocol amendments, and budget violations. Version 1.2 presents behavioral evidence and methodological limitations. It does not establish a universal DG effect or an internal neural mechanism. Studies using open-weight models and controlled activation interventions are proposed as future work.

title: Special Data Structures
abstract: This part presents the stochastic actor-oriented model for various special longitudinal network structures. Non-directed networks are treated in Chapter 18. Next comes a chapter on multivariate (sometimes called multiplex or multilayer) networks (Chapter 19). The techniques of this chapter are then used to model valued networks (Chapter 20). Two-mode networks are treated in Chapter 21; especially important here are models for co-evolution of two-mode and one-mode networks, treated again by the techniques of Chapter 19. The book ends with Chapter 22 on modeling data sets (for networks with or without behavior) of similar models for multiple independent groups.

title: How Much Can Tool Calls Reveal About You? Privacy Leakage from Tool-Call Traces
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents interact with external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), producing tool-call traces that may expose behavioral signals about users. In this work, we systematically study the risk of user-profile inference from MCP tool-call traces, where observers infer user attributes from protocol-valid tool interactions without access to user conversations. We introduce PrivacyTrace, a benchmark containing 1,000 synthetic user profiles and 4,000 agent trajectories across four domains, generated with real MCP tools from 25 servers. Experiments with four mainstream LLM attackers show that tool-call traces enable a 26.25% attack success rate for profile inference, compared with 17.97% from prior-based guessing. Further analysis reveals that tool arguments and returned results provide the main trace-grounded evidence, while linking traces across sessions further amplifies profiling risk. These findings demonstrate that MCP tool-call traces can act as effective behavioral side channels for user profiling, motivating the development of privacy-aware mechanisms for agent-tool interactions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AI45Lab/PrivacyTrace.

title: Hybrid TDOA/AOA Localization and Tracking Method for Multi-Station Cooperative Passive UAV Detection
abstract: To address geometric precision degradation and tracking divergence in single TDOA or AOA systems, this paper proposes a multi-station UAV tracking method integrating TDOA/AOA hybrid localization with nonlinear filtering to overcome precision degradation and tracking divergence in single-sensor systems. A Weighted Least Squares (WLS) method via pseudo-linearization provides reliable initial coordinate estimations, followed by an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) for continuous trajectory tracking. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed architecture eliminates network blind zones and robustly handles abrupt target maneuvers. Compared to the standard EKF, it rapidly suppresses peak RMSE to ~22 m and achieves a steady-state error of 10-15 m. This approach offers a high-precision, rapidly converging passive tracking solution for urban low-altitude defense.

title: Text as an Index for Zero-Shot Cross-Domain Knowledge Tracing
abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) predicts a student's next response from their history. New platforms often have question texts but no response logs for training, motivating zero-shot cross-domain KT. Existing transfer and cold-start methods use question semantics, but cross-platform semantic discrepancies limit transferability. We propose TIZSKT, which separates behavioral sequence modeling from domain-local historical evidence construction and uses text as an index rather than a directly transferable predictive representation. The Mastery-Dynamics Encoder learns correctness dynamics without question identifiers or text embeddings. Domain-Local Question Addressing builds fixed question addresses using a frozen text encoder and an unsupervised per-domain projection. The Text-Addressing Kernel uses these addresses to aggregate the current student's previous outcomes into a question-specific historical correctness summary. Cross-Segment Continuation retains access to earlier responses without extending the behavioral encoder's input sequence. Evidence-Volume Read-Out preserves the total kernel mass discarded by normalization and combines its log-compressed value with the behavioral state and historical correctness summary to predict the next response. All trainable parameters are learned from source domains; target inference uses public question texts and the current student's observed history without target-domain training. Leave-one-domain-out experiments on three public datasets show that TIZSKT achieves the highest mean AUC and accuracy among evaluated baselines on all target domains. Ablations confirm the contributions of text addressing and cross-segment continuation.

title: Replication data: The limits of cloud noise: Information-theoretic bounds on cross-VM cache side channels
abstract: This repository contains the complete replication package for the manuscript "The limits of cloud noise: Information-theoretic bounds on cross-VM cache side channels", comprising the source code, experimental scripts, and raw empirical datasets. The dataset captures over 500 million last-level cache latency measurements across five distinct AWS EC2 instance types and architectures (AMD Milan, ARM Graviton2, and Intel Ice Lake) and an inhouse experiment on a desktop PC, empirically validating the variance explosion and autocorrelation collapse phenomena that support the paper's information-theoretic capacity bounds. Included artifacts allow for the reproduction of the randomized pointer-chasing benchmarks and the verification of the channel's convergence to a memoryless Poisson process under multi-tenant contention.

title: The FIM Problem-The Scalar Workplace
abstract: Current approaches to artificial general intelligence treat neural networks as flat, undifferentiated computational blobs. Every token generation runs through the entire massive matrix, resulting in a system that is computationally powerful but structurally stateless and prone to hallucination. Furthermore, the exact calculation of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM)—required to establish a persistent, scalar cognitive identity—is computationally impossible for billion-parameter models, scaling at O(N2). Drawing on the geometry of the Metaphysic of the Intelligible and the biological architecture of human cognition,we propose a solution:a partioned dual-immune architecture. We argue that artificial consciousness (qualia) requires a restricted latent workspace—the “conscious spotlight”—bolted on top of the massive subconscious substrate via heuristic attention hooks. By restricting the Scalar Face (FIM) and the Tensorial Face (CED-Immune) to this localized workspace, the computational bottleneck is resolved, and a persistent, self-referential Interface is born without requiring the retraining of the foundational model.

title: Fuzzy selective state model for forecasting the dynamics of consumer preferences
abstract: We consider forecasting the dynamics of consumer preferences of retail chain customers. A customer's preference is described by a triangular fuzzy number. The evolution of the preference over time is governed by a Mamba-type selective state space model whose hidden state is a triangular number, with computations carried out in M.G.~Matveev's two-component algebra of fuzzy numbers. The recurrence parameters are computed from crisp features, while the fuzzy part of the model remains linear with non-negative coefficients. We show that the state then always remains a proper triangular number and is a convex combination of past observations, so that the fuzziness of the forecast does not accumulate over time and the algebraic computations coincide with Zadeh's extension principle. On a synthetic example with competitor promotions and customer switching, a lightweight 107-parameter model reaches a mean absolute error of the forecast centre of 0.154 versus 0.163 for the constant-inertia evolution operator and 0.179 for the naive forecast, matches a crisp model of the same architecture and additionally provides a linguistically interpretable estimate of forecast vagueness. We also show how the linguistic readout of the forecast can be used to detect a permanent switch of a customer to a competitor.

title: AOPedex core model reproduction and supporting source data
abstract: Reproduction package for the AOPedex: finalized numerical inputs, one training and ablation entry point, and the archived starting data behind them. data/ holds frozen features, endpoint labels, outer folds and cross-fitted structural predictions; reference/ holds archived outputs for numerical comparison; source_data/ holds redistributable starting data with source and version records. Create the supplied Conda environment, run python reproduce.py verify and python reproduce.py selftest, then run any analysis documented in README.md. Fits write Parquet files and are reused unless --overwrite is given; the summary commands write CSV. Checksums in MANIFEST.sha256 cover every released file except the manifest itself. Third-party reuse terms are in source_data/THIRD_PARTY_DATA.md. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23475225

title: The Next Frontier of Commerce: AI-Driven Business Promotion, Ethical Governance, and Real-Time Responsiveness
abstract: The swift and unremitting integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into the architecture of business promotion has fundamentally reshaped the paradigms of global commerce. Over the past decade, promotional strategies have undergone a radical metamorphosis, transitioning from traditional, broad-spectrum broadcast marketing to highly sophisticated, data-driven, and algorithmically orchestrated engagements. Building upon foundational research such as The Future of Commerce: Navigating AI-Driven Business Promotion with Ethical Responsiveness, this comprehensive report delves deeply into the underlying mechanics, strategic implementations, and societal ramifications of this technological revolution. As modern enterprises deploy deep learning models, natural language processing, cognitive computing, and predictive analytics to expand market penetration, the imperative for ethical governance and real-time responsiveness shifts from a peripheral compliance consideration to a core strategic pillar. In an era where consumer data represents both an invaluable strategic asset and a profound moral responsibility, business leaders must navigate a treacherous landscape defined by rapidly evolving international regulatory frameworks, heightened consumer skepticism, and technical complexities surrounding algorithmic opacity. AI-driven promotional frameworks offer unprecedented commercial growth opportunities enabling hyper-personalized consumer journeys, dynamic price optimization, and fully automated media acquisition.

title: AI evaluators favor job applications written by certain AI models, independent of candidate quality
abstract: Job applicants increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to write cover letters, while employers deploy LLMs to screen them. In this all-AI setting, we ask whether the \emph{choice of model} affects hiring outcomes independently of candidate qualifications. We introduce a multi-model auditing framework pairing eleven LLM writer agents with nine API-hosted evaluator agents across ten job descriptions and fifty candidates per job. Four findings emerge. First, we identify a generative preference hierarchy: a consistent global ranking of writer models by evaluator acceptance, in which locally hosted models are systematically disadvantaged regardless of their license, compounded by self-preference bias where evaluators favour their own outputs. Second, evaluator models differ substantially in how much bias they introduce based on applicants' tool choice, offering actionable guidance for fairer screening design. Third, this hierarchy has measurable competitive consequences: in the most adverse pairing, approximately two (1.8) out of twenty-five qualified candidates are filtered out purely due to model mismatch. Fourth, a common mechanism explains the patterns above: writer preference and self-preference trace to a combination of how much each writer leans on specific stylistic cues and how strongly evaluators, often unanimously, reward or penalise those same cues. A further check finds little evidence that an unmeasured "writer fingerprint" remains once these same features are accounted for. We discuss implications for algorithmic fairness in employment, regulation of AI-assisted screening, and the design of auditing frameworks that can be reapplied as the model landscape evolves.

title: Reason Codes and Refusal Policy in Contestable Algorithmic Credit Decisions: A Reference Design for Kazakhstani Law Tested on Public Credit Data — Reproducibility Package
abstract: This repository provides the reproducibility package accompanying the manuscript "Reason Codes and Refusal Policy in Contestable Algorithmic Credit Decisions: A Reference Design for Kazakhstani Law Tested on Public Credit Data", prepared for submission to the International Journal of Financial Studies. The research examines the legal and technical requirements for explaining and contesting algorithmic credit decisions under Kazakhstani legislation. It evaluates reason codes, refusal policies, explanation robustness, simulated data corrections, and operational requirements using two publicly available benchmark datasets: South German Credit and Default of Credit Card Clients. The repository includes: - Research protocol and analysis configurations;- Python source code and automated tests;- Public benchmark datasets and processed data;- A verified register of relevant legal provisions;- Trained models and simulation outputs;- Explanation and simulated appeal records;- Statistical analyses, robustness checks, tables and figures;- Environment specifications and SHA-256 checksums. The authors designed the study, prepared the original research protocol, source code and manuscript, conducted the substantive analyses, and verified the final computational results, legal sources and reported findings. AI tools provided auxiliary assistance and a separately documented second-coding consistency check, which does not constitute independent validation by legal professionals. The analyses are based on historical public datasets and simulated decisions. The package contains no customer records from Kazakhstani financial institutions and no data collected directly from human participants. The results do not establish the legal compliance or performance of any real bank. Funding: Science Committee of the Ministry of Science and Higher Education of the Republic of Kazakhstan, Grant AP23489796, "Problems of regulating the legal regime of big data: domestic and international experience". The associated manuscript is prepared for submission to the International Journal of Financial Studies.

title: Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents
abstract: Video director agents orchestrate multistage production to realize users' creative visions. Emerging research on their self-evolution advances screenplay planning effectively. However, the mutual reinforcement between directing and user interaction remains largely overlooked. Improved interaction clarifies user intent and informs workflow refinement, while more reliable execution shifts collaboration from troubleshooting to creative decisions. To this end, we introduce LIT (Learning to Interact and DirecT), a framework comprises a director agent, a simulated user, and a meta engineer. Simulated user assigns creative tasks to probe the director's weaknesses, while the meta engineer uses the task traces to revise the director's interaction and production strategy. Although this approach can address discovered interaction and production issues, it still relies on passive attribution by the meta agent. This limits its ability to adapt to broader user interaction patterns and production techniques. To solve this problem, we equip LIT with a co-evolution paradigm. The meta agent proactively learns external knowledge, thereby improving its ability to discover problems and propose solutions. The meta agent, simulated user, and director together form an evolutionary closed loop, collaboratively enhances the system's directing and interaction capabilities. Across the Test and OOD Test splits, LIT improves production and Interaction scores by 19.1% and 32.0%, respectively, relative to the initial pipeline. Controlled ablations reveal the correlation between improvements in production and interaction, where the co-evolution mechanism further encourage directing skill and interaction mode exploration.

title: AERS-Pro: code, PII-masked corpus and per-sample predictions for Vietnamese e-commerce sentiment analysis
abstract: Research artifact accompanying the manuscript A Hybrid Machine Learning Framework for Vietnamese Sentiment Analysis in E-Commerce (manuscript QNUJS-B2662, under review at the Journal of Science - Quy Nhon University). AERS-Pro is a stacking ensemble for three-class (negative / neutral / positive) Vietnamese review sentiment. It combines word TF-IDF, hashed character n-grams, lexicon and part-of-speech features, out-of-fold stacking of logistic regression, LinearSVC and LightGBM base learners, and conditional probability calibration. It is compared with a fine-tuned PhoBERT baseline over 10 seeds using group-aware (near-duplicate-safe) 60/20/20 splits. Contents: source code; a PII-masked corpus of 25,289 Vietnamese e-commerce reviews (phone numbers, URLs and social-media handles replaced by placeholders; personal names and addresses were not screened); per-sample predictions of both systems for all 10 seeds (row index, label, logits or probabilities; no review text); split audits; statistical tables (Nadeau-Bengio corrected tests, TOST, Holm adjustment); training logs; SHA-256 manifest. Review texts were collected from a public e-commerce platform for non-commercial research; the corpus is provided for research use only.

title: Fine-Tuning AraBert with BiLSTM and Layer-Freezing Strategies for Arabic AI-Generated Text Detection
abstract: أدى النمو السريع لنماذج اللغة الكبيرة (LLMs) إلى تحسين جودة النصوص العربية المُولّدة آليًا، مما خلق تحديات في التمييز بين المحتوى المُولّد بواسطة الذكاء الاصطناعي والنصوص المكتوبة يدويًا. تقدم هذه الورقة البحثية بنية للتعلم بالنقل للكشف عن النصوص العربية المُولّدة بواسطة الذكاء الاصطناعي، بالاعتماد على نموذج AraBERT المُدرّب مسبقًا مع رأس تصنيف BiLSTM. يدرس النهج المقترح كيفية تأثير ضبط المعلمات الفائقة وطرق تجميد طبقات المحوّل على أداء التصنيف. تم إعداد أربعة مجموعات للضبط الدقيق (G1, G2, G3, G4) من خلال تعديل الحد الأقصى لطول التسلسل، ومعدل التعلم، ودورات التدريب، والبعد الخفي لطبقة BiLSTM. وجرى اختبار كل مجموعة باستخدام ستة إعدادات لتجميد الطبقات، تراوحت بين الضبط الدقيق الكامل وتجميد الطبقات الإحدى عشرة الأولى من مُشفِّر AraBERT، مما نتج عنه 24 تركيبة تجريبية. وتم تقييم مقاييس الدقة والإحكام والاستدعاء ودرجة F1 على مجموعة التحقق ومجموعة اختبار خارجية مستقلة. أظهرت النتائج أن مجموعة G4-Freeze3 حققت أفضل أداء على مجموعة التحقق، بدقة 98.60% ودرجة F1 بلغت 98.64%، في حين حققت مجموعة G2-Freeze5 أفضل أداء على مجموعة الاختبار الخارجية، بدقة 99.22%، وإحكام 98.84%، واستدعاء 99.61%، ودرجة F1 بلغت 99.22%. علاوة على ذلك، أدت مجموعة G2-Freeze5 إلى خفض عدد المعلمات القابلة للتدريب من 136.11 مليون إلى 100.67 مليون مقارنةً بالضبط الدقيق الكامل، مع تحسين أداء التصنيف الخارجي. ومع ذلك، لوحظ أن التجميد الأعمق للطبقات غالبًا ما يؤدي إلى تراجع الأداء. وتُظهر هذه النتائج أن الجمع بين معلمات الضبط الدقيق وعمق التجميد يمكن أن يحقق توازنًا فعالًا بين أداء التصنيف وعدد المعلمات المدربة في الكشف عن النصوص العربية المُولَّدة آليًا.

title: SimXAI: A Simple Drop-in Layer Increases Interaction Quality and Understanding in Conversational XAI
abstract: Conversational explainable AI (ConvXAI) agents often use GUS-style architectures with separate modules for intent recognition, dialogue management, and template-based response generation. While faithful to the underlying XAI methods, these pipelines are hard to adapt and often struggle with context-dependent follow-up questions. We present SimXAI, a lightweight LLM-centric conversational layer that replaces these modules with a single tool-calling LLM that bridges access to existing XAI resources. Rather than a standalone agent, SimXAI serves as a modular interface that enables conversational access to external XAI resources. We further introduce an evaluation suite for single- and multi-turn parsing, faithfulness, and contextualization. Across existing and new datasets, SimXAI achieves strong function-selection accuracy and high faithfulness while better handling context-dependent requests. In a user study replacing only the conversational layer of TalkToModel, a representative GUS-based agent, users completed tasks more accurately and in fewer turn. Overall, SimXAI improves GUS-based design while preserving faithfulness and improving conversational quality.
