title: Replication package for: Verification-Gated Hybrid Negotiation for Decentralized Multi-Agent Planning under Temporal Uncertainty
abstract: This package contains the code, data and results needed to reproduce the experiments of the paper “Verification-Gated Hybrid Negotiation for Decentralized Multi-Agent Planning under Temporal Uncertainty.” The paper proposes Hybrid Flexibility Negotiation (HFN), a coordination framework in which agents with private temporal plans (Simple Temporal Networks with Uncertainty) repair a loss of dynamic controllability by escalating from direct negotiation to broker-mediated recommendations and then to a decentralized cascade. Every state is committed only after an exact dynamic-controllability check succeeds at every agent. The package includes: a Python implementation of the dynamic-controllability checker, the network and crisis generator, all negotiation strategies, and two distributed constraint-optimisation baselines; one script per experiment, a script that regenerates all tables and figures, and unit tests; the ICU length-of-stay table from the MIMIC-IV Clinical Database Demo used to calibrate durations (ODbL licence); all result files reported in the paper. All instances are generated from fixed random seeds. See README.md for instructions and for the mapping between scripts and research questions.

title: GLTF-FEDformer: an adaptive time-frequency fusion method for multivariate time series anomaly detection enhanced by prediction error embedding
abstract: Abstract Multivariate time series are widespread in scenarios such as industrial IoT, smart manufacturing, energy systems, and medical monitoring. Their anomalous behaviors often involve complex patterns like long-range dependency changes, local dynamic shifts, transient spectral perturbations, and variable-association mismatches. Existing reconstruction-based and attention-based methods can learn the overall evolution of normal sequences but still lack fine-grained characterization of local time-frequency changes; moreover, relying solely on point-wise prediction errors for anomaly scoring struggles to fully reflect structural shifts in the error distribution. To address these issues, this paper proposes GLTF-FEDformer, a multivariate time series anomaly detection method that jointly models global and local time-frequency features. The method learns temporal dependencies, trend changes, and periodic candidate patterns from long-window contexts via a global temporal representation module, and enhances the modeling of temporal evolution through a continuous dynamic refinement mechanism. It also builds a lightweight local time-frequency feature extraction module that uses short-time Fourier transform, 2D convolutions, spectral gating, and inverse transforms to enhance the perception of local morphological changes, spectral perturbations, and time-frequency coupled features within local windows. A gated fusion mechanism performs data-dependent integration of global temporal information and local time-frequency information to obtain more discriminative prediction representations. Additionally, we design an anomaly scoring strategy based on a prediction-error-embedded profile, mapping prediction residuals into an embedding space and measuring structural deviations of test prediction-error embeddings from the normal error profile through variable-level standardized distances. The profile score is further combined with point-wise prediction errors to form anomaly responses with temporal localization ability. This strategy not only uses amplitude information of prediction errors but also captures structural shifts of the error distribution relative to normal patterns, thereby improving detection robustness in complex anomaly scenarios. Experimental results show the proposed method effectively enhances multivariate time series anomaly recognition and demonstrates strong detection performance and stability across various public datasets.

title: Iterated Integrals as Lexical Fingerprints: Path Signature Embeddings for Lexical Similarity
abstract: While sentence embeddings are primarily designed for semantic generalization, their latent geometry implicitly encodes surface-level lexical properties, a relationship that remains poorly understood. Shallow pooling methods discard word order, while deep Transformer models obscure these lexical alignments behind computational complexity and uninterpretable spaces. We propose constructing sentence embeddings via the path signature of Word2Vec trajectories, leveraging the iterated integrals of rough path theory to create representations that explicitly capture sequential and lexical structure in a geometrically tractable manner. Through extensive ablations spanning Word2Vec dimensions, signature depths, and PCA compression, we correlate embedding distances against five lexical string metrics: Levenshtein, Jaro-Winkler, word Jaccard, phoneme Levenshtein, and character TF-IDF. We reveal that while average pooling almost entirely fails to capture character-level edit distances, path signatures strongly align with them, with depth 2 signatures optimally balancing character and word-level sensitivities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the critical lexical variance is concentrated in a highly compact PCA subspace, and unlike pooling, signatures structurally preserve and quantify word order. These findings establish path signatures not as semantic generalizers, but as rigorous mathematical lenses that explicitly encode discrete lexical structures and word order, offering an interpretable alternative to opaque deep learning for lexical tracking.

title: Artificial intelligence, emotional well-being, and difficult dialogues in school settings
abstract: Attention to students' emotional dimension represents a key determinant of both academic success and future personal and social development (Weber et al., 2016). Within this perspective, the design of emotionally meaningful learning experiences, including those supported by Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based conversational technologies, can enhance students' well-being and engagement by recognizing emotions as a fundamental component of learning processes. Through Natural Language Processing techniques and affective computing models, intelligent conversational systems can detect and interpret users' emotional states and dynamically adapt interactions accordingly. In particular, so-called empathic conversational agents (Ortega-Ochoa et al., 2024) are artificial entities designed to elicit empathic responses from users (Hall & Woods, 2006) and to generate highly personalized simulated environments by modulating content, feedback, and task difficulty according to identified emotional factors. Such artificial conversations enable learners to engage in adaptive learning experiences in which their emotional state becomes an active variable in the regulation of the educational pathway. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 116-117. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Hybrid and "Emotionally Aware" Learning Environments.

title: Interpretable Deep Learning for Ovarian Cancer Subtype Classification Using Histopathology Images
abstract: Abstract Ovarian cancer is a histologically heterogeneous malignancy in which accurate subtype classification is essential for prognosis and treatment selection. Manual interpretation of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)–stained histopathology slides remains time-consuming and subject to inter-observer variability, particularly for morphologically overlapping subtypes. In this study, an interpretable deep learning framework was developed for automated ovarian cancer subtype classification using a fine-tuned ResNet50 architecture. A publicly available histopathology dataset comprising five major ovarian carcinoma subtypes was employed. Model training incorporated optimized strategies including data augmentation, selective layer unfreezing, label smoothing, and test-time augmentation. Classification performance was benchmarked against established convolutional neural network architectures. Visual interpretability was assessed using Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) to examine model attention patterns. The proposed framework achieved high classification performance, with strong accuracy and macro-averaged F1-scores across subtypes. Grad-CAM analysis demonstrated that model attention was consistently localized to histologically relevant tissue regions in correctly classified samples, while misclassifications were associated with morphologically ambiguous structures. These findings suggest that classification errors primarily reflect intrinsic histopathologic overlap rather than spurious model behavior. Overall, this work establishes a reproducible and interpretable deep learning benchmark for ovarian cancer subtype classification and provides clinically meaningful insight into model decision processes. The proposed framework is well-suited for use as a second-reader decision support tool in digital pathology workflows.

title: Dynamical Memory Transformer: Selective Recurrent Memories with Constant Cost Attention
abstract: Transformers retain an explicit history of the sequence, allowing attention to directly retrieve past representations. However, the size of the KV-Cache and the cost of a new token increase with the context length. State Space Models compress the past into a fixed-size recurrent state, at the cost of reduced addressability. We present the Dynamical Memory Transformer (DMT), a hybrid architecture that separates sequence encoding from information reading. The encoder uses several memory units, each implemented by a dynamical system with a complex diagonal recurrent matrix. An input-dependent leak rate controls their updates. The decoder then uses attention to read and combine their outputs, without going through the token history. The formulation of the recurrence allows an associative scan with O(T ) total work and O(log T ) parallel depth, with fixed dimensions. During autoregressive inference, the recurrent states and the convolution cache remain fixed in size. We compare DMT with Mamba and Transformer on cognitive and language modeling tasks, and show its strengths and limitations: DMT achieves the best results on several cognitive tasks and language modeling performance close to that of Transformer, but remains behind Mamba in language modeling. On selective copy, DMT also shows stronger length extrapolation than Mamba and Transformer. These results demonstrate that parallel dynamical memory units are a promising mechanism for retaining and using information over sequences.

title: Source code for: Virtual Immunohistochemical Staining for Pathological Complete Response Prediction in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
abstract: This record contains the source code supporting both the article (submitted to Bioinformatics, 2026) and the master's dissertation (PPGCC/UFMG, 2026) entitled "Virtual Immunohistochemical Staining for Pathological Complete Response Prediction in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer". The project predicts pathological complete response (pCR) in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) by combining H&E images with Ki-67 and PHH3 stains (real or virtually generated) through a biomarker-based spatial attention mechanism. Contents: bcs-kedro/ - Kedro project implementing the full pCR prediction pipeline: image preprocessing, generation of biomarker-based spatial attention maps, and a ResNet-based classifier with attention. virtual_staining/ - models for generating Ki-67 and PHH3 stains from H&E images, including CycleGAN, conditional GAN (cGAN), and diffusion-based approaches. Requirements: Python 3.8+, dependencies listed in requirements.txt. Training is GPU-optimized.ob scripts are configured for SLURM clusters. Installation and execution instructions are provided in README.md. Trained models: Hugging Face | Digital Pathology Models Source repository: Github | PCR Classification Repository Main author: Henrique Colonese Main contributor: Daniel Ayala

title: ipi-bench: a reproducible, utility aware benchmark for adaptive indirect prompt injection in multi document LLM screening
abstract: Code, configuration, synthetic corpus generator, attack taxonomy, defense implementations, metrics, statistics and figure scripts accompanying the manuscript 'Beyond Detection: A Reproducible, Utility Aware Benchmark for Adaptive Indirect Prompt Injection in Multi Document LLM Screening'. The archive includes an OpenAI compatible client for live runs, a documented synthetic responder for offline validation of the pipeline, the trial level results and aggregated tables of the reported run, the LaTeX source of the paper, and a Colab notebook. Results produced with the synthetic responder validate the pipeline and are not measurements of any real language model.

title: Open-Weight MLLMs Cannot Compare What They Cannot Name
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly capable of understanding images and performing complex visual reasoning, suggesting the possibility of using them to automate biological image analysis. This need is becoming increasingly urgent as advances in technology continue to generate ever larger and more diverse microscopy datasets, already exceeding the scale at which manual visual analysis is feasible. With the final aim to use MLLMs for visual comparison of complex phenotypes, we investigate a very simple baseline: comparison of the size of body parts in synthetic images of ants. We find that state-of-the-art open-weight MLLMs fail for some body parts, but not for others, even though the comparison itself is visually trivial for all of them. We evaluate different in-context learning strategies and analyze performance on the related object recognition task. Our results suggest a recognition-driven grounding failure: structures that the models cannot recognize are instead associated with a recognizable semantic concept, impairing the grounding and comparison of both. Further analysis of the vision encoder is consistent with the hypothesis that fine-grained visual structure may be less well preserved without semantic support. Together, our results reveal a surprising limitation of current MLLMs: semantic recognition can gate simple visual comparisons that do not intrinsically require semantic understanding. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/kreshuklab/Open-Weight-MLLMs-Cannot-Compare-What-They-Cannot-Name

title: BURIDAN: the ambiguous picture, decided by a 144-qubit collective with its controller in the loop. A registered experiment
abstract: On the IBM Heron processor ibm_fez, 144 qubits form 36 domains of four. A field law running on a microcontroller (an ESP32-S3, firmware v4.12) turns the measured populations of every cycle into the rotation angles of the next, and a Hebbian coupling matrix of two images, a unicorn and a heart, makes the two images attractors of the collective: cued with part of either, the field completes it. The experiment writes a blend of the two: of the 16 pixels on which the images differ, k are taken from the unicorn and the rest from the heart (which pixels: fixed in the registration, per trial), the 20 shared pixels as they are. The blend is held for two cycles and released, and the field runs six free cycles on its own. Resolution is the first free cycle in which the field's majority picture agrees with one image on at least 90 percent of the pixels. Lines, thresholds and rules were fixed and hashed before the first registered job (registration SHA-256 81398e6660c6538ebcf1566b3a2ebb6ecbaaefe29da074894848516b5749acda; a first registration was refused by its own budget guard after four burn jobs and is part of the deposit). Results, as they fell: of 13 field-on trials 11 resolved into one of the two images; the fraction resolved to the unicorn was 0.00, 0.00, 0.33, 0.50, 1.00, 1.00 for k = 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, a monotone curve with a single flip whose interpolated crossing lies at k* = 9.0; the censored decision time was 4.4 cycles at the two levels nearest the flip against 1.0 at the levels far from it; the two field-off controls, the same blend with the inter-domain coupling off, never resolved. The device's lean, read from the cycles in which the field was off, pointed to the heart and moved the fair point up by about one pixel, as the registered exploratory line asked. All five binding lines and the exploratory line held. The decision dynamics is the one a textbook predicts, a mean-field quench of 16 domains from the blend's magnetisation; the content of the experiment is that it runs, pre-registered to the pixel, on a quantum collective with the controller in the loop. Two chips were in the loop: the controller (ESP32-S3, with the field, the coupling matrix and the agents drawn on its display during the run) and a witness (ESP32-C3) running the byte-identical kernel source, compiled with the same arctangent and without fused multiply-add, so that the RISC-V chip in software arithmetic and the Xtensa chip with its floating-point unit produce the same bits: a seeded programme of 527 exchanges over every kernel path gave the same vector on both before the run, and on every one of the 148 ticks of the run the witness returned the same bytes as the controller. 148 jobs of 2048 shots, one device, one night. The deposit holds the registration (and the refused first registration with its burn log), the model and registration script, the runner, the verdict script, the kernel replica, the rehearsal on the noiseless simulator with both chips in the loop under the hashed registration, the run log with the measured populations of every qubit in every cycle and the witness flag of every tick, the job ids, the verdict (formed once), the bit-check vectors of the two chips, the write-up (buridan_paper_v1.pdf) and the scripts and figures that build it. The firmware sources and binaries are not deposited; their SHA-256 are in the registration.

title: Understanding and improving language models through interpretable decompositions
abstract: The interpretability of a machine learning model refers to the degree to which a human can understand the model's internal structures and reasoning processes. While the quality of natural language processing (NLP) models has traditionally been measured by predictive accuracy, this overlooks the demands of real-world deployment, where interpretability underpins trust and accountability in sensitive domains, supports systematic debugging, and enables the detection of undesirable biases. However, the scale of modern large language models (LLMs) and the distributed nature of their learned representations make it difficult to attribute any behavior to localized, human-understandable components. While local explanation methods can audit individual predictions, they neither reveal the global organization of a model's representations nor suggest what interventions might improve the model. This thesis investigates globally interpretable decompositions of language model representations, breaking opaque representations into human-interpretable components that can be understood and exploited for model improvement. We organize our investigation around three core constructs. Structures are the discrete computational patterns that organize how information is aggregated within a model's internals. Topics are the latent thematic variables that capture what a model or corpus is about. Features are the monosemantic directions in activation space that disentangle the concepts superimposed in model activations. Specifically, we propose a series of methods that discover and inject interpretable attention patterns as explicit priors, adaptively encode linguistic and dialogue structures through parameter-efficient adapters, align topic model training with the properties that make topics interpretable, recover the latent themes underlying LLM generation through explicit Bayesian inference, construct semantically grounded supervision from LLMs, and improve sparse dictionary learning through probabilistic feature selection and constrained optimization. A comprehensive set of experimental results demonstrates that our methods enhance not only the interpretability of language models, but also their performance, establishing interpretable decompositions as actionable foundations for both understanding and improving these models.

title: ReuScope: Auditing Data Reuse and Evaluation Sensitivity in Capsule Vision 2024
abstract: We develop ReuScope, a protocol for auditing data reuse and evaluation sensitivity, using Capsule Vision 2024 as a case study. It combines measurements of data relationships with two comparisons: changing the evaluation population while holding predictions fixed, and changing training data while holding evaluation fixed. Byte-identical files cross the public training-validation boundary, and all 41 Kvasir-Capsule recordings that contribute frames occur in both partitions. Shared source recordings establish cross-split overlap; missing cross-recording patient identifiers prevent counting unique shared patients. Across ten paired seeds, removing all training rows attributed to Kvasir-Capsule, plus five rows from other sources flagged as near-matches to it, lowers public-validation balanced accuracy from 82.5% to 61.2%. Evaluating the same fitted models on the validation rows of the other sources reverses the comparison: removal improves balanced accuracy by 1.38 percentage points. The public-validation drop measures sensitivity to source removal, not an amount of leakage-induced inflation. Matched controls show that sample size and class counts alone do not explain the observed score differences. An exploratory experiment removes the training neighbors of validation frames that have close training matches, or equally many distant training rows, and yields a difference-in-differences estimate, relative to matched unflagged frames, of -0.355 percentage points in true-class probability; the paired-t interval for accuracy spans zero. The resulting procedure distinguishes observed reuse from conditional performance sensitivity and specifies the population, class support and uncertainty unit for each conclusion.

title: An Upper-Bound Inequality for the Calculation Time in Simulated Annealing: A Classical Analogue of the Adiabatic Theorem
abstract: It has recently been reported that classical systems have a speed limit for state evolution, although the concept of a speed limit had previously been considered to be unique to quantum systems. Owing to the speed limit for classical systems, a lower bound on the calculation time of simulated annealing for a desired calculation accuracy can be derived. However, such a lower bound does not provide a practical criterion for determining whether a calculation can be completed within a reasonable time. In this paper, we derive an inequality for classical systems analogous to the quantum adiabatic theorem, which provides a calculation time that guarantees a specified accuracy for fluctuation-exploiting computation. For a Fokker–Planck evolution with a spectral gap, the error is bounded by a relaxation term and, for a genuinely driven annealing protocol, by an additional driving term proportional to the speed of the instantaneous stationary distribution. The trade-off relation between calculation time and accuracy is given in a form that is tolerable for practical use. The result clarifies the roles of the relaxation gap and annealing speed, as well as the possible acceleration caused by detailed-balance-violating dynamics.

title: DHR-OD: Dynamic Heterogeneous Redundancy for Robust Object Detection
abstract: Object detection underpins safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving and intelligent surveillance, yet the inherent vulnerability of object detection models exposes them to the dual threat of adversarial and backdoor attacks. Existing defense methods are mostly passive, relying on prior knowledge of known attacks and thus failing to defend against unknown attacks. To address these problems, we introduce Dynamic Heterogeneous Redundancy (DHR) into object detection and build the Dynamic Heterogeneous Redundancy for robust Object Detection (DHR-OD) framework. DHR-OD defends against both threats through four modules, namely a heterogeneous executor pool, dynamic scheduling, multi-model arbitration, and closed-loop feedback, of which the multi-model arbitration module is the core. It fuses the box-level outputs of multiple heterogeneous detectors and identifies anomalies, turning the output differences among heterogeneous models into a defense. Experiments on COCO and PASCAL VOC show that DHR-OD retains 88.9% accuracy under PGD-20 attack and reduces the BadDet backdoor attack success rate from about 100% to about 35% without a dedicated detection module, making it a defense framework that covers both adversarial and backdoor threats while not relying on prior knowledge of specific attack forms.

title: ObjectGuidedMap: An Object-Aware Model for Robust Bird's Eye View Map Prediction in High-Occlusion Scenarios
abstract: Accurate BEV map prediction is a critical component of autonomous driving systems, enabling downstream planning and control. Recent approaches such as Mask2Map achieve strong performance by predicting vectorized, instance-level map elements directly from multi-view images. However, existing BEV map prediction models operate largely independently of object-level scene understanding, despite the fact that traffic participants frequently occlude or implicitly encode information about road geometry. In this work, we propose a multitask architecture that jointly predicts BEV maps and 3D objects, explicitly enabling information exchange between the two tasks. Building upon Mask2Map, we introduce an object detection branch and incorporate cross-task feature fusion at both the BEV feature level and the instance-query level via deformable attention and cross-attention mechanisms. This design allows map instances to leverage object context while remaining robust to occlusions caused by traffic participants. Experimental results on the nuScenes and Argoverse 2 datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently improves BEV map prediction accuracy, with particularly significant gains of 21% mAP in scenes containing heavy object occlusion.

title: Vigenère-Squad : cryptanalyse de chiffrements classiques par agents LLM encadrés
abstract: Système multi-agents (Classifieur, Cryptanalyste, Linguiste, Pédagogue) qui casse des chiffrements classiques (César, affine, Vigenère, Beaufort, autoclave, substitution) avec des outils déterministes, un orchestrateur explicite et des traces JSONL rejouables. Comprend l'ablation (sans modèle, petit modèle, second modèle), un modèle de menace évalué, les données brutes, les métriques et le rapport. Projet individuel bonus du cours Cryptographie appliquée et IA agentique, SUP DE VINCI, 2026.

title: GNES: Neural-Guided Evolutionary Program Search for Interpretable UAV Swarm Control
abstract: Synthesizing interpretable velocity controllers for decentralized unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms requires optimizing discrete symbolic programs from sparse, expensive, long-horizon simulator feedback. Evolutionary program search preserves interpretability but often spends many evaluations on weak random variation, whereas deep multi-agent reinforcement learning can learn effective policies that are difficult to inspect. We propose GNES, a neural-guided evolutionary program search framework for symbolic UAV swarm controller synthesis. GNES casts controller design as a program-edit decision process: gene growth trees are program states, validity-preserving genetic operators are actions, simulator fitness provides the return, and policy–value graph neural networks learn edit signals over controller topology. Monte Carlo tree search performs look-ahead planning in controller-program space before simulator validation, closing the loop between evolution, learned guidance, and verified rollouts. Case studies on three simulated UAV swarm tasks produce compact, inspectable velocity controllers with non-obvious coordination motifs such as density-normalized radial gains and motion-compensating terms. In a six-method line-formation comparison over three seeds, every program-search variant exceeds the evolutionary and reinforcement-learning baselines on every seed with roughly one third of their evaluations, and ablations indicate that graph-structured policy–value learning and MCTS look-ahead each contribute, most visibly in search efficiency once final scores approach the task ceiling.

title: PGGT-Loc: Primitive-Grounded Geometry Transformer for Feed-Forward Camera Localization
abstract: Camera localization methods are mostly multi-stage pipelines relying on dedicated and complex maps that are costly to construct, store, and maintain over time. Alternatively, well-structured maps that organize scenes with compact yet expressive primitives are often readily available, providing rich structural and semantic cues that humans can interpret. However, their potential for direct camera localization remains largely unexplored due to the significant modality gap between map primitives and visual observations. This motivates a new concept for localization, which estimates camera poses by grounding query observations to map primitives. In this paper, we instantiate the concept in the context of planar primitives with PGGT, the Primitive-Grounded Geometry Transformer network. Given a single query image and a set of planar map primitives, the network is trained to predict multiple localization targets for feed-forward 6-DoF camera localization that generalizes to unseen environments. With this straightforward and scalable architecture, our method pushes the state-of-the-art localization performance on both dense surface maps and minimal layout models. The code and models are available at https://github.com/3dv-casia/PGGT-Loc

title: Three instruments for evaluating AI audio tools: professional usefulness, creator-protection strength, and commercial disclosure
abstract: The three evaluation instruments used in the research report at 10.5281/zenodo.23476695, self-published and deposited in an open repository, with a DOI. They are a six-criterion Professional Usefulness scale with published anchors and a consent gate for voice technologies, a creator-protection evaluation with five columns and three 0-3 ratings, and a twenty-field commercial-disclosure checklist. They are published so that the report’s ratings can be checked, disputed or reproduced against the same anchors. The instruments have been applied by one analyst and have not been scored by a second rater. Section 7 gives the inter-rater protocol. Section 8 states the limitations, including that the band thresholds were reconstructed and may not reproduce every published rating, and that the creator-protection ratings are the author’s assessment, not legal advice.

title: Overcoming the Representational Limitations of Amplitude Encoding for Quantum Neural Networks
abstract: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) offer a framework for learning functions from classical data, but their expressive power depends critically on how inputs are encoded into quantum states. Angle encoding can require resources that scale with the number of features, whereas amplitude encoding represents $d$ features using only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2 d)$ qubits. This compactness comes at a representational cost: normalization makes conventional amplitude encoding invariant to nonzero real rescaling of the input, up to an unobservable global phase. We show that this invariance induces an exact, architecture-independent restriction on the resulting hypothesis class. No downstream quantum circuit can distinguish inputs differing by nonzero real scaling. We develop a general condition under which deterministic preprocessing can remove this ambiguity and show that nonlinearity alone is insufficient. Based on this analysis, we introduce a fixed nonlinear feature map that provably distinguishes all real inputs under subsequent amplitude encoding, without adding trainable parameters and while retaining logarithmic qubit scaling. We evaluate the resulting QNN on three canonical classification benchmarks and a nonlinear synthetic dataset against conventional amplitude and angle encoding, as well as a classical neural network. Across these tasks, the proposed encoding consistently improves classification accuracy over both quantum encoding baselines by 21$-$44 %. Our results establish normalization-induced scale invariance as a concrete representational bottleneck of amplitude encoding and demonstrate that it can be removed while preserving a compact quantum representation, marking a step toward quantum models capable of capturing arbitrary relationships in classical data.

title: A Domain Label Is Not a Treatment: Why Specialist and General-Purpose Language Models Trade Places Across Studies, What a 'Medical' Checkpoint Leaves Unspecified, and the Matched Contrasts That Would Assign the Gain
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research A September 2026 study compares an 8B general-purpose instruction-tuned model with a medically fine-tuned checkpoint built on the same base and finds that the general model scores higher both at selecting the meaning of medical jargon and at recognising when a word is being used as jargon, significantly so on the second, and that the medical checkpoint's deficit on the second task sits in a few pre-existing components it over-weights. The finding joins a run of 2024-2026 results in which medical models fail to beat their bases, set against an older and still-growing record in which domain-adapted models in code, mathematics, chip design, law and clinical text beat general ones by wide margins. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that these verdicts are not answers to one question, because a specialist-versus-generalist comparison is indexed by five things that the studies set differently: the treatment (what was trained, on how much text the base had not already seen), the comparator (the starting checkpoint, a post-trained sibling, or a model of another lineage), the elicitation (whose prompt format and whose decision threshold), the target skill (recall, terminology, extraction against labels, or multi-step computation), and the statistic (paired tests, intervals, calibration). Read through those indices, the negative medical results hold in one well-populated cell - a modest post-training or continued-pretraining treatment on a web-trained base, compared with a strong sibling under independent prompting on recall or terminology - and the large positive results hold in cells where the domain data are large relative to the base's exposure, absent from the public web, or labelled for the exact task. The paper argues that the anchor's mechanistic result is better read as a shifted decision prior than as lost knowledge, consolidates 27 published results in a table, maps fourteen studies onto four of the five indices, states a classification procedure, and specifies five matched contrasts that would decide what a domain label buys.

title: FeDLRT: Federated Dynamical Low-Rank Training
abstract: Abstract. We propose a federated dynamical low-rank training (FeDLRT) scheme to reduce client compute and communication costs—two significant performance bottlenecks in horizontal federated learning. Our method builds upon dynamical low-rank time integration schemes for manifold-constrained optimization to create a global low-rank basis of network weights, which enables client training on a small coefficient matrix. This global low-rank basis allows us to incorporate a variance correction scheme and prove global loss descent and convergence to a stationary point on a low-rank manifold. FeDLRT features dynamic augmentation and truncation of the low-rank bases to optimize computing and communication resource utilization. Notably FeDLRT only trains a small coefficient matrix per client. We demonstrate the efficiency of FeDLRT in an array of computer vision benchmarks with both independent and identically distributed (IID) and non-IID data and show a reduction of client compute and communication costs by up to an order of magnitude with minimal impacts on global accuracy. FeDLRT performs as well as classical methods such as FedAvg and FedLin, with a fraction of the memory and compute requirements.

title: Trainable Vector Quantization for Large Language Models
abstract: Vector Quantization (VQ) is a rapidly evolving technique for compressing Large Language Model (LLM) weights, reducing memory usage, and speeding up inference. However, extreme compression deteriorates model performance, which is challenging to recover due to the discrete nature of VQ parameters. Existing methods employ training-free approaches that are limited to layer-wise reconstruction loss minimization. To address this limitation, we propose TVQ, a novel method that leverages straight-through estimation to enable gradient descent-based optimization of vector-quantized LLMs. By reformulating VQ LLM optimization with trainable latent weights, TVQ enables arbitrary objective minimization. We constitute our approach by applying TVQ in a block-wise knowledge distillation paradigm, which balances quality and training efficiency, and propose several practical solutions to accelerate training. In experiments on modern LLMs, we demonstrate that TVQ is compatible with modern VQ schemes. As a result, TVQ achieves state-of-the-art quality in low-bit post-training quantization settings with a modest training budget and straightforward PyTorch implementation. For instance, TVQ achieves near-lossless 2-bit quantization for LLaMA2-70B with only 1% accuracy drop on popular Question-Answering benchmarks.

title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm
abstract: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.

title: BURGER: Benchmarking and Understanding Robotic Generalization via Embodied Drawing
abstract: How effectively can vision-language-action (VLA) models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviors as training data scales? Investigating this question requires large and varied robot datasets, whose collection on physical robots remains costly. We introduce BURGER, a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a scalable, prompt-driven pipeline for generating continuous drawing trajectories, both in simulation and the real world. In BURGER, an agent starts from the same blank canvas and controls a robot arm to draw the object or spatial composition specified by language, while each instruction allows an open-ended variety of valid drawings and stroke orders. Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations spanning 282 drawing tasks, we evaluate five representative VLA models across data scales, language grounding, and multimodal behavior. BURGER supports fine-grained analysis of language grounding, spatial composition, and action generation, revealing distinct failure patterns across VLA models. Our experiments suggest that some VLA models can benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale, capture multimodal drawing behaviors, and generalize to unseen compositions of familiar objects. Finally, we deploy a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm, demonstrating the ability to draw reactively under human intervention. Project homepage and code can be found at https://siyingzhao.github.io/BURGER/.

title: How I Aligned Your Model: Scaling Up Multilingual Safety Training with Templates
abstract: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As a result, we release MSafeTemp, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. title: LucidLyra: Feed-Forward Generative 3D Scene Reconstruction and Joint Understanding via Multi-Task Distillation
abstract: We present LucidLyra, a framework that makes generatively reconstructed 3D scenes directly queryable for semantics and instances in a feed-forward manner from video latents. While generative 3D reconstruction can synthesize virtual environments from a single image, downstream applications in robotics and physical AI require not only visual realism but also access to scene semantics and object identities. Existing 3D understanding approaches, however, require captured multi-view scenes, have limited generalization capabilities, or rely on expensive per-scene processing and optimization. To bridge this gap, our method distills complementary knowledge from a camera-controlled video diffusion model and frozen 2D vision foundation models into a unified model to jointly infer 3D Gaussians encoding geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantics, and class-agnostic instance cues. The resulting scenes support novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, and object grouping without per-scene optimization, while training requires neither manual 3D annotations nor captured multi-view data. Our method outperforms baselines combining state-of-the-art 3DGS segmentation approaches with generative 3D scene reconstruction on curated synthetic and real-image-conditioned benchmarks, while preserving reconstruction quality. Furthermore, our latent formulation naturally extends to monocular video, reconstructing structured dynamic 3D scenes across time. By turning renderable but unstructured outputs into queryable 3D worlds, LucidLyra enables downstream applications including 3D scene editing, 3D asset mining, and robotic simulation.

title: Glance: The Generator Is Its Own Reranker
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation commonly serves separate models for reranking and answering, duplicating model residency and passage processing. We introduce Glance, which equips the generator with a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to score candidate passages from a shared prefill. Short relevance probes branch from the cached context, producing one score per passage without separately prefilling each query-passage pair. A single resident 9B backbone supports generation, general decisions and reranking, with approximately 0.1 GiB of additional memory per decision skill. After 39 minutes of MS MARCO fine-tuning, Glance achieves nDCG@10 of 0.741 on SciFact and 0.345 on NFCorpus, compared with 0.721 and 0.326 for bge-reranker-v2-m3. On 300 HotpotQA questions, its selected context improves answer F1 by 0.045 over cross-encoder-selected context under the same base generator (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.014, 0.076]). In a scaling study, reranking quality keeps rising up to 200 candidates (43k tokens) scored from one shared prefill, where it exceeds the cross-encoder by 0.058 nDCG@10, and a probe-only activated adapter lets generation continue from the original passage cache. These initial results demonstrate generator-based reranking with one resident backbone; evaluation currently covers two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset and one backbone family.

title: Elucidating the Design Space of LM Data Attribution
abstract: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation. We introduce the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT) for fact tracing, in which we fine-tune LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge, providing unambiguous ground truth for attribution. This synthetic setup allows us to systematically alter one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors. With this configurable evaluation, we demonstrate that redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution performance. Rather than proposing a new estimator, we examine two design choices that are underexplored: the loss used to compute gradients and how per-token attribution scores are aggregated into a document score. We find that the true causal evidence within a training document is highly localized, but standard methods dilute this evidence into noise by averaging attribution scores across the entire document. We find that replacing standard cross-entropy loss gradients with the negative log-odds gradients surfaces the critical tokens from other uninformative ones. We can then aggregate only the top token scores to improve ground truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines on our diagnostic benchmark. The negative log-odds correction also generalizes to FTRACE-TREX, improving counterfactual retraining performance for every method we test, by up to 4.9x.

title: PhysInsert: Physically Plausible Object Insertion with Geometric Priors and Bidirectional Object-Scene Interactions
abstract: We present PhysInsert, a framework for physically plausible reference-based object insertion that jointly adapts objects and their surrounding scenes. Existing methods often rely on masked inputs, generation-based pairs, or training pairs with limited viewpoint variation, leaving pose and illumination adaptation and bidirectional object-scene interactions insufficiently constrained. We construct the Insert World dataset with strictly aligned Blender-rendered counterfactual pairs and object references across viewpoints and lighting conditions. Building on these data, Geometry-Guided Adaptation couples a VGGT geometry stream with image and text streams under target-scene feature supervision to guide spatially consistent insertion. Complementary 2D Object-Scene Spatial Supervision jointly supervises object occupancy and environmental changes while grounding spatial instructions in object regions through image-text attention. We introduce PhysInsert-Bench with dedicated cross-environment and cross-view cases requiring illumination and pose adaptation beyond appearance copying. Experiments on PhysInsert-Bench and DreamBooth demonstrate improved image fidelity; a user study further shows more accurate placement and improved lighting integration, perspective, and pose plausibility.

title: Probing Spatial State Representations in Visual Foundation Models
abstract: An observer sees only part of the surrounding world, yet must keep track of what lies beyond the current view. Spatial perception therefore involves more than recognizing individual images: it calls for a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action. Do visual foundation models provide representations that support such a state? We study this question through four levels of spatial capability---spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability---using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments. The resulting capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers, and prefix lengths: strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval. Matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer to predicted features unchanged. Finally, goal-dependent candidate selection does not establish reliable continuous action utility: predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress. Across the four levels, object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial representations not only by what can be decoded from them, but by whether that information is maintained beyond observation, updated predictively, and used for goal-directed action.

title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers
abstract: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.

title: Continuous-Action World Models: Learning Cross-Embodiment Spatiotemporal Dynamics Priors
abstract: We introduce Continuous-Action World Models (CoAWM), a framework for learning cross-embodiment spatiotemporal dynamics priors that support robot action generation across embodiments and execution frequencies. At its core is a shared latent function space that captures the spatial and temporal structure of robot actions. We learn this space through two stages. First, function pretraining brings trajectories from different embodiments and sampling frequencies into a common representation, learning shared dynamics priors through action reconstruction and consistency across temporal sampling views. By accommodating heterogeneous robot trajectories, this stage broadens the range of data sources available for pretraining and facilitates scaling to larger and more diverse datasets. Second, we connect the pretrained function space to a world-model backbone, enabling observations, language instructions, and the current robot state to condition the prediction of a latent action function. A single decoder takes any query time and returns the corresponding end-effector action. By separating shared dynamics priors from task-conditioned action selection and temporal sampling, our approach provides a unified foundation for transferring robot experience across embodiments and control frequencies.

title: HiFOR: Hierarchical Foresight with Action-Guided World Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Model
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Recent advances have further incorporated future prediction to enhance the understanding of environmental dynamics and task progression. However, existing methods often model short-term dynamics and long-term task objectives separately, while directly incorporating predicted futures into action policies without sufficiently considering their relevance to current action requirements. To address these limitations, we propose HiFOR, a hierarchical foresight framework with action-guided world retrieval. Specifically, Hierarchical Foresight Prediction jointly predicts short-term state evolution, semantic milestones, and final goal states through a Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), establishing dependencies across temporal horizons. Building upon these predictions, Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling organizes future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to facilitate fine-grained retrieval. Furthermore, Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval adaptively retrieves relevant future information from the structured latent world based on evolving action representations during denoising, providing targeted guidance for action generation. Extensive experiments on two simulation benchmarks and six real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

Specifically, Hierarchical Foresight Prediction jointly predicts short-term state evolution, semantic milestones, and final goal states through a Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), establishing dependencies across temporal horizons. Building upon these predictions, Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling organizes future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to facilitate fine-grained retrieval. Furthermore, Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval adaptively retrieves relevant future information from the structured latent world based on evolving action representations during denoising, providing targeted guidance for action generation. Extensive experiments on two simulation benchmarks and six real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

title: Your LR Schedule May Not Be Principled: Effective Learning Rate Scheduling in Weight-Normalized Training
abstract: Weight-normalized (WN) training is emerging as a compelling alternative to conventional weight decay (WD), with recent studies reporting substantial pretraining loss gains. We show that these gains are driven primarily by the induced effective learning rate (ELR) trajectory rather than by normalization alone. Matching ELR trajectories largely collapses the training loss dynamics of WN and WD. Schedule design should therefore target ELR rather than the nominal learning rate (LR) alone. Building on this principle, we propose AIR (Affine Inverse-square-Root decay), which combines a theoretically derived $1/\sqrt{t}$ decay with an affine adjustment to satisfy prescribed peak and terminal LRs over a finite training horizon. We further identify late-stage ELR scheduling as a key source of its gains, because a shared late schedule attenuates the effect of earlier LR choices. Experiments on 128 B-token Mixture-of-Experts pretraining demonstrate that AIR outperforms cosine and other candidate schedules in training loss, downstream performance, and hyperparameter robustness, reducing terminal training loss by approximately 0.01 relative to cosine at matched cumulative LR. Applying the same ELR trajectory to WD reproduces the corresponding training dynamics, showing that the benefits extend beyond fixed-norm training and establishing ELR as the principled scheduling object.

title: world2vec: Mechanistic world models through latent dynamics learning
abstract: World models can achieve strong control performance without faithfully capturing the dynamics of their environment, limiting their potential for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. Here, we introduce world2vec to learn mechanistic world models without reward information directly from observations and actions. World2vec learns latent dynamics that faithfully reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons, with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM. This enables state of the art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors, demonstrating how world models are amenable to scientific discovery.

title: Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control
abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled the generation of increasingly realistic and interactive virtual environments, opening new possibilities for player-customizable gameplay. Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured representations. We leverage these representations as intermediate proxies to condition a video generation model, together with an adaptive masking mechanism that improves alignment between the conditioning signals and generated video rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce an agentic framework that explicitly maintains and updates game states, allowing players to freely configure their virtual worlds and exercise fine-grained control over character motions while preserving visual quality and gameplay consistency. By combining agentic control with structured proxy-based generation, our framework unlocks new possibilities for player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.

title: L3G-World: Real-Time Infinite World Generation with Latent 3D Gaussian Memory
abstract: Interactive world models generate visual content conditioned on user actions, yet maintaining spatial consistency over long-horizon exploration in real time remains challenging. Existing approaches rely on either temporal context or explicit 3D memory, both of which scale poorly because memory grows with the length of the generated stream. Moreover, explicit 3D memories condition latent video generators by re-encoding RGB renderings, which precludes real-time generation. In this paper, we introduce a Latent 3D Gaussian Memory (L3G) that combines the efficiency of feed-forward reconstruction with a compact, rapidly renderable scene representation. Building on this memory, we propose L3G-World, in which a memory updater and a video diffusion transformer (DiT) alternate autoregressively to generate spatially consistent worlds. The memory updater spawns Gaussians in newly observed regions and refines existing ones, so that the memory grows with scene extent rather than stream length. Each Gaussian further stores a VAE latent feature, allowing the memory to be rendered directly into the DiT's latent space without VAE re-encoding. Experiments show that L3G-World achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and long-horizon spatial consistency, with up to $38.6\times$ fewer 3D primitives, $3.2\times$ faster memory updates, and $359\times$ faster memory rendering relative to the most efficient prior 3D-memory baseline for each metric, enabling real-time world generation at 9 FPS.

title: HairDeck: Animation-Ready Stylized Hair Cards from a Single Image
abstract: The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is built from hair cards: artist-placed ribbons whose geometry is the visible hair, animated by spring bones. Existing image-based methods produce realistic hair or a single fused mesh, while CHARM, the only generator of stylized hair cards, decodes a hairstyle autoregressively as a long sequence of control points. Observing that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, we propose HairDeck, which generates it as one: each card is a single token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all cards together. From a single image, HairDeck generates the cards and the spring-bone chains that drive them, yielding an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats. On CHARM's own test set, it lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster, and from single images it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand-based methods. Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/HairDeck

title: Multi-View MoE: Letting Every Router Shape Expert Computation
abstract: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models expand parameter capacity by activating a small subset of experts per token. Expert selection directly affects model capabilities under a fixed active-expert budget. Dense evaluation of all experts reveals weak agreement between single-router rankings and expert-utility evaluation rankings, especially in middle and deep layers. Richer signals for selection and computation incur additional cost: selection based on internal expert activations requires preliminary computation, while processing multiple full representations separately through the same expert repeats its computation. We propose Multi-View MoE to improve expert selection with multiple routers and reuse their preferences to modulate expert computation under a fixed expert budget. Its Multi-Router submodule aggregates sigmoid scores from independently initialized routers. These routers develop highly differentiated expert preferences during training, allowing experts strongly favored by one router or jointly supported by several routers to be selected. Multi-View further uses each selected expert's relative scores across routers to mix learned latent views into its input, reusing routing preferences for both selection and computation. Each selected expert executes one forward pass, preserving the active-expert count, expert FLOPs, and all-to-all communication volume. On a 24-layer 10B-A1B model trained on 708B tokens, full Multi-View MoE improves the nine-task downstream mean by 1.18 percentage points over the baseline. Multi-Router alone yields a 0.6-percentage-point gain and improves the rank correlation between router scores and evaluated expert utility, with relative increases of 8.1% globally and approximately 58% in the layer with the lowest single-router alignment. Controlled mixing interventions show the model uses input differences that depend on both the expert and the token.

title: Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-distillation
abstract: On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) has proven effective for post-training large language models by constructing a teacher conditioned on privileged references. However, existing approaches keep the teacher fixed either throughout training by consistently exposing it to the full reference, or within each response by adaptively varying partial reference exposure only across responses. In this paper, we argue that neither of them is sufficient. Instead, every token needs its own teacher, as the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response. Through a teacher-intervention pilot study, we validate that the teacher preference differs across tokens, and reveal that a preferred teacher can be identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection. Motivated by these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. Our method constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, and enables every token to adaptively select its preferred teacher during training. Experiments with Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks show that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to $+5.9$ over the base model, highlighting the importance of adapting teacher supervision at the token level. The code is available at https://github.com/xingzhejun/MTA-OPSD.

title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
abstract: Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world. However, despite decades of progress, available simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena. The core bottleneck is that creating better simulations requires significant expert effort and therefore does not scale. To address this, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations. Our core insight is that simulation creation is a coding agent task, so improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations. We select simulations based on U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, define what makes a good simulation and a good task, and develop an adversarial creation-audit loop that checks each simulation and task against these definitions. Using this pipeline, we build RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty. Even the best frontier models fail on every RoboWorld test task, achieving an average reward of only 0.06. Building on RoboWorld, we introduce several new ways for frontier models to improve, including in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher that reads the simulator state and teaches a student in context, self-assisted learning from the model's own privileged experience, and code policies that generate demonstrations across varied scenes to train vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as $π_{0.5}$. Each of these substantially improves performance. We release our pipeline, RL environments, and benchmark to facilitate future research. Code and data are available at https://gym-anything.github.io/robotics

title: rTaste: Do Research Agents Have Taste? Evaluating Early Stage Research Judgment
abstract: Do research agents have taste, the judgment of which experiments are worth running before their outcomes are known? We give six frontier models seven recent NLP papers. Each model, working as a research agent alone or as a team, proposes minimum viable experiments (MVEs), forecasts whether each will pass a threshold it sets and ranks them. A separate executor then attempts every MVE, including those ranked last, and three model auditors judge the results. Of 415 MVEs, 194 are judged sound, valuable and new, but fewer than half of these (73) are also judged beyond the seed paper and non obvious. The agents' first choices match the auditors' most valued experiment more often than a random pick, but are not shown to improve on choosing the experiment written first. Their forecasts beat a base rate but are not measurably more accurate than those of a fresh instance of the same model given only the paper and registrations. Teams cost more without a clear overall improvement in proposal quality. The agents produce many worthwhile experiments, but the evidence that their rankings improve the choice of which to run remains limited. The evaluation harness and a dataset of all 415 MVEs, with their forecasts and audited outcomes, are available at https://github.com/ArtKanke/rTaste.

Teams cost more without a clear overall improvement in proposal quality. The evaluation harness and a dataset of all 415 MVEs, with their forecasts and audited outcomes, are available at https://github.com/ArtKanke/rTaste.

title: Preserving Utility in Continual LLM Unlearning via Orthogonal Projections
abstract: Unlearning concerns the task of removing the influence of a sensitive portion of the training data, such as protected, copyrighted or private text, from a model without retraining it from scratch. While unlearning requests happen continuously during a model's lifetime, the vast majority of LLM unlearning methods are ill-suited for iterated removal, yielding steep decay in forgetting and utility upon sequential unlearning. This decay stems from interference between successive updates, as each new deletion can undo earlier ones or push the model further along directions already degraded by them. To address this, we introduce Continual Orthogonal Projection (COP), a gradient-projection scheme that restricts each update to the orthogonal complement of activation subspaces cached from prior forget sets. This approach provably guarantees first-order non-interference with earlier deletions. COP stores only a low-rank basis per layer, requiring neither past gradients nor previous forget sets, and plugs into unlearning methods that update the model through gradient steps on a differentiable loss without modifying its objective. Experiments on standard LLM unlearning benchmarks (TOFU and RWKU) show that COP preserves utility across sequential requests without weakening forgetting, preventing the collapse of standard objectives and forgetting more effectively than continual-specific baselines.

title: Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering
abstract: An estimator can be accurate and stable on typical data, yet sensitive to a few possible records. Differentially private mechanisms commonly scale their noise to the worst-case influence of a single record, which lets these records dictate the noise even when the remaining data would allow far less. Removing them first would restore the smaller scale, but the removal must itself be private. We introduce \emph{propose-filter-release} (PFR), which, by privately filtering its input, turns a mechanism that protects the addition or removal of a typical record, one that fits the remaining data, into one that is differentially private in the standard sense, on every input. Using our novel filtering step, PFR requires only a concave friendliness score, which measures how well a record fits a dataset, and a release mechanism that is friendly-DP, that is, private when the changed record fits the remaining data. For every such score and release mechanism, it guarantees differential privacy under public conditions on the number of records, so it is a general privacy primitive, comparable to propose-test-release, and FriendlyCore can be viewed as one of its implementations. We illustrate the generality of PFR by instantiating it for scalar statistics, principal subspace estimation, the KL divergence of user histograms, the effective resistances of a graph, and treatment-rule selection.

title: Micro-Edits: Computational Support for Fine-Scale Edits in Film
abstract: In film editing, every frame matters. While macro, content-level edits shape the high-level narrative of a film, small local edits often control timing and direct visual attention. For example, editors can adjust the precise timing of clips to control the length of a meaningful silence, or cut to shots that highlight a specific character's reactions to important moments. These small, detailed edits are slow and tedious to make in standard editing tools because users have to map high-level narrative goals to low-level frame-by-frame adjustments. At the same time, these fine-scale adjustments, which we call micro-edits, can be nuanced and expressive, with different choices serving different creative goals. In this work, we start by conducting a formative study with professional editors to understand the structure of micro-edits and how they are used. We then derive a mathematical formalization for this structure to develop tools that leverage AI and optimization to make exploring micro-edits simpler and more efficient for users. Finally, we validate our tools in multiple user studies and a wide range of video examples.

title: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations
abstract: The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions. This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision.

title: Learning developmental dynamics from lineage context
abstract: A central goal of biology is to predict the dynamics of multicellular systems. Lineage context (the states of a cell's sisters, cousins, etc.) could inform these predictions, but how best to leverage it remains unclear. Here we introduce lineage inpainting, a generative modeling approach that uses lineage context with tree-structured transformers and stochastic interpolants to model cell state dynamics across lineage trees. Applied to a lineage-traced transcriptional atlas of mouse embryogenesis, it recovers dynamics not resolved by gene expression alone, including multiple transcriptional convergence events where distinct lineages are drawn to a common state. Despite being fit on unperturbed development, lineage inpainting can generate hypotheses about perturbation responses by simulating counterfactuals. These simulations agree in many cases with observed developmental phenotypes, including a single-cell measurement of the Tbx5 knockout response. Our results show that lineage information provides a rich source of context for learning multicellular dynamics.

title: Adaptive Scenario Generation for KL-DRO Around a Learned Density Model
abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) hedges data-driven two-stage stochastic programs against error in the distribution estimated from a finite record, and standard ambiguity sets differ in how they treat realizations absent from that record. A divergence ball around the empirical distribution contains only reweightings of the record, whereas a transport ball also contains distributions supported off the record, including on realizations the data-generating process cannot produce, against which the decision is then hedged as well. We instead propose a Kullback-Leibler (KL) ball centered at a density model fitted to the record, the learned nominal, which lets the adversary up-weight costly unobserved realizations in proportion to the probability the model assigns them. Solving the resulting problem poses a second difficulty, because it can accommodate only a few scenarios, and an independent sample of that size is likely to omit the rare realizations on which the worst case concentrates. We therefore build the scenario set adaptively, alternating between solving the finite problem and drawing new realizations from the learned nominal, steered toward the worst case at the current decision, with importance weights that correct the draws back to the model. On a multi-item newsvendor problem and a capacity expansion problem on realistic grid data, centering the ball at the learned nominal rather than at the record lowers cost under distribution shift, at comparable in-distribution cost, when the record is scarce and the model class captures structure that lets it extrapolate beyond the record. The advantage fades as the record grows or as the shift departs from the structure the model has learned.

title: Luggage re-identification: A study of strategies towards a real-world application
abstract: Luggage re-identification (ReID) is a critical task in video surveillance for forensics, security or border management (suspicious or abandoned luggage recognition), as well as luggage management (lost luggage recovery). It enables the association of observations of the same luggage across disjoint camera views in complex environments such as airports, train stations and border crossing. While existing approaches primarily focus on appearance-based cropped image matching under relatively clean conditions, real-world scenarios are characterized by frequent occlusions, cluttered background and crowded scenes which significantly degrade performance. Yet, strategies leveraging the complementarity of multiple shots and views from different video streams is overlooked. In this paper, we study strategies for an end-to-end pipeline that operates from multiple video streams to detect and re-identify luggage. We evaluate different variants on a benchmark dataset acquired in real-world environments to address the questions of selecting and merging different views and shots of the same luggage as well as training on different environment datasets for an overall ReID performance improvement in practical applications.
